Supporting the repair and refurbishment of electronics is important for several reasons. It helps cut down on waste, saves people money, and pushes back against a culture that encourages tossing out devices too soon. Nowadays, we rely heavily on phones, laptops, and appliances. It doesn't make sense that we often have to replace them just because a battery dies, a screen breaks, or a small part stops working.

Electronic waste is growing fast globally. Old devices often contain toxic stuff like lead and mercury, which can pollute the environment if not handled properly. On the other hand, electronics also have valuable materials that are hard and energy-intensive to mine and produce. Fixing a device so it can be used for a few more years means we avoid making new ones, which cuts down on the environmental impact of getting raw materials, shipping, and disposal.

Repairing electronics also makes them cheaper. A new phone or laptop can cost a lot, but replacing a battery or a screen is usually much less. Refurbished electronics are also a good option for students, families, and small businesses who need working technology without paying for new. Making repaired devices more available can help bridge the digital gap by giving more people access to essential tools.

Some people might say newer devices are more efficient or secure, and sometimes replacing a device is necessary. But that doesn't excuse companies for making products that are hard or impossible to fix. Businesses should make spare parts, repair guides, diagnostic tools, and software updates available. Laws that support the right to repair can ensure that independent repair shops and individuals can fix the products they buy.

In the end, the movement to repair and refurbish electronics encourages responsibility over convenience. It means seeing electronics as valuable tools to be maintained, not as disposable items. Supporting repair helps the environment, gives consumers more options, and leads to a more sustainable way of using technology.

Community-supported fisheries (CSFs) are a newer way to get seafood. They link people who eat seafood directly with local fishermen. This skips the usual long and often unclear way food gets to us.

Think of it like community-supported agriculture (CSA), but for fish. People pay for a share of what a fishing boat will catch, usually ahead of time. This gives the fishermen money upfront, stable prices, and a sure market. In return, people get fresh seafood that they know where it came from and that was likely caught sustainably.

The first CSFs in the US started in the mid-2000s. Now, this model has spread to coastal areas in North America, and also a bit in Europe and elsewhere. This growth shows that people care more about where their food comes from, if it's caught sustainably, and if it helps local economies.

As CSFs have grown, so has the research about them. People from different fields like economics, sociology, marine policy, and food studies have looked at CSFs. They've studied them as ways to help small fishing communities make money when facing big competition and dwindling fish populations. They've also looked at how CSFs can encourage better fishing practices because fishermen and consumers are more connected. And, they see CSFs as part of a larger movement to create different food systems that push back against the industrial food model.

Even though there's more research now, we still don't fully understand a few things about CSFs. We need to know more about whether they can be financially successful in the long run. We also need to see what their actual impact is on the environment and conservation efforts. And, we need to understand the social and cultural factors that make some CSFs succeed and others fail in different places and with different rules.

This review brings together what we know about CSFs. It looks at where they came from, how they work, and what effects they have on fishermen, consumers, and marine life. By looking closely at what previous studies did well and where they fell short, this review hopes to point out the main topics, research methods, and unanswered questions. This information can help guide future research and policies for this growing way of getting sustainable seafood."

I want to study social psychology because I’m curious about how our relationships and surroundings affect what we think, feel, and do. It’s interesting how people act differently in groups, meet social expectations, and form opinions about others, often without realizing why. Learning about this would let me look into important topics like identity, prejudice, conformity, relationships, and how we make decisions.

I’m especially interested in using what social psychology research finds to help with real problems. Figuring out why people have stereotypes, how opinions change, and what makes people cooperate could help build better communities and improve how people and groups communicate. I’m also curious about social media’s effects, where people constantly shape how they present themselves, compare themselves to others, and see ideas that might change what they believe and how they act. These things make social psychology really important today.

What I like most about this field is how it combines scientific research with real-life importance. I want to learn how researchers set up studies, look at evidence, and use psychology theories to explain complicated actions. I’m eager to get better at thinking critically, understanding data, and seeing things from different angles, while also understanding the ethical side of studying people.

Studying social psychology would let me understand human interaction better and see how our social situations affect us and society as a whole. My goal is to gain the knowledge and skills to contribute meaningfully to conversations about social behavior and use what I learn in my future studies or career.

How to Paint Your Kitchen in Just a Weekend

Start on Friday evening by clearing everything out of your kitchen. Take off hardware from cabinets, light fixtures, and any appliances you can move. Use drop cloths and plastic sheeting to cover countertops, floors, and anything else that will stay. This keeps your stuff clean and saves you time later.

On Saturday morning, clean all surfaces well. TSP (trisodium phosphate) is good for cutting through grease and grime. Let everything dry completely. If you have any stains or dark walls you're painting over, put on a coat of primer. Lightly sand any shiny surfaces so the paint sticks better. Doing this groundwork makes the final paint job look much more professional.

Saturday afternoon is for the first coat of paint. Use a roller on the ceiling and the main parts of the walls to work faster. Use a brush for the trim and any tricky spots. Using good quality paint means it'll cover better and last longer. Make sure you let each coat dry fully before starting the next one; this usually takes about 4 to 6 hours, depending on how humid it is.

On Sunday, apply the second coat to the walls and ceiling. You can also paint doors and trim now if you want. Use painter's tape to get clean lines around windows and along the baseboards. Peel the tape off when the paint is still a little bit wet, not completely dry. This helps create sharp edges.

For the final steps, from Sunday evening into Monday, put back the light fixtures and cabinet hardware once the paint is totally dry. Move the appliances back into place. Carefully remove all the drop cloths and plastic sheeting so you don't accidentally drag dust onto your fresh paint.

Here are some helpful tips:
Buy all your supplies on Thursday so you don't have to shop on the weekend.
Consider using paint with low VOCs (volatile organic compounds) for better air quality.
Spend a bit more on good brushes and rollers – they really do make a difference in how the paint goes on.
Have a damp cloth nearby for wiping up small spills right away.
Make sure there’s good airflow in the kitchen while you’re painting.

If you plan well and work efficiently, your kitchen will look like a freshly painted room by Monday morning, all ready for the new week.

Here are 10 ways to help you wind down at night and get to sleep more easily:

1. Stop using screens an hour before bed. The light from devices can make it harder to fall asleep.
2. Lower the lights in your home as it gets dark. This signals to your brain that it's time to relax.
3. Taking a warm bath or shower can relax your body. When you get out, your body temperature drops, which helps with sleep.
4. Read a real book instead of an e-reader. It's a more relaxing way to wind down.
5. Do some light stretching or yoga to release muscle tension without becoming too active.
6. Drink a cup of herbal tea, like chamomile or lavender. Avoid anything with caffeine.
7. Write down your thoughts, worries, or things you need to do. Getting them on paper can help clear your mind.
8. Listen to calm music, nature sounds, or a soothing podcast.
9. Get things ready for the next day, like choosing your clothes or packing your bag. This can make your mornings less stressful.
10. Try to go to bed and wake up around the same time every day. Your body likes consistency.

It takes time to form new habits, so be patient with yourself. Try adding one or two of these ideas each week to see what helps you most.

When deciding between bike lanes and street parking, cities should generally choose bike lanes if they make transportation safer, more efficient, and greener. While parking is handy for drivers and can help local shops, public streets are more useful for everyone when they're used for moving around instead of just storing cars.

Bike lanes that are protected from traffic can lower the number of injuries, encourage people to exercise, and make it easier for kids, older people, and those without cars to bike. They also help cities cut down on air pollution and greenhouse gases. In busy neighborhoods, replacing parking spots with bike lanes could mean more people can get around without adding to traffic jams. Businesses can also gain from this, as people who bike or walk tend to shop more often, and nicer-looking streets can boost business.

Still, cities shouldn't just get rid of parking without thinking about people with disabilities, delivery drivers, tradespeople, and others who really need cars. A well-planned approach could keep accessible parking, loading zones, and some short-term parking while turning other spots into protected bike lanes. Cities should also improve public transit and manage the remaining parking with permits or fees, instead of letting free curb parking take up valuable public space.

The right choice really depends on the specific situation in each city. A bike lane might not be very helpful if it's not connected to other routes, is unsafe at intersections, or is built in an area where not many people cycle. Before changing how space is used, officials need to look at traffic patterns, talk to the people who will be affected, and track the results. However, in busy cities, the long-term public advantages of safe cycling usually outweigh the convenience of having lots of street parking. Cities should make bike lanes a priority as part of a larger plan for transportation, while still offering reasonable ways for people to access places by car when necessary.

Community libraries are changing to become key places for digital access, helping many people who don't have much tech access.

With more people working remotely, taking online classes, and using online services, public libraries are doing more than just lending books. Now, they provide free fast internet, computers, and classes on how to use technology. This is really important for people who don't have much money.

Maria Chen from the American Library Association said that libraries are making technology available to everyone. She noted that for many, the library is the only place they can get reliable internet and computer access.

This change was especially important during the pandemic. Libraries helped students taking online classes and people looking for jobs online. Now, many libraries offer special programs like coding classes, lessons on being safe online, and help with government websites and online doctor visits.

It's not just about providing computers and internet. Librarians are now like tech tutors. They help people with everything from sending emails to understanding online security. They know that just having access to technology isn't enough if people don't know how to use it.

But this bigger role puts a strain on libraries that already have tight budgets. It's hard for them to buy new equipment, hire staff with special skills, and keep up with fast-changing technology, all while their funding might get cut.

Even with these problems, community libraries are still very important. They offer a cheaper option than paying for internet and computer labs elsewhere. They are safe places to learn, and they remain central to their communities.

Experts say libraries need to keep changing. Working with tech companies, getting more government money, and using new technologies like virtual reality and AI could help them offer even more.

As long as there's a gap in digital access, community libraries will be leading the way, making sure everyone, no matter how much money they have or where they come from, can get the tools and knowledge they need to succeed in today's digital world.

University lectures are definitely going to be a mix of online and in-person from now on. This change will actually make the learning experience better, not worse. Some people miss the old-style lectures, but that's just holding back progress. The traditional lecture format, with set times and places, doesn't work for today's students who often have jobs, families, or live far away.

Hybrid learning is a practical fix. It combines live online classes, materials people can access anytime, and specific in-person sessions. This flexibility isn't a step down; it's an upgrade. Things like recorded lectures or online activities let students learn at their own speed, go back over tricky parts, and study when they're most focused. This also means the time spent in person can be used for more active and group-based work, like in-depth talks, problem-solving sessions, and getting individual help – things that often get lost in large, one-way lectures.

Plus, using technology for hybrid learning helps students develop digital skills, which they'll really need after graduation. Universities need to get students ready for a world that relies on technology, and using various online tools in classes is a big part of that. A well-planned hybrid approach doesn't lower educational quality. Instead, it can give students more control, make education more accessible, and create a more engaging and effective learning environment than the old, often one-sided, university lecture. Higher education isn't just getting by with technology; it's getting better because of it.

Keeping employees is a big deal for companies, especially now with lots of job openings, higher costs when people leave, and employees wanting more flexibility and better well-being. One policy getting a lot of attention is unlimited vacation, sometimes called discretionary paid time off or unlimited PTO. Instead of a set number of days off each year, employees can take time when they need it, as long as their manager agrees, their work is manageable, and it fits with what the company expects. Supporters say this shows trust, gives employees more control, and creates a culture focused on results, which could make employees more dedicated to their jobs.

The idea that unlimited vacation helps keep employees comes from a few areas in how we study organizations. Social exchange theory suggests that if employees feel the company supports and is flexible with them, they might be more loyal and less likely to quit. Also, self-determination theory highlights how important autonomy is for motivation. Giving employees more say in when they take time off could make them feel more in control, happier, and better overall. Unlimited vacation can also be a way for companies to stand out when hiring and keeping people, especially in fields that rely on knowledge workers who really value flexibility and balancing work with their lives.

But, how unlimited vacation actually affects keeping employees isn't always clear. Some point out that getting rid of official vacation days can make it confusing to know how much time off is okay. Employees might end up taking less time off when the rules aren't clear, particularly in places where people work really hard and worry about looking less committed than others. In some situations, unlimited PTO might put the responsibility for taking breaks and recovering squarely on the employee, which defeats the purpose of improving well-being. So, how managers act, how much work there is, what the team is used to, and whether people feel things are fair are likely to shape whether the policy is seen as a real benefit or just something that sounds good but doesn't amount to much.

This review looks at unlimited vacation policies as a way to keep employees by bringing together research on employee autonomy, company support, work-life balance, and why people leave jobs. It explores what could be good about these policies and what might not work, focusing especially on when unlimited vacation might actually lead to employees staying committed long-term, instead of just being a nice-sounding perk at work.

Living in a coastal city, I saw up close how economic growth and protecting the environment often clash. When local industries grew, jobs increased, but it really hurt our oceans and made the air worse. This made me wonder from a young age: how can we build an economy where people can thrive without destroying the planet?

In college, I studied economics and learned a lot about how markets work, how to analyze data, and how to judge policies. But often, it felt like environmental damage was just something extra to consider, not a major problem. That changed when I worked on a project about how to share resources. I looked at how charging companies for carbon emissions affected their actions. I figured out that the problem isn't that economics and sustainability can't go together, but that we've historically failed to put a proper value on nature.

To fix this, I want to get a degree in environmental economics. I want to get really good at using advanced statistical methods and ways to measure value, so I can create practical, market-based ways to deal with climate change. I'm especially interested in how we can use local incentives and systems for biodiversity credits to get companies to care about conservation while still making a profit. This is particularly important in developing areas where economic growth is badly needed.

Your program really appeals to me because of its tough coursework and how it combines different fields for policy research. Being able to learn from your respected professors and cutting-edge research centers would be the perfect place for me to figure out workable solutions that can be applied widely. My ultimate aim is to be a policy advisor for a global development group, creating economic policies based on solid evidence that encourage sustainable growth. Studying environmental economics is the crucial next step to making our markets the strongest tools we have for bringing back nature.

Starting a book club in your neighborhood is an easy way to meet people, find new books to read, and create a regular event that neighbors will enjoy.

To start, invite a small group of people. You can use neighborhood email lists, social media, flyers, or just tell people you know. Aim for about six to twelve members. This size keeps discussions interesting but not too hard to manage. At your first meeting, decide on the basic rules: how often you'll meet, where you'll meet, how you'll pick books, and if everyone needs to finish the book.

Pick a regular meeting time, like the first Thursday of each month. You can rotate which house you meet at to make hosting easier, or you could meet at a library, coffee shop, community center, or park. Sometimes, offering a way to join online can be helpful for people who can't make it in person.

For picking books, you can take turns choosing or have members suggest books and then vote. If you want, set a page limit. Try to pick different kinds of books, authors, and viewpoints. Include popular fiction and nonfiction, memoirs, mysteries, books by local authors, and shorter reads. Make sure everyone knows the next book and meeting date before they leave.

To help conversations go well, think of a few questions that don't have simple yes or no answers. Ask what people liked, didn't like, or found surprising. Ask which characters or ideas were most convincing, and how the book relates to life today or things happening in your area. Having a different person lead the discussion each time can help share the work.

Try to keep the club friendly and easygoing. Be open to different opinions, don't let one person talk too much, and understand that people might miss a meeting or not finish the book. Having snacks and drinks can make it cozier, but don't make hosting too complicated.

To keep things going, send out reminders, acknowledge when the club reaches a milestone, and sometimes try new things like a potluck with a theme, a talk with an author, a trip to a bookstore, or a book swap. A good book club doesn't need perfect attendance or deep literary analysis. It just needs to be consistent, friendly, and pick books that make people want to keep coming back.

Weeknight dinners can be tough. Having meals ready in the fridge makes things so much easier. Here’s how to handle weekend batch cooking without it feeling overwhelming.

1. Pick recipes that hold up well in the freezer. Things like curries, chili, soups, and roasted meats are good choices. Avoid anything that gets mushy when frozen.

2. Decide on your meals before you go grocery shopping. Writing down your menu helps you save money and avoids wasting ingredients or time.

3. Get your prep work done on Friday. Chop your veggies, measure out seasonings, and get your ingredients organized. This will make Saturday cooking much smoother.

4. Use all your cooking appliances at once. Running the oven, stove, slow cooker, and rice cooker at the same time can help you get more done faster.

5. Make extra when you cook. Since the oven or stove is already on, make double or triple batches to freeze for later.

6. Get good food storage containers. Glass or sturdy plastic ones are best. Make sure to label them with the date so you know what's what in the freezer.

7. Start by cooking your proteins. Get your chicken, ground meat, or beans cooked first. Once they are done and cooling, you’re well on your way.

8. Think about breakfast too. You can also make things like egg muffins, oatmeal, or breakfast burritos ahead of time. It’s a lifesaver on busy mornings.

9. Clean up as you cook. It’s easy to let the dishes pile up, but cleaning as you go means you won’t have a huge mess to deal with later.

10. Don’t be too hard on yourself. Some weekends you’ll get a lot done, other times just one meal is a victory. That’s still better than relying on takeout.

You’ll feel much better during the week when you have these meals ready to go.

Making financial literacy a required subject for graduation is important for getting students ready for today's world. Many young people start their adult lives having to make tough money choices—like handling student loans, credit cards, budgeting, and investing—without ever being taught how. This often results in them getting into high-interest debt, having bad credit, and struggling financially for a long time. If schools teach financial education as part of the high school curriculum, they can give all students the basic skills they need to manage their money well throughout their lives.

Also, making financial literacy a requirement helps create a more equal society. Wealthier students often learn about managing money from their parents, but students from poorer families might not have that same kind of help. A standard curriculum gives everyone the same chance. All students, no matter how much money their families have, will get access to important life skills. This helps young people escape poverty that might have been passed down through generations and allows them to build their own financial future.

Some people might say that adding another graduation requirement will make school schedules too full and cost too much. But financial literacy doesn't have to be a separate, long course. It could be taught as part of existing math or social studies classes. Or, a focused one-semester class for seniors could offer a lot of practical benefit without messing up their other studies.

In the end, the main job of public schools is to get students ready to live on their own and succeed. Not understanding basic money principles costs individuals and society a lot. Requiring financial literacy means that a high school diploma shows that students are not only academically prepared but also truly ready for real life.

As more people buy electric cars, folks in older neighborhoods are running into a problem that newer places were usually built to avoid: figuring out where to charge.

A lot of older communities were built before garages, driveways, and places to park off the street were common. With narrow streets, old electrical systems, and houses packed close together, charging at home can be tough. People who have to park on the street might have to use public charging spots, and even those with garages might end up paying a lot to get their electrical systems upgraded.

Cities are trying different things to solve this. Some are putting charging stations right on the curb in areas where people don't have much off-street parking. Others are experimenting with chargers built into lampposts or parking meters, which cuts down on the need for new poles and construction. In a few towns, officials are also looking at changing rules that let people run charging cords across sidewalks, but there are still worries about safety and making sure everyone can get by.

This shift has also brought up questions about fairness. People with more money tend to have an easier time putting in their own chargers, while renters and people living in apartment buildings might not have as many choices. Some people argue that public money should go to neighborhoods where residents don't have driveways or garages, instead of putting chargers mostly in newer or wealthier areas.

Trying to keep historic buildings looking the way they should makes things even more complicated. Putting in equipment on older buildings or in historic districts might need extra approvals. Power companies also have to check if the local transformers and power lines can handle the extra load, especially when many drivers charge their cars overnight.

Even with these challenges, transportation planners say that older neighborhoods can make the switch if they plan carefully. They suggest a mix of curbside stations, charging at work and in public, and giving owners of apartment buildings reasons to install shared charging equipment.

For the people living there, how fast things change will depend on local money and the existing infrastructure. As more drivers move to electric cars, communities built long before charging was a thing will need to update their systems without losing the unique character that makes them special.

Recommendation algorithms have changed how we find products, but they actually limit our choices instead of broadening them. These systems are supposed to make things convenient, but they end up showing us fewer different options and strengthening our existing tastes in ways that aren't great.

The problem with algorithms is that when they learn what we like, they create bubble effects that stop us from seeing new things. For example, when Netflix suggests movies based on what you've watched, or Amazon shows you products based on what you've bought, the system is trying to guess what you'll like, not help you stumble upon something new. This means we don't often see truly different options that the algorithm didn't predict. Real choice means seeing all kinds of possibilities, but algorithms deliberately cut down this range.

These systems also give more power to big companies because they tend to push popular products and sellers. New or small items have a hard time getting noticed because algorithms focus on how much people click on things and buy them. A small bookstore's new book is unlikely to show up in recommendations compared to a bestseller from a big publisher. This leads to a situation where everyone ends up seeing pretty much the same things.

It's also hard to know why algorithms make the recommendations they do. Consumers can't easily see why some options are hidden or how the order of suggestions was decided. Without this openness, we can't make truly informed choices because we don't know what else is out there or why we're seeing what we're seeing.

On top of that, recommendation algorithms can play on our psychology. They strategically show us things designed to keep us clicking, often the most extreme or addictive content. This means they focus on making money rather than truly satisfying what consumers genuinely want.

Even though recommendation systems are convenient, they really do take away from our freedom to choose. Instead of helping us make choices, they shape them to benefit companies. To truly give consumers power, we need to rely less on algorithms, make them more transparent, and create spaces where we can discover unexpected things. Only then can our choices truly be our own.

With so much noise on social media, people trusting traditional news less, and public arguments getting more divided, something new is happening: independent newsletter writers are becoming really trusted voices. This paper will look at why this is happening. We’ll see how platforms like Substack, Ghost, and Patreon have helped individual writers, researchers, and experts connect directly with their readers, without needing to go through big media companies.

Before, being a trusted commentator usually meant being a columnist for a major newspaper, a TV personality, or a well-known academic. Their authority often came from their association with big institutions and the fact that editors approved their work. But the internet has made it easier for more people to share their views. Plus, many people are becoming more doubtful of what mainstream media reports. This has created an opening for different kinds of voices. We’ll explore how newsletters, with their personal delivery, feeling of closeness, and often reader-supported model, create a sense of realness and independence that readers connect with. We’ll also look at how newsletter writers use their specific knowledge and detailed viewpoints to provide deep analysis and new reporting, making them stand out from the often shallow or attention-grabbing content found elsewhere online. By bringing together current research on media trust, how platforms make money, and how audiences engage, this introduction will prepare us to fully examine the role of the newsletter writer as an important and increasingly powerful voice in today’s public conversations.

To train for a 100-mile bike ride in 16 weeks, you need to be consistent, gradually increase your effort, and eat well. This plan works if you can already ride about 20 to 25 miles without much trouble.

First Phase: Building a Base (Weeks 1–4)
For the first four weeks, aim for three or four rides each week. Do two shorter rides during the week, about 10 to 15 miles at a steady pace. Include one ride for recovery or another type of exercise. Then, do one longer ride on the weekend. Start this long ride at 25 miles in the first week and add 5 miles each week, so you're riding 40 miles by week four.

Second Phase: Gaining Endurance (Weeks 5–8)
Keep up with your weekday rides, but try to make them a bit harder during the week with some hills or speed intervals to improve your fitness. For the weekend rides, start at 45 miles in week five and work up to 60 miles by week eight. Use these longer rides to figure out your eating and drinking strategy. Aim to have 30 to 60 grams of carbohydrates and one bottle of water or sports drink every hour.

Third Phase: High Mileage (Weeks 9–12)
This is when you'll be riding the most miles. Your weekday rides should be between 15 and 25 miles. The weekend rides will go from 65 miles up to a maximum of 75 to 80 miles in week 12. You don't actually need to ride 100 miles before the actual event; hitting 80 miles shows you have the endurance to complete the full distance.

Fourth Phase: Resting Up and The Event (Weeks 13–16)
Cut back on your mileage during these weeks so your muscles can recover and you feel fresh.
Week 13: Long ride of 60 miles.
Week 14: Long ride of 45 miles.
Week 15: Long ride of 30 miles.
Week 16 (Event Week): Rest for most of the week. Do a short, easy 10-mile ride two days before the event, and rest the day before that.

Important Advice: Consider getting a professional bike fitting to help prevent injuries from doing too much. Make sure you get enough sleep. And whatever you do, don't try any new food or equipment on the day of the event.

Here are 10 tips for using a standing desk at home.

Standing desks can make your home office more adaptable, comfortable, and lively, but you need to use them correctly. These 10 tips will help you make the most of yours.

1. Ease into it. Don't try to stand all day at first. Start with 15 to 30 minutes at a time, then slowly stand for longer periods.

2. Position your monitor at eye level. The top of your screen should be about the same height as your eyes. This helps avoid neck pain and keeps your posture looking natural.

3. Adjust your keyboard and mouse. Your elbows should be near your sides, bent at about a 90-degree angle. Keep your wrists mostly straight when typing.

4. Wear supportive shoes. Standing in bare feet or unsupportive slippers can be uncomfortable. Wear comfortable shoes, or use an anti-fatigue mat.

5. Use an anti-fatigue mat. A cushioned mat can relieve pressure on your feet, knees, and lower back, especially on hard floors.

6. Move around, don't just stand. Shift your weight, stretch, walk during calls, or do some calf raises. Standing still for hours isn't much better than sitting still.

7. Change positions often. Aim to switch between sitting and standing every 30 to 60 minutes. Pay attention to your body instead of sticking to a strict schedule.

8. Keep frequently used items nearby. Arrange your desk so your keyboard, mouse, phone, and other items you use often are easy to reach. Constantly reaching can cause new pains.

9. Pay attention to your posture. Keep your shoulders relaxed, your head aligned with your spine, and your weight evenly distributed on both feet. Don't lean on the desk.

10. Make moving easy. Keep a water bottle close, have walking meetings when you can, and consider a small footrest or balance board for variety.

The best standing desk setup isn't about standing constantly. It's about having more choices during the day and changing positions before you start to feel uncomfortable.

Mentorship is key to making remote apprenticeships work. It fills in for the lack of physical closeness that would normally make learning harder. In a normal workplace, apprentices learn by being around their mentors – seeing how they do things, overhearing how they solve problems, and getting corrected on the spot. When you’re remote, these natural learning moments disappear, so mentorship has to be much more planned out than when everyone is in the same office.

A good mentor working remotely needs to intentionally build the kind of structure that would happen on its own in person. This means setting up regular meetings, clearly explaining their thinking out loud during screen-sharing sessions, and making it easy for apprentices to ask questions that they might normally just ask in passing. The mentor has to actively design the learning space instead of just being someone the apprentice can watch.

Building trust is also much more important. Without those casual chats in the hallway or eating lunch together, mentors have to put in more effort to make apprentices feel safe enough to admit when they’re confused or have made a mistake, using text or video instead of face-to-face. This often means mentors need to show their own vulnerability and check in on how the apprentice is doing overall, not just on their technical skills.

Furthermore, remote mentors often act as bridges to wider professional connections that apprentices can’t easily reach without being in an office. Introducing apprentices to other people in the company, including them in virtual meetings that aren’t directly related to their current tasks, and making sure they get noticed within the organization all become important parts of a mentor’s job.

In the end, remote apprenticeship mentorship changes from something that happens naturally because people are together to a planned, structured activity. It requires more deliberate effort, but when done right, it can lead to learning relationships that are deeper and more thoughtful.

Governments around the world are trying to make laws for facial recognition technology. But experts are saying that the rules they are coming up with aren't keeping up with how fast the technology is changing.

The European Union has its big AI Act, and some cities in the U.S. have banned it. Mostly, these rules focus on how the government, like the police, can use this technology for watching people in real-time. But some legal experts and tech people think these rules give us a false sense of safety because they miss many important areas.

The main problem is that this technology is everywhere now. Facial recognition isn't just on police cameras on streetlights anymore. It's in private security systems, stores use it to track shoppers, and it's in phone apps and social media. Current laws have a hard time dealing with this in the private sector. Often, you have to agree to it in long terms-of-service agreements that people just click through without reading.

Also, laws don't work well when data crosses borders. Companies can build their facial recognition software in places with weak privacy rules and then sell it everywhere. When people try to make companies be more open about how they train these systems, they often can't because of trade secret laws.

Things are even harder because of new technology. Generative AI and fake biometrics make it tough to tell if an image is real or artificial. This makes old definitions of "biometric identifiers" useless in many laws. By the time a law is even made, the technology has often changed, making the law ineffective.

Banning police use in some places might help for a short time. But experts say that just having a few separate rules won't stop a technology that is used globally for business. We need international rules that cover both private use and how the technology itself is built. If we don't, facial recognition will keep growing much faster than the laws trying to control it.

The community-supported fisheries model has become a new approach to seafood distribution, which allows consumers to be in direct contact with fishermen and avoid long and opaque supply chains. CSFs can be seen as analogous to the community-supported agriculture approach; consumers purchase shares of a fishing operation's catch beforehand, which provides the fishermen with funds and price security and gives consumers access to sustainable, fresh, and traceable seafood. The first cases of CSF program implementations have been registered in the USA in the mid-2000s, and since then, they have developed in North American coastal areas and, to a smaller degree, in Europe and other parts of the world, driven by rising demands of consumers to trace back the origin of their food and protect environment.

The interest of scholars in CSFs has increased along with that and comes from several disciplines, such as economics, sociology, marine policy, and food systems. Scholars investigate CSFs from various angles: as a means of helping small fishing communities compete in a globalized economy and sustain depleted fish stocks, as a way to encourage sustainable fisheries management through improved interaction between producers and consumers, and as an element of alternative food network movement against industrial food system. Still, there are many issues left unsolved in the sphere of the economic viability of CSFs, their true impact on environment and fisheries conservation, and the socio-cultural aspects of their functioning in various settings.

This paper reviews the literature related to CSFs in order to understand their background, functioning, and effects on fishers, consumers, and marine ecosystems. The aim of the review is to identify main themes and methods of the current research and possible gaps in the field.

Overall, cities should give priority to installing bicycle lanes as opposed to street parking if the latter contributes to safer, more efficient, and more sustainable transportation system. Though parking is beneficial for drivers and businesses in general, the streets will be more useful to a larger number of people if they promote transportability rather than accommodate private vehicles.

Protected bike lanes help cities decrease the number of injuries on the roads, encourage physical activities and make bicycles available to kids, older citizens and those who don't have cars. Moreover, these lanes are effective means for reducing air pollution and greenhouse gases. In densely-populated neighborhoods, removal of some parking spaces and replacement of them with bike facilities might make possible to decrease the amount of congestion created by residents. The cyclists and pedestrians often come to local businesses and make them more active.

On the other hand, city governments shouldn't remove parking without considering needs of people with special needs, delivery services, tradespeople and people who depend on automobiles. The good way would be keeping accessible parking places, loading spaces and limited short-term parking while creating bicycle lanes. Moreover, the city administration should consider development of public transportation system and management of remaining parking by permit system or parking charges rather than unlimited free parking.

Finally, there is no universal solution to this problem. If the bike lane is not continuous and safe enough at the intersections or if there is little desire to cycle, such re-allocation of spaces is not reasonable. However, before making any changes the authorities should conduct researches, listen to suggestions from affected communities and measure their results. But in general terms, bike lanes would bring more long-term benefits to cities than abundance of street parking.

The retention logic behind unlimited vacation policy is based on a set of theoretical perspectives widely discussed in the organizational literature. According to the social exchange theory, the perception of organizational support and the provision of flexibility may be returned by the employees through higher loyalty and lower intentions to quit the job. Additionally, according to self-determination theory, autonomy can have important motivational effects; unlimited vacation may thus help increase autonomy and satisfaction of people working at companies. # 10 Tips for Weekend Batch-Cooking Strategies

Let's face it—weeknight dinners are a mess. But do you know what's not? Having meals prepared in advance and stored in the refrigerator. And here's how to master this kind of cooking strategy on weekends without going crazy.

**1. Pick Simple, Freezer-Friendly Recipes**
Avoid any recipe that doesn't freeze well because it gets soggy or becomes weird. Curries, chili, soups, and roasted proteins? You got this.

**2. Plan Your Meals in Advance**
Write down the recipes you're going to make before heading to the supermarket. This way, you'll save money and won't be second-guessing yourself while cooking.

**3. Pre-Prepare All Ingredients the Night Before**
Cut all vegetables, measure spices and other ingredients. By the time you start cooking in the morning, you will have no need to be busy with all this stuff.

**4. Make Sure You're Using Your Entire Kitchen**
Your oven, stovetop, slow cooker and even rice cooker should work at once. This is how you can get the most out of your weekend.

**5. Double or Even Triple Your Recipe Amounts**
Anyway, you're heating up your oven, why not cook a few extra portions to store in the freezer for future use?

**6. Invest in High-Quality Containers**
Good quality glass or plastic containers should be in the center of your attention. Label each portion with the date, and you won't have to play the game of guessing in three weeks' time.

**7. Cook Your Protein First**
Roast your chicken, ground beef, and other proteins first. Then all you have to do is to wait for them to cool down.

**8. Take Care of Your Breakfast**
Batch-cook your breakfast, too—egg muffins, oatmeal, breakfast burritos. You'll thank yourself in the morning of the next week

It has been observed that the use of recommendation algorithms changed the way in which people used to find products, however, in reality, this change in the system limited the choice available to the consumers instead of broadening it. These algorithms offer personalization and convenience to consumers, but this is done at the cost of limiting the variety of the options.

Algorithms have a basic contradiction that while learning consumer behavior, they build up an echo chamber that limits exposure to any alternative. For example, when Netflix recommends films that you like, or Amazon recommends you products based on your previous purchases, algorithms make predictions for your satisfaction and not for discovering something new. As a result, people will hardly be offered alternatives that are not predicted in algorithms. In order to have true choice, one should be exposed to all the possible options, but these algorithms specifically filter out options.

Furthermore, recommendation algorithms have concentrated power on some products and vendors because they cannot reach a lot of people. An alternative will not be able to appear in algorithms in case the product is not popular and does not provide enough profits to the seller. Thus, it will be hard for a debut novel of a small bookstore to appear in algorithms, but not a bestseller from a major publisher. In such a way, consumers' choice becomes homogenized throughout the population.

The lack of transparency in algorithms also worsens this situation. People do not know what options were filtered and how the ranks were formed. Consequently, people cannot make informed choices as they need to know what is the whole range of alternatives and how they were offered.

Community-supported fisheries (CSFs) are a new direct-to-consumer seafood marketing approach that establishes a relationship between fishers and consumers and offers an alternative to the long, complex, and sometimes opaque supply chains of the commercial fishing industry. Similar in concept to community-supported agriculture (CSAs), CSFs typically buy shares of a fishing enterprise before the season begins and help fishers bridge financial gaps while obtaining fresher, traceable, often more sustainable seafood. CSFs have been around in the US since the mid-2000s, and while the concept is gaining popularity in coastal North America and Europe, few data exist on how widespread the model truly is.

With the exception of studies considering conservation and environmental impacts, academic research on CSFs has expanded considerably in recent years and takes inspiration from a range of disciplinary approaches, from economics and sociology to marine policy and food systems analysis. Scholars have studied CSFs as a potential way to strengthen the economic sustainability of small-scale fishing communities, threatened by a globalization-driven competition and declining marine stocks; as a potential pathway to develop more sustainable fisheries management through a closer relationship between producers and consumers; and as an element of broader alternative food network movements that may intersect with or deviate from industrial food systems. However, despite this growing literature, important gaps remain regarding the long-term economic viability of CSFs, their actual environmental and conservation impacts, and their socio-cultural dynamics.

This review draws together previous research on community-supported fisheries to identify what is known about their origins, models of operation, and effects on fishers, consumers and marine ecosystems. Through a comparative analysis of previous research, this review aims to highlight the strengths and gaps of past studies, and to identify key themes, methodologies and research gaps to contribute to future work on this new paradigm of sustainable seafood provision.

# Repaint Your Kitchen in a Weekend

## Preparation (Friday Evening)

Make sure to clear everything out of your kitchen. Take down cabinet hardware, light fixtures and any appliances if you can. Use drop cloths and plastic sheeting to cover counters, floors and other fixtures so that you don't have to wait to get around to cleanup.

## Priming and Cleaning (Saturday Morning)

Clean all surfaces with a solution of TSP (trisodium phosphate) to get rid of grease, dirt, and grime. Wait until dry. Add primer to darkened or discolored walls and spots. Sand the shiny paints to ensure paint to stick well. That is how you get a professional work.

## First Paint Coat (Saturday Afternoon)

Start painting your ceiling and upper walls first with a roller for faster application. Detail trims with a brush. Use good quality paints because the richer the pigment, the more it covers and the longer it lasts. Let it dry!

## Final Coat & Details (Sunday)

Apply on wall and ceiling. Paint doors and trim if required. Use painter's tape to get clean lines on around window and skirting boards, then peel off while paint is still a little tacky.

## Wrapping Up (Sunday Night into Monday)

Rehang light fixtures and cabinet hardware as soon as the paint is completely dry. Replace appliances. Gently remove plastic to prevent dragging dust onto new paint.

## Pro Tips

- Order materials Thursday to bypass shopping delays on the weekend
- Purchase low-VOC paint for a healthier home
- Quality brushes and rollers â€“ invest in them, you will see the difference (and so will your paint!)
- Have a damp cloth ready for easy cleanup
- Ensure proper ventilation throughout the process

If you plan, work efficiently, and stick to the plan, you will have a freshly painted kitchen waiting for you on Monday morning to start the week.

## 10 Tips for a Focused Evening Wind-Down Routine

What's up, guys! Feeling awake and alert even at 10 pm and staring at the ceiling wishing you had a remote that would turn your mind off? Well, you're not alone. Sometimes our days are so packed that we just don't get time to relax and rest before a good night's sleep.

Here are 10 tips to help you create a more targeted nightly routine and get to sleep more quickly:

1. Pick a "Digital Sunset" Time: Make screens go dark an hour before sleeping – the blue light suppresses melatonin.
2. As it gets dark outdoors, lower the interior lighting to prepare your body to wind down. Turn the lights off or dim them when it gets dark outdoors.
3. Taking a warm bath or shower will help your muscles relax and will also help to bring your temperature down a little - great for sleeping.
4. Put away your electronic device and read a real paper book. It's relaxing and distraction free.
5. A gentle, slow stretch or yoga sequence to relax tension but not fire you up.
6. Herbal Tea Time: Chamomile or lavender tea can be a relaxing treat. But steer clear of anything with caffeine!
7. When your mind starts to race, write down your worries or your to do list. Clear your mind by writing it down.
8. You can also try listening to an instrumental soundtrack, nature sounds, or a lighthearted podcast.
9. Lay out your clothes, pack your bag-getting these things done the night before helps you make fewer decisions in the morning and cuts down on your day's stress.
10. Set a Bedtime: Routine is the best! Even on weekends, try to get yourself to bed at about the same time and wake up at about the same time each day.

It takes time to develop a new habit, so be patient with yourself. Try implementing one or two of these tips at a time each week and see what works for you. Sleep well!

Cities should normally prefer bike lanes to parking on the street where that decision supports safer, more efficient, more sustainable transportation. While parking is convenient to drivers and provides additional business to adjacent stores and businesses, more public street space is reserved for movement and not to store the vehicles of its residents.

Protected bike lanes can help prevent traffic crashes, lead to more physical activity, and enable children, seniors, and those without cars to cycle. They can also help lower traffic-related air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions. Replacing parking with bike lanes and paths in dense neighborhoods can enable more people to get around without adding to traffic congestion. Cities can also use bike lanes to bring more customers to local businesses-cyclists and pedestrians tend to make frequent stops, and great streets attract customer traffic.

But cities shouldn't eliminate parking at the expense of those with disabilities, delivery workers, tradespeople and anyone else who truly needs a car. An equitable plan might retain parking for people with disabilities, loading zones and some short-term parking in dense areas, while establishing protected lanes for bikes and buses in the place of other parking spots. Cities could also push for more transit and control the free curb parking with permits or pricing, rather than allowing free curb parking to hog city space.

The best choice for your city will always come down to a number of considerations. For example: a bike lane does little good if it's disconnected, dangerous at intersections, or located in an area with low demand. Municipalities should research traffic patterns and community opinions, and monitor outcomes before changing allocations. In most dense city centres, the benefits to the public of safe cycling far outweigh the benefits to individual vehicle owners of free parking. Cities should embrace bike lanes as part of a comprehensive transportation plan, while offering modest accommodations for people who need to drive.

# Local Libraries Transition into Digital Centers in the Era of the Internet

Community libraries are transforming into vital digital portals, narrowing the tech divide for millions of underserved residents.

With more and more work, education, and service now occurring online, public libraries have grown well beyond their traditional functions. They now provide free high-speed internet, computers, and digital literacy programs that are critically important to low-income communities.

"Libraries are the equalizers of technology," says Maria Chen, director of digital initiatives for the American Library Association. "For some populations, a library is the only way they'll have internet access or computers."

In the midst of the pandemic, this change has become especially important, as libraries have become one of the only places where students who are learning from home, and jobseekers whose job applications are completely online, can turn for help. Now many branches are providing coding classes, digital literacy classes, and support with government websites and telehealth.

Aside from technology and internet access, librarians are now serving as digital coaches. Librarians support and guide users in how to use their devices for basic email function to how to be safe online, realizing that giving someone internet access isn't enough.

But it's a costly mission. Libraries cannot afford to update their hardware and software, hire highly trained staff, or keep up with the speed of technology - all under the threat of lost funding.

Even with these challenges, community libraries are still vital. They offer low-cost alternatives to computer labs and commercial internet providers, safe spaces for people to learn without judgment, and they stay community anchors.

Next, professionals see libraries evolving through: Forming alliances with technology firms. Boosting government support. Introducing virtual reality and artificial intelligence to make their holdings more diverse.

In the face of the digital divide, community libraries are this nation's buffer, making sure all folks - no matter their income or zip code - have the resources and skills they need to succeed in a digital age.

The university lecture of the future will be hybrid – and it should be, as this is where it is going. The traditionalists who mourn the demise of the archetypal face-to-face lecture are fighting a losing battle. The inflexible model of one mono fix-time fix-place lecture that only works for a minority of students seeking a traditional career does not meet the needs of many of today's students who are juggling work, family and location considerations.

Hybrid learning really is the way forward, with a mix of synchronous online learning, asynchronous content and some focused in person content. Far from a half-measure, asynchronous content allows for flexibility in the way students can access the content, including pausing a pre-recorded lecture to absorb and reflect on the information at their own pace, optimising their learning. It also allows them to keep face to face time for what it's best at: reactive, practical sessions, in-class discussions, brainstorms and tutorials, the elements that aren't possible with 50, 80, or 150 students sitting passively in a lecture hall.

In addition, the technological foundations of hybrids can underpin digital literacies that are relevant for today's graduates. Universities have a duty to equip students for the interconnected world into which they will graduate; engaging a suite of different online resources into education should be part of that. Not only will such a hybrid, well-structured approach raise levels of student independence and access, but it can provide a much more dynamic and engaging learning environment than the monologues that lecturers from previous generations have tried to speak to students during. The future of university is not simply to survive in the digital age, but to thrive in it.

Retention of staff is a pressing issue for employers facing fierce competition for workers, escalating turnover costs and shifting employee attitudes towards flexibility and health. One strategy that has become increasingly popular in the debate about how best to retain top talent is that of limited is that of unlimited vacation, also known as "discretionary paid time off" and "unlimited paid time off (PTO)." A traditional leave program provides employees with a predetermined number of days off each year, whereas unlimited vacation policies allow employees paid time off that is granted without a predetermined limit, subject to manager approval, workload considerations, and organizational expectations.

There are several widely accepted organizational theories and perspectives that can support a retention explanation for unlimited vacation policies. Based on the social exchange perspective, which often underpins organizational support and discretionary behavior theories, the provision of flexible time off policies like unlimited vacation might lead to less turnover and greater loyalty to the employer. Likewise, based on self-determination theory, greater autonomy in the form of unlimited vacation should bolster participants' feelings of control, intrinsic motivation, and general psychological health, which could then lead to greater job satisfaction and lower intention to leave. Finally, universities and organizations might use unlimited vacation as a symbolic benefit that is attractive for recruitment and retention purposes, especially when competing for knowledge workers who are prone to value work-life flexibility.

But the link between unlimited vacation and retention isn't cut-and-dried. Detractors argue that doing away with hard-earned PTO entitlements adds a little confusion to time off. Employees will take even less time off when the conditions aren't perfectly clear, particularly if they are in a high-stress, high-performance environment and don't want to be perceived as less hardworking than their peers. Unlimited PTO might even just shift some of the burden of staying healthy and well from employers to employees, stripping the policy of any potential positive effects. Managers, workload, team culture, and perceived fairness are all likely to determine whether unlimited PTO is seen as an employee benefit or a hollow promise.

Increasingly, companies are considering the implementation of unlimited vacation policies as a business practice to help attract and retain workforce talent. Although unlimited vacation can serve as a symbol of a workplace perk, such practices are being studied to evaluate whether they can actually function as an employee retention strategy. This review explores the literature on the topics of employee autonomy, organizational support, work-life balance and intent to leave and synthesizes the information related to the positive and negative outcomes of unlimited vacation policies.

Create a neighborhood book club. It's a low-pressure way to connect with new friends, learn about new authors, and establish a recurring event that neighbors will enjoy.

Start by launching a small gathering through neighborhood email forums, social media, flyers, or friends. Intentionally seek to have 6 to 12 people to keep the conversation vibrant without it being unwieldy. During your first meeting, lock in simple things like frequency, location, method for choosing books, and if you will all read the same books through.

Pick a regular schedule, maybe the first Thursday of each month. Switching the location could ease the burden of hosting, or you could meet at a library, a coffee shop, a community center or a park. Allow for a virtual option for people who are unable to come in person.

If possible take turns selecting books or have members suggest books and hold a vote. When applicable, establish a page limit. Offer a wide variety of styles and writers from different backgrounds and time periods. Suggest bestsellers, non-fiction, memoirs, mysteries, local writers and short stories. Announce the next book and date of meeting before dispersing.

Have a few open-ended questions ready to prompt discussion. What did members like/dislike/surprise them? Which characters/ideas seemed most convincing? What does the book have to do with their lives today, or what happens in their community? A discussion leader may rotate.

Maintain the club's welcoming spirit and flexibility. Allow for diverse opinions, encourage participation from all members, and be aware that readers may not be able to attend all meetings or read the entire book. Beverages and snacks are nice but keep the hosting schedule manageable.

Last but not least, keep the momentum going by sending reminders, celebrating wins, and having fun with it now and then - maybe a themed book swap or meeting, author event or visit to a bookstore. A good book club isn't about perfect attendance or even deep discussion: it's about friendliness and having a book to come back to.

# 10 Tips for Weekend Batch-Cooking Strategies

Come on - weeknights are mayhem. But you know what isn't? An organized fridge filled with ready-made food. Here's exactly how to crush weekend batch cooking without losing your mind.

## 1. Select Easy, Freezer-Friendly Dishes

Skip foods that turn soggy or off-taste when frozen. Curries, chili, soups and roasted proteins are perfect.

## 2. Plan Your Menu First

Write your recipe down before you go shopping. It helps you to save money and to avoid the "why did I buy that?" feeling halfway through a dinner.

## 3. Prep Everything on Friday Night

Prepare your vegetables, measure out your spices and put everything in order before you start. If you get everything prepped on Saturday morning then you can avoid having onion skins everywhere.

## 4. Use Your Whole Kitchen

Oven, stovetop, slow cooker and rice cooker all running at the same time? The culinary equivalent of a kiss. This is how you get the most bang for your buck.

## 5. Double (or Triple) Recipes

It's already warm in the oven, so you're heating it already. Make a batch for the freezer.

## 6. Invest in Quality Containers

Bottled glass or great plastics - so you use these as your MVPs. Label everything with date - so you're not playing freezer roulette in three weeks.

## 7. Cook Proteins First

Get your ground beef, chicken, or beans out of the way. By the time they're cool, you're at the halfway point.

## 8. Don't Forget About Breakfast

Batch-cook egg muffins, oatmeal, or breakfast burritos as well. The you who tackles those things on Monday will thank you later.

## 9. Clean as You Go

Oh yeah, it's almost easier to block out the sink but ultimately it's better to get it over with than tackling Mount Dishmore Sunday night.

## 10. Give Yourself Grace

You're going to have good weeks, bad weeks. Some weeks you'll get one meal that you cook and feel like it's a victory. That's still, like, four takeout days.

Your future self for weekdays will be extremely healthy.

The consequences of requiring high school financial literacy out weigh any cost. As a nation, we have no written financial strategy, and students take on complex financial responsibilities in their to-days without prior education: credit cards, car loans, budgeting, planning for education, planning for retirement and investing. Not only does the nation have little financial literacy when we leave high school, those students quickly learn the effects of poor credit and a mountain of high interest debt.

In addition, mandating financial literacy also has the potential to reduce social and economic disparity. Children of prosperous parents are much more likely to develop an understanding of money management from their family early on, while children from disadvantaged family environments do not get this same support. A standardized framework ensures all children, regardless of background, are given the same tools to succeed.

One concern is that another graduation requirement might seem unnecessary given the number of other graduation requirements and limited school hours available. But the addition of a financial literacy requirement need not be a multi-year course. Given the ability to incorporate financial literacy concepts into mathematics and social studies curricula, it could be a one-semester course offered in senior year.

Finally, the bottom line. How can our public education system help better prepare our high school graduates for reality? Lack of understanding of fundamental financial skills, it seems, results in a tremendous loss, both at a personal and societal level. Requiring financial education with a high school diploma is thus the right call.

With more people owning EVs, residents in older neighborhoods are facing a dilemma that newer communities were often designed to dodge: Where to plug in.

Most older neighborhoods were developed long before garages, driveways and off-street parking were common. Close-together houses, small electrical panels and narrow roads can make home charging a challenge. If you park on the street, you may need to use public chargers, or if you have a garage, you might have to upgrade your electrical system.

Cities are taking a variety of approaches. Several cities are deploying curbside chargers in neighborhoods that have few off-street parking spaces. Others are experimenting with chargers embedded in streetlights or parking meters to limit new utility pole installation and construction. A handful of municipalities are reevaluating policies that let residents run extension cords across sidewalks, amid safety and accessibility issues.

The switch has also prompted concerns about equity. Wealthier homeowners are more likely to have driveways or garages to install private chargers, and renters or those in apartment buildings may have limited options. Critics argue that public investments should be targeted toward communities that don't have driveways or garages to park in, not richer or newer parts of town.

Historic preservation might complicate things further. It is required for equipment installations in historic districts or on historic buildings to seek extra review. Utility companies will have to check the capacity of local transformers and power lines, especially when many drivers charge through the night.

Even with the roadblocks, transportation planners say aging neighborhoods can transition with proper planning. They advocate a "blend of curbside stations, workplace and public charging, and inducements for owners of apartment buildings to retrofit shared gear."

For residents, the speed of change will also depend on the level of investment and infrastructure in their area. Communities that already exist long before a driver is charging their first electric vehicle will need to evolve without sacrificing their identity.

# The Constraining Effect of Recommendation Algorithms on Consumers' Choice

Recommendation engines have transformed consumer behavior by broadening access to products and services. But the real extent of the shift is just the opposite: recommendations, well as they are presented, constrict traditional options and repeat, and in some ways restrict, consumers' tastes.

Algorithms face a key contradiction: their effectiveness depends on exploiting user behavior, which leads to paradoxically us ensuring customers never see any new options. So when Netflix recommends films closely aligned with one's past choices, or Amazon suggests products based on past orders, algorithms seek to maximize the probability of consumption, rather than experience for the individual. Customers are seldom presented with a truly novel alternative that doesn't fall within the algorithm's predictive range.

Secondly, these systems concentrate market power and skew them towards the existing products and vendors. New niche product can hardly appear to compete with the popular ones, because the algorithms put more priority on engagement or conversion rates. A debut from a small bookstore has next to no chance to appear through algorithmic recommendations as a bestseller from a mega publisher.

This is made worse by the opacity of algorithmic decision-making. Consumers are unable to explain why some options were not presented to them or how particular choices were ranked. This lack of explainability prevents consumers from making an informed choice, which the law defines as understanding the alternative options and how they were presented.

Additionally, algorithmic suggestions take advantage of our psychology by manipulation. They choose and display options that best drive engagement (and the most addictive or incendiary options in the case of content), for the sake of profit, regardless of whether they even satisfy demand.

Recommendation systems may feel like a convenience, but they come with a real price. They aren't giving us choice, they're forcing it upon us. To make it possible for real consumer choice, we need less mediation from algorithms, more transparency, and more "inconspicuous" spaces to encounter the unexpected.

In the last twenty years, digital media has experienced an unprecedented upheaval, fueled by rapid pluralization of new platforms and the profound transformation in the circulation of information. In the midst of social media noise, the declining credibility of legacy news organizations, and the growing polarization of the public debate, there is one phenomenon to which little media attention has been paid: the emergence of independent newsletter authors as most trusted commentators. In this literature review, I will examine the trend of newsletter writers' quick rise to prominence, focusing on the rise of platforms such as Substack, Ghost and Patreon that enable journalists, academics and subject-matter experts to develop meaningful relationships with their audiences outside the legacy media.

In the past, the trusted commentator role was essentially limited to established print columnists, TV pundits, and prominent academics, who often relied on institutional ties or gatekeeping editing practices to lend credibility. Today, the internet's sense of democratizing power, combined with an eroding trust in traditional media sources, have created the ideal conditions for alternative media creators to emerge as trusted commentators. This review will explore how the affordances of the newsletter format (personal delivery, feeling of closeness, the typical subscriber-funded model) often create a perception of authenticity and neutrality that is highly compelling for consumers. In addition, we will examine how newsletter creators emphasize their own expertise and unique perspective to provide rich analysis and original reporting that is absent from other online news sites. Drawing from research on media trust, platform economics, and audience engagement, this introduction will lay out the foundation for a detailed understanding of the newsletter writer as a pivotal emerging figure.

Building up for a century ride (100 miles) in 16 weeks should be set up with you showing up consistently, increasing intensity/time, and fuel up correctly. We are going to assume you can already comfortably ride 20-25 miles.

Phase 1 – Foundation (Weeks 1-4)
Prioritize 3-4 weekly rides: Two weekday rides of 10-15 miles at an easy to moderate pace Two recovery rides or cross training A long ride on the weekend. Begin with a 25-mile long ride in the first week and add 5 miles every week till week 4 where you'll be riding 40 miles.

Phase 2: Endurance Building (Weeks 5–8)
Stick to your weekly schedule, with a bit more mid-week effort on hill-climb or interval days to develop cardiovascular strength. Ramp up your weekend long ride from 45 miles in Week 5 to 60 miles in Week 8. Try to replicate your race-day eating plan by eating for 30–60 grams of carbs an hour, plus one bottle of water/electrolytes per hour.

Phase 3: Peak Volume (Weeks 9–12)
The second phase involves the bulk of your mileage. Your weekday rides should be between 15-25 miles, your long weekend rides can start at 65 miles, and eventually get up to about 75-80 miles in Week 12. No need to ride 100 miles before the race. Just ride at least 80 miles and you will have enough in the tank.

Phase 4: Taper and Event (Weeks 13–16)
Lower your volume and allow your muscles to recover so that your legs stay fresh.
* Week 13: 60-mile long ride.
* Week 14: 45-mile long ride.
* Week 15: 30-mile long ride.
* Wk16 (Event Week): Rest early in week, one easy 10 mi two days before, rest day before.

Key Tips: Go for a professional bike fitting, always spend time on your core strength, eat well and never trial any new equipment or food during race day.

# 10 tips for standing desks for home offices

A stand-up desk can help your home office become a more versatile, comfortable, and energizing space - if you use one mindfully. Here are 10 simple tips for getting the most out of your stand-up desk.

## 1. Start slowly

Avoid standing all day from the start. Start off standing for 15-30 minute durations, then build it up gradually.

## 2. Maintain your monitor at your eye level

You also want the top of your screen to be approximately eye level. When your screen is at eye level you won't bend your neck down while working.

## 3. Modify Your Mouse and Keyboard

Keep your elbows near your sides and use a relaxed "90 degree" bend. Keep your wrists fairly straight as you type.

## 4. Wear supportive shoes

Bare feet or in unsuitable shoes or slippers make standing uncomfortable. Wear comfortable shoes or use an anti-fatigue mat.

## 5. Use an anti-fatigue mat

A padded mat will take some of the impact off your knees, feet and lower back (particularly on hard floors).

## 6. Move instead of simply standing

Move your body. Shift your weight, reach and stretch, walk while you talk, or do some calf raises. Because standing still all day isn't really an improvement over sitting still.

## 7. Switch positions frequently

Aim to alternate sitting to standing every 30â€“60 minutes. There's no right time to change. Listen to your body.

## 8. Keep essentials within reach

Position your desk so that your phone, mouse, keyboard, and other essentials can be close to you. Keep in mind how much you have to reach all the time can cause some fresh pain.

## 9. Mind your posture

Maintain a relaxed shoulder posture, keep your head aligned with your spine and your weight distributed equally on your feet, and never lean into the desk.

## 10. Facilitate the movement

Keep a water bottle handy, take walking meetings as often as you can, and bring in a small footrest or balance board to switch things up.

The best standing desk setup isn't standing all day. It's making the best use of the options you have during the day and switching between sit and stand before you get sore.
