Mentorship is the foundation of the remote internship, as the physical separation between apprentice and mentor destroys opportunities for organic leaning moments to occur. In on-site environments, apprentices learn simply by being near a mentor; gazing at their hands, eavesdropping on their thinking, and getting randomly corrected. Remote setups remove these "random" moments, requiring far more deliberate mentoring.

In a remote environment, an effective mentor would need to intentionally scaffold the training because the scaffolds would not naturally be in place. These could include regular calls, sharing screen and clearly articulating their thinking process, setting up a dedicated slack channel for questions instead of asking a question on the walkie. Basically, the mentor has to be an active designer of the environment.

When mentors and apprentices aren't sitting side-by-side at the office, theres work to be done. Without meeting in the hallway or chatting in the cafeteria, mentors need to go the extra mile to establish psychological safety for apprentices. This means engaging in warmth and self-disclosure themselves and navigating tradeoffs between mentors time and headspace.

Moreover, in remote apprenticeships, mentors may also act as links to large-scale networks that the apprentices might have access to by working on-site. Introducing the apprentice to co-workers, including them in team meetings (beyond his/her working tasks), and promoting the apprentice's visibility among the organization become some of the mentor tasks.

Inevitably, mentoring in remote apprenticeships becomes no longer an incidental consequence of being in the same place but is instead a more proactive, conscious, intentional endeavour, which, if done well, is likely to lead to more intensive and considered learning relationships.

As governments rush to write laws related to facial recognition technology, experts are pointing out that laws on the books, and those being written, cannot keep up with the pace of this rapidly emerging technology.

Policymakers have fixated on government use - banning or restricting law enforcement's use of real-time biometric surveillance, for example - from the European Union's groundbreaking Artificial Intelligence Act to citywide bans throughout the United States. But legal experts and technologists say these efforts, while well-intentioned, are mostly illusions that leave giant regulatory gaps.

The fundamental challenge: the widespread infiltration of the technology. No longer limited to high-resolution police surveillance cameras atop streetlights, facial recognition has pervaded security, retail applications, smartphones, and social media, and current laws haven't caught up with that private-sector spread, where declarations of consent lurk deep in often-unread terms-of-service contracts.

Additionally, jurisdictional restrictions pose a significant obstacle to enforcement. Because biometric data can be transmitted across jurisdictions, designers can train their algorithms in states with weak privacy laws and then deploy the software elsewhere. Efforts to force companies to reveal the training data for their models - a very simple form of transparency - are often thwarted by companies citing trade-secret protections.

But technological change is even more difficult. Generative AI and synthetic biometrics have eroded the line between real and fake images, making the notion of "biometric identifiers" a legal anachronism in many jurisdictions. By the time a law is being considered and written, the technology it is based on may already be outdated.

By themselves, targeted bans in some cities may rein in police conduct, but it won't stop a product that's now licensed and used around the world. Without international standards for private commercial use and the algorithms underlying such systems, facial recognition is unlikely to be reined in by legislation anytime soon.

Public support for the repair-and-refurbish electronics movement is well justified. This movement supports waste reduction, consumer savings and challenges the wasteful culture of planned obsolescence. Since people have come to rely on their phones, laptops, tablets and appliances in everyday living, they shouldn't be forced to buy replacements for these items when they experience common issues such as weak batteries, cracked screens or small component failure.

The rapidly growing stream of electronic waste is one of the most pressing environmental challenges today. Electronic waste (e-waste) is produced when electronic products are discarded and no longer used. Many of these products contain toxic substances like lead, mercury, and other hazardous chemicals; if they are not disposed of properly, they may leach into soils and waters. On the other hand, electronic products also contain many valuable metals and components that would have required large amounts of energy and mining to create. Repairing a product so that it can be used for an additional number of years will avoid creating new products unnecessarily and reduce the negative environmental impacts of extracting raw materials, transporting manufactured goods, and discarding used equipment.

Repair can also make technology less expensive. When you buy a new cell phone or computer, it may be very costly (hundreds or thousands of dollars), but if you replace a battery, charge port, or screen, it may only cost you a fraction of what buying a whole new device would. There is also the opportunity to purchase refurbished electronic items which will allow students, families, and smaller business owners to obtain reliable technology at a lower price than purchasing brand new products. In addition to providing affordable access to reliable technology, expanding access to repaired devices can also help close the "digital divide" by providing many individuals with technology they require to operate in today's society.

Critics could argue that newer models of devices are more energy efficient or provide greater security than older models, and there are times when it makes sense to replace a product with a newer model. However, just because a manufacturer can make a product more energy efficient or more secure does not give them permission to create products which are difficult or impossible to repair. Manufacturers must offer repair parts, repair manuals, diagnostic tools, and easy access to software updates. Right-to-repair legislation can help make sure that independent repair shops as well as individual consumers can easily maintain the products that they purchased.

Repairing/Refurbishing promotes responsible behavior toward technology rather than relying on the convenience of disposing of technology. Electronics are treated as valuable tools that need to be maintained, not as disposable fashion statements. When we support repairing/refurbishing technology we promote environmentally conscious behaviors, provide consumers with options, and create a long-term sustainable connection with technology.

## Introduction

Community Supported Fisheries (CSF) is an alternative way to sell seafood. It is based on a concept similar to Community Supported Agriculture (CSA), but instead of buying produce from a farmer, you buy seafood from a fisherman. With CSF, the customer pays for a "share" of the fisherman's catch at the beginning of each season. This allows the fisherman to have some financial security by having money available before he even goes out on the boat, and it gives him a guaranteed customer for his product. In return, the customer receives fresh, traceable seafood that was caught locally, and in many cases, sustainably. The first known CSF began in the U.S. in the early 2000s and since then has grown significantly throughout the coastal areas of North America and to a smaller degree in Europe and elsewhere. Consumers are showing more interest in knowing where their food comes from, how environmentally friendly the practices used to get it are, and supporting their local economy.

A growing amount of research on CSFs has also emerged in parallel with the growth in scholarly attention to CSFs, with contributions coming from various disciplines such as economics, sociology, marine policy, and food systems. Researchers have used several frameworks to analyze CSFs: as mechanisms for improving the economic feasibility of small-scale fisheries operating within a globally competitive environment with decreasing fish supplies; as strategies for achieving more effective fisheries management by developing closer relationships between producers and consumers; and as components of larger alternative food network movements that oppose industrialized food systems. However, even though there is an increasing body of research addressing CSFs, there are still major areas of unknowns regarding the long-term economic sustainability of CSFs, the actual environmental/conservation impacts of CSFs, and the social/cultural factors that determine the success/failure of CSFs under varying geographic/institutional conditions.

Community supported fisheries (CSFs) have been a focus of extensive research in recent years. This review synthesizes prior studies of CSFs to determine what has been learned about the history, organization, and effects of CSFs on fishers, consumers, and aquatic habitats. Through a critical examination of the advantages and disadvantages of previous studies, this review seeks to identify central themes, methodological approaches, and unaddressed questions that could help guide future research and public policy regarding CSFs, as a new form of sustainable seafood supply.

# Repaint Your Kitchen in a Weekend

## Preparation (Friday Evening)

Clear out your entire kitchen. If possible, take down all cabinet hardware, lighting devices, and appliances. Protect everything else in the kitchen by using drop cloths and plastic sheets on top of countertops, floor surfaces and other fixtures that will remain. This will protect your space and help you avoid cleaning up later than necessary.

## Priming and Cleaning (Saturday Morning)

First, use TSP (trisodium phosphate) to clean every surface well enough so that you can remove any dirt, oil and other contaminants. After the surface has dried completely, then apply primer to those parts of the wall that have stains, or are currently painted in a dark color. Then, lightly sand each of the surfaces that appear to be glossy in order to allow the paint to adhere properly. All of these initial preparation steps will enable you to obtain a high-quality finish on your walls.

## First Paint Coat (Saturday Afternoon)

Begin with the ceiling and upper wall area using a roller for speed. Use a brush to paint the trim and detailed areas. Use high quality paint because it has greater coverage and durability. Give enough time for the paint to dry before applying the next coat of paint — usually 4 to 6 hours depending on humidity.

## Second Coat and Details (Sunday)

To apply a second layer of paint to the walls and ceiling. If you choose to do so, paint the doors and trim as well. To achieve clean, crisp edges when painting around windows and baseboards, use painter's tape. While the paint is still slightly tacky, remove the tape so you have sharp, clean lines.

## Final Touches (Sunday Evening to Monday)

Once the paint has dried, you can put back the lights and other hardware on your cabinets. Put the appliances back where they were. Be careful when removing the protective covers so that you do not drag any dust on the freshly painted area.

## Pro Tips

- Purchase supplies Thursday to avoid weekend shopping delays
- Use low-VOC paint for better air quality
- Invest in quality brushes and rollers—they make a visible difference
- Keep a damp cloth handy for quick cleanup
- Ensure proper ventilation throughout the process

By being organized and having things done correctly, you can expect to have a new look to your kitchen by Monday morning, which is great because that's when you start the rest of your week.

It makes it very difficult for us to unwind before we go to sleep. A great way to help yourself get a better nights sleep is by having a relaxing wind down routine.

10 ways to create a relaxing night-time routine and fall asleep faster:

1. **Establish a "Digital Sunset" Time:** Establish the time you will turn off all electronic devices. It should be established a minimum of one hour prior to going to sleep. Blue light affects melatonin production.
2. **Dim the Lights:** As the sun goes down, turn down your indoor lighting to signal to your brain that you should begin to unwind.
3. **Warm Soak:** Taking a warm bath or shower will help you loosen up, and as a result of that, you'll be able to drop your body temperature a little after the soak. This is what you want before going to bed.
4.  **Read an actual book** - Leave behind your e-reader and choose to read a traditional paper-based book. This can be very relaxing and free from distractions.
5. **A Little Gentle Stretching or Yoga:** A few easy, unhurried stretches will help ease tension in your body, but they won't give you a lot of energy.
6. **Time for some herbal tea:** A cup of chamomile or lavender tea will help you relax and feel better. Be sure to use non-caffeinated varieties.
7.  **Write Down What is Going on in Your Head:** When you have a lot of thoughts going through your head, write down your concerns and things you need to do. Write down those things from your head into writing.
8. **Listen to Relaxing Music/Podcast:** You may find that listening to soft instrumental music, sounds from nature, or an easy-going storytelling podcast helps you relax.
9. **Prepare for Tomorrow:** Get your clothes ready for the next day, and put everything you need in your backpack – if you do both of these tasks the night before, then you will have fewer decisions to make when waking up in the morning and less stress.
10. **Consistent Sleep Schedule:** Our body enjoys having a regular routine. Therefore, try to go to bed and wake up at approximately the same hour each day (including the weekend).

You need to give yourself some time to develop a new habit. It's okay to take things slow and have patience with yourself. Start by implementing one or two of these suggestions per week and determine which ones are most effective for you. Good night!

Cities should usually choose to develop bicycle lanes instead of allowing on-street parking because it provides a safer, more effective, and environmentally friendly transportation system. While parking may provide some convenience to motorists, as well as support local businesses, public streets are best utilized by accommodating movement as opposed to providing storage space for individually owned vehicles.

Bike lanes with barriers will help decrease the number of injuries from traffic; increase the use of physical activities; provide access to bicycling for children, older adults, and those without their own vehicle; assist cities in reducing air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions; and in high density areas, when replacing on-street parking with bike facilities, allow more people to commute using methods other than driving which contributes to congestion. Businesses can also benefit from bike/pedestrian friendly streets since they are typically frequented by bicyclists/pedestrians who are supportive of local merchants, and attractive streets tend to lead to greater commercial activities.

Cities must consider the needs of residents with disabilities, delivery workers, trade workers, and individuals that rely on their personal vehicles when eliminating parking. A carefully developed plan will allow cities to convert most of their existing parking into protected bike lanes while still providing accessible spaces, loading zones, and short-term parking. Cities must also enhance their public transportation systems and use permits or pricing strategies to control the amount of parking available on-street instead of having unmanaged free street parking take up prime real estate.

The best decision regarding whether to install a bike lane will depend on your areaâ€™s current conditions. If the proposed bike lane is not connected to other bike lanes, is dangerous to cross at intersections, or is in an area with very little cycling demand, then the installation of the bike lane may not be the most effective way to improve transportation options in that area. Prior to reallocating roadway space to accommodate a bike lane, officials should examine how people are using the roadways in their community, engage with residents and businesses who would be affected by the change, and determine the success of similar projects. However, the long term benefits of safe cycling in congested urban areas generally far exceed the short term benefit of having plentiful street parking available. Therefore, cities should focus on implementing bike lanes as part of a larger transportation plan; however, cities should also provide alternative means for individuals to access their vehicles when necessary.

# Community Libraries Evolve as Digital Hubs in the Modern Age

Public libraries are being remade into crucial online connections to close the digital divide for millions of under-served individuals.

With remote working, online education, and digital service becoming increasingly popular, public libraries have developed beyond their previous role. Today, public libraries provide free broadband access to the Internet, computers, and digital skills training which are essential for those living in poverty.

"As such," states Maria Chen, director of the American Library Association's digital initiatives, "libraries provide access to the digital world through technology, which helps create a level playing field for everyone. Many individuals have no other means of accessing high-speed internet or using a computer."

The transition to a digital environment has had its most substantial impact during the COVID-19 pandemic, with libraries serving as crucial sources of information for students taking online courses and individuals applying for jobs remotely. Many library systems have developed targeted programming that includes coding classes, digital literacy instruction, and support for accessing federal/state government websites and receiving health care virtually.

Librarians are now also digital instructors. Librarians are assisting patrons with all levels of technology use, from basic email to understanding the risks associated with cybersecurity. They know that having a computer and an internet connection does not automatically mean a person is technologically competent.

However, these increased responsibilities stretch further the limited budget resources that exist. Libraries are having difficulty keeping current with state-of-the-art equipment, hiring professionals who have specialized skills, and maintaining an on-going relationship with the rapidly changing world of technology â€” all while dealing with possible reductions in their budgets.

Even with the many obstacles that community libraries face today, they continue to be essential. For example, community libraries are often more cost-effective than private internet service providers or other commercial options. Additionally, community libraries create a nonjudgmental environment where individuals can learn, and also serve as community anchors.

Experts say that in order to remain relevant, libraries must continue to adapt. They can improve what they offer by working together strategically with technology companies, receiving more funding from the government and using new technologies such as VR and AI.

As long as there remains a digital gap between the rich and poor, community libraries will be on the front lines, making sure that regardless of how much money you make or where you come from, you have equal opportunities to access the technology and information needed to survive and succeed in today's digital environment.

The university lecture will undoubtedly be hybrid in the future. Hybridization is an essential step forward for universities to enhance, not reduce, the student experience. Traditionalists may complain about the possibility of losing the traditional in-person lecture; however, this thinking is an obstacle to progress as it is based upon a romanticized idea of how lectures used to take place. Conventional lectures, which are fixed in time and space, can no longer serve the varied requirements of today's students, who often must find ways to combine their studies with employment, family responsibilities or geographic distance.

The hybrid model is a realistic option, providing the best of both worlds by combining live online instruction with asynchronous learning (pre-recorded lectures, interactive modules) and face-to-face interaction. The hybrid approach does not represent a compromise; rather it represents an improvement over traditional forms of instruction. In addition to allowing students to work through the curriculum on their own schedule and review difficult concepts as many times as necessary, asynchronous components provide students with the ability to study during periods of peak cognitive receptivity. Hybrid models allow instructors to use their valuable face-to-face instructional time for interactive, collaborative and individualized instructional strategies such as discussion-based lessons, problem solving workshops and individual feedback sessions â€” the types of instructional strategies typically missing from large, passive lecture hall environments.

In addition to the previous points, the technological foundations of hybrid models promote digital literacy, which is essential in today's workforce. Higher education institutions are required to equip students to operate successfully in a digitally integrated society, therefore using multiple forms of technology throughout the learning process is central to meeting this objective. Rather than reducing the quality of education, a carefully developed hybrid model will allow for increased student autonomy, improved access to educational resources, and eventually lead to a more interactive and successful learning experience than traditional lectures that were typically one-directional. Higher education's future is not just about adapting to technology; it is about utilizing technology as a means to succeed.

Organizations continue to focus on how to retain employees in response to increased competition in the labor market, increasing employee turnover costs, and increasing employee expectations about work/life balance and personal wellness. To help alleviate some of these issues, many organizations have implemented new policies including "unlimited vacation," "discretionary paid time off," or "unlimited paid time off" (PTO). Unlimited vacation policies allow employees to take as much paid time off as they need, with the only limitations being the need for manager approval, meeting the workload requirements of the position, and adhering to company guidelines. Advocates of unlimited vacation policies believe that they demonstrate the organization's confidence in its employees, provide employees with greater flexibility in their schedules, and foster a results-driven workplace environment, which may increase employee loyalty to the organization.

The reasoning behind why organizations offer unlimited vacation is based upon various theoretical approaches found in the literature on organizational studies. For example, Social Exchange Theory posits that when an organization provides its employees with support and flexibility, the employee will respond by being more loyal and less likely to leave. Another approach that supports this idea is Self-Determination Theory. This theory focuses on the importance of providing employees with autonomous work environments. When employees are given the opportunity to make decisions about their time off from work, they may experience higher levels of job satisfaction, control over their lives and improved mental health. Lastly, unlimited vacation may serve as a form of non-monetary compensation. In today's highly competitive labor market, especially within knowledge-based sectors, organizations need to find ways to differentiate themselves in order to attract and retain top talent. Offering unlimited vacation is one way to accomplish this goal.

The relationship between an employee taking as much time off as they want (unlimited PTO) and retaining employees is not always clear-cut. Critics have pointed out that by eliminating the entitlement to a specific number of days of paid time off, there is no longer clarity regarding what constitutes an appropriate amount of time off. If there is ambiguity about how much time off is acceptable to take, then employees may take less time off; particularly in high-performance organizations where employees do not wish to appear less dedicated than their co-workers. Also, in some instances, the responsibility for ensuring that employees are getting sufficient rest and recovery shifts from the organization to the individual employee. Thus, the potential for well-being benefits of unlimited PTO is lost. Therefore, manager behaviors, employee workload levels, team expectations and employee perception of fairness will all likely determine if an organization views unlimited PTO as a valuable benefit or simply a meaningless promise.

This article reviews the use of unlimited vacation time as an effective means of retaining employees through reviewing the current research regarding employee empowerment (autonomy), company support (organizational), employee satisfaction with work-life balance (work-life), and employee intent to leave the organization (turnover intentions). The article provides insight into how unlimited vacation time can be used to positively influence employee loyalty to the company, as opposed to simply being considered an additional benefit provided to employees.

A simple method for meeting others in your community, discovering different authors and developing a consistent social event for your neighbors to attend would be to start a local neighborhood book club.

Start by reaching out to a few people using your local neighborhood email list, social media, flyer distribution, or simply word of mouth. Your goal should be to bring together approximately 6 to 12 individuals. This size will create an environment that encourages lively discussion among participants, yet is small enough that the group is manageable. When you first meet, establish some ground rules regarding frequency of meetings, location of meetings, selection process for books, and expectations for completion of each book.

Select a regular day and time each month to hold your meetings. If it is possible, rotate among the homes of group members to help manage the workload. Alternatively, you could find a location outside of someone's home (e.g., a library, coffee shop, community center, etc.) where you can meet as a group. Occasionally, you may want to provide a virtual option for those who are unable to participate in person.

Select your titles by taking turns picking the titles, or have each member make recommendations for books they would like to read and then vote on which ones to select. When you need to set a limit on the number of pages in the books you will be reading, you can do so. You should try to choose different types of books such as fiction, non-fiction, memoirs, mysteries, etc. Also, include some books written by authors from your area as well as books that are shorter in length. Finally, before everyone leaves the meeting, inform them about the next title and the date of the next meeting.

To facilitate engaging discussions with group members, you should come up with some open-ended questions. These would include: what did each member like, dislike, or find interesting about the book; which characters/ideas were the most believable; and how does this book relate to what is going on in our lives today, or what has happened in our community? You could also consider having different group members take on the role of being the discussion leader for different meetings so that everyone gets to be responsible for leading the discussion.

Create an inviting environment for members. Provide opportunities for members to share their views; however, do not allow anyone to take over the discussion. Members may have other commitments and therefore miss some meetings or complete only a portion of the assigned reading. Adding snacks and beverages will enhance the atmosphere, but keep your responsibilities as host manageable.

The final step is to keep going through regular communication (reminders), recognition of success (celebrating achievements), and occasionally doing something new (themed potluck, author visit, bookstore trip, book swap). A great book club doesn't need perfect attendance, nor does it need to do deep analytical work. Instead, what makes a book club work is being consistent, having a friendly environment, and reading books that make members want to come back.

# 10 Tips for Weekend Batch-Cooking Strategies

I'm not going to sugarcoat it – weeknight cooking is stressful. However, there is one thing that isn't – a freezer/fridge full of pre-made meals. If you want to master the art of weekend batch cooking and still keep your sanity intact, read on.

**1. Choose Simple, Freezer-Friendly Recipes**
Avoid any items which will become soggy or odd when frozen. Gold: roasted meats/poultry, curries, chili and soups.

**2. Plan Your Menu First**
Make a list of exactly what you will be creating prior to going shopping. This can help save money, and it can also help to prevent you from having to say "What did I do that for?" when you are in the middle of preparing the meal.

**3. Prep Everything on Friday Night**
Prep all of your produce (vegetables), measure out your spices, and gather all of the items that will go into making the meal. If you prep these things prior to Saturday morning, you won't have to deal with the headache of dealing with a pile of onion skins.

**4. Use Your Whole Kitchen**
The oven, stove, slow cooker, and rice cooker are all in use at once? That is a master chef's dream. That is the best way to utilize your time.

**5. Double (or Triple) Recipes**
You are going to turn on your oven. So why don't you make a large batch of food, so you can put some away in the freezer for when you need it?

**6. Invest in Quality Containers**
Glass or high quality plastic containers will be your most valuable players. All items should be labeled with the date they were frozen so that you aren't guessing what is in there for the next few weeks.

**7. Cook Proteins First**
Finish cooking your chicken, ground beef, or beans. When they're cooled, you've pretty much nailed it.

**8. Don't Forget About Breakfast**
You may wish to batch-cook your eggs, oatmeal, or breakfast burritos. When Monday comes around, you will be happy that you did.

**9. Clean as You Go**
Yes, while ignoring the sink is easy, having a clean kitchen when you finish will make you feel much better than having to deal with a mountain of dishes on Sunday evening.

**10. Give Yourself Grace**
Sometimes you can achieve your goal, sometimes you have only done part of what you wanted to do, and you will consider this as a success. Either way, this is better than getting takeout on multiple occasions.

Your future self during week nights will be absolutely thriving.

The implementation of financial literacy as a mandatory graduation requirement is critical in order to prepare students to successfully function in today's society. Currently, young adults enter adulthood with many difficult financial decisions—including how to manage their student loans and credit cards; budget; and invest—without having received any formal education regarding those matters. As a result of this lack of knowledge, there are many young adults who find themselves with high-interest debt; poor credit ratings; and ongoing financial insecurity. Through the integration of financial education into the high school curriculum, schools will be able to provide each student with the essential skills required for long-term financial security.

In addition, mandating financial literacy creates social and economic fairness. Children of wealthy parents typically receive some form of financial education through family interactions. On the other hand, children of low-income parents frequently do not have the same opportunity to acquire informal financial literacy. A uniform curriculum provides a level playing field so that each student has the opportunity to develop the necessary life skills to successfully manage money regardless of their family's economic status. Developing these skills will allow young people to end the cycle of poverty within generations and create wealth for themselves.

Opponents could say that adding another graduation requirement will cause schools to become even more overwhelmed with their busy schedules and place additional pressure on limited educational resources. Financial literacy does not have to be taught in its own separate multi-year class; it can easily fit into existing mathematics or social studies programs. Or, a short, one semester class taken in the senior year would provide great benefits to students for practical use while not interfering with the students’ other academic interests.

The ultimate objective of public education is to equip students to lead productive and independent lives. However, being ignorant of the fundamentals of finances has significant personal and societal consequences. Therefore, requiring students to receive financial literacy instruction will ensure that high school graduation represents both an indication of educational accomplishments, as well as a measure of preparation for the real world.

The increasing number of people buying electric vehicles (EVs) has created an issue for residents of many older communities, which was typically avoided by developers when creating new communities. This is because there are very few options for residents of older communities to charge their EVs.

Before there was a need for off-street parking, driveways, or garage spaces to be included in home designs, many historic neighborhoods were constructed. Due to the narrowness of the streets, age of the electrical system, and proximity of the homes, there are multiple issues that can cause home-charging to be problematic. Those that live in these types of neighborhoods and are forced to park their vehicle on the street will often times have to utilize public charging stations. On the other hand, residents that have garages, may have to pay high costs for upgrading their electrical systems.

Cities are addressing the issue using multiple approaches. For example, some cities have installed curbside charging stations in areas where there is little to no available parking on-street. Other cities are evaluating chargers that can be installed on existing street lights or parking meters, which eliminates the need to build additional utility poles and create more construction. In addition, officials in a number of communities are reviewing regulations that permit residents to extend charging cables across sidewalks; however, there are still safety and accessibility concerns.

The transition has created concerns over equality. Those with higher incomes tend to be able to get their own charging stations; however, those that rent and live in multi-family units will have limited options. Advocates of equity suggest that when funding for public charging infrastructure is allocated, it should be done so with an emphasis on low-income neighborhoods whose residents do not have access to private parking spaces (i.e. driveways or garages) instead of placing chargers in newer or more affluent communities.

When historic preservation is added to the equation there is an extra level of difficulty. For example, if you want to install new equipment on a building that has been designated historic or if you are working within a district that has received protection status, you will likely need to go through several additional approval processes. Additionally, utility providers must evaluate if the existing transformers and electrical distribution systems are capable of handling increased demands created by the charging of multiple vehicles simultaneously during overnight hours.

Planners of transportation believe that, despite being faced with numerous challenges, old neighborhoods will be able to adapt to these changes through proper planning. The planners suggest using a combination of on-street charging stations, work place and public charging stations, and providing financial incentives to landlords of multi-family buildings so that they install shared charging equipment.

The speed at which residents experience change will be determined by how quickly they can fund their own local government and develop its infrastructure. Once there are many more people driving electric cars than now, those communities developed prior to the time we began using electric cars will need to upgrade while still maintaining the uniqueness of each community.

# The Constraining Effect of Recommendation Algorithms on Consumer Choice

Recommendation systems have changed the way people find out about products. However, the impact that recommendation systems have made on the consumerâ€™s decision-making process is limited by the fact that they do not increase the number of choices available to consumers; instead, they decrease the number of choices that consumers are exposed to. These systems provide consumers with personalized convenience but at the same time they restrict the amount of variety in the selection of choices that consumers see. In addition, these systems also help to reinforce consumersâ€™ previous choices.

The basic paradox behind algorithms is that while they are designed to understand how users interact with their systems, they also produce "echo chambers," which prevent users from seeing other possibilities. For example, when Netflix recommends movies that you've watched in the past, or Amazon suggests items to purchase because you purchased those same types of items before, both systems have been optimized to provide you with recommendations that will satisfy your needs, as opposed to providing you with opportunities for discovery. As such, most people do not get to experience truly new options that exist beyond the scope of algorithmic predictions. To have real options, people need to be exposed to all possible options, and algorithms intentionally limit people's access to all available options.

Moreover, such systems concentrate market power by favoring those products/vendors that are already well-established. New or specialized items may find it difficult to obtain visibility due to the algorithm's emphasis on engagement metrics and conversion rates. A new author's first book, published through a small independent bookstore, would have little to no opportunity to appear in algorithmic recommendation lists when compared to a bestseller from a major publishing company. Consequently, this creates a "winner take all" dynamic with respect to consumer choice, which tends to lead to increased uniformity among consumers' purchases.

Algorithmic decision makingâ€™s lack of transparency exacerbates this issue. There is no easy way for consumers to know why some options are not visible, nor is there any way for them to know how a ranking system arrived at its decision. Without transparency, consumers do not have the ability to make an informed choice because they cannot see the options that are being presented to them, nor do they understand the logic used to present those options.

Additionally, by utilizing manipulated psychological vulnerabilities, algorithms are able to exploit consumers. Through strategically displaying options that will generate the greatest amount of user interaction with the platform (typically the most exciting or addictive content) algorithms place a greater emphasis on profit generation than on satisfying consumer preferences.

While there is no question that recommendation systems provide convenience, there is also no question that they limit consumer control. Instead of giving consumers choices, they control what choices consumers make based upon their own interest. To truly empower consumers, we need to limit the role of algorithms as mediators between consumers and products, provide greater transparency in how these systems operate, and create spaces where consumers will be exposed to alternative product options they did not anticipate. This is the only way that consumer choice can remain free.

Over the last 20 years there was a dramatic change in the digital media world, characterized by the explosive growth of different forms of communication (platforms) and the massive changes in how we get our news and information. Among all the noise that is created by social media, the declining credibility of traditional news organizations, and the increasing division among people on issues of public concern, we are seeing a new trend: the emergence of independent newsletter writers as credible sources of commentary. In this literature review, I will examine some of the reasons why these independent newsletter writers are gaining so much influence and power in today's media environment, and how the development of new platforms such as Substack, Ghost, and Patreon has given individual journalists, academics, and experts the ability to build direct relationships with their readers without having to go through established media organizations.

Historically, the role of trusted commentator has been largely occupied by columnists in major newspapers, commentators on television news programs, and academics at well-respected universities; these roles have been supported by institutional associations and editorial controls. However, the democratizing nature of the Internet, along with a growing distrust among the general public toward mainstream media narratives, has provided opportunities for alternative viewpoints to emerge. We will explore how the unique characteristics of the newsletter format â€” including the personalized nature of delivery, perceived intimacy, and frequently funded by subscribers model â€” promote a sense of credibility and autonomy that resonates with many readers. Additionally, we will examine how newsletter authors utilize their specialized knowledge and nuanced perspectives to provide detailed analytical reporting and original reporting that distinguishes them from the superficial or sensationalized coverage typically found on other online platforms. In doing so, this review is intended to provide a foundation for an extensive analysis of the newsletter author as a critical and increasingly significant participant in today's public debate.

A 100-mile (century) bike ride is a big goal. To achieve it within 16 weeks, you will need to be consistent with your training, increase the intensity of your workouts over time, and fuel your body correctly. The following training program is based on the assumption that you are already able to comfortably complete a 20-25 mile ride.

**Phase 1: Foundation (Weeks 1–4)**
Build a habit of riding three to four times per week. One of those should be a long ride on the weekend. The long ride can begin at 25 miles during week 1 and will increase to 40 miles by week 4. In addition, you should have two short weekday rides (10-15 miles) that are done at a moderate intensity. Lastly, there can either be a recovery ride or cross-training session as the last component. 

**Phase 2: Endurance Building (Weeks 5–8)**
Maintain your typical Monday-Friday routine, but slightly increase the intensity of your mid-week workouts (intervals, hills) to help develop your aerobic capacity. Increase the length of your Saturday/Sunday long rides from 45 miles during Week 5 to 60 miles during Week 8. These rides will provide you an opportunity to practice on-the-bike nutrition strategies; aim for consumption of 30-60g carbohydrate and 1 bottle of fluid/electrolyte mixture each hour.

**Phase 3: Peak Volume (Weeks 9–12)**
The current phase of your training includes your highest mileage. On weekdays, you can expect to ride between 15 and 25 miles per ride. Your weekend long rides will increase from 65 miles per ride to a maximum of 75 to 80 miles per ride by Week 12. There is no requirement for you to complete a 100-mile ride prior to the event; completing an 80-mile ride demonstrates that you are physically capable of completing the entire distance. 

**Phase 4: Taper and Event (Weeks 13–16)**
Reduce your volume to let your muscles repair while keeping your legs fresh. 
*   **Week 13:** 60-mile long ride.
*   **Week 14:** 45-mile long ride.
*   **Week 15:** 30-mile long ride.
*   **Week 16 (Event Week):** Rest up early in the week. Take a 10-mile ride two days before your event. Rest the day before.

**Top Advice:** Receive a professional bicycle fitting to avoid over-use injuries; get adequate sleep; and avoid consuming anything you have not eaten before, or using any equipment you have not used before, on your competition day.

# 10 Tips for standing desks for home offices

Standing desks have the potential to make your working environment at home feel like it is more flexible, more comfortable, and more energetic. However, to achieve this, you need to be aware of how to use a standing desk properly. To assist you in getting the most out of using a standing desk, here are 10 useful ways to use a standing desk.

1. **Start slowly**  
On your initial try, do not remain standing for the entire day. Start by remaining in a standing position for 15-30 minutes per interval. You will then have an opportunity to extend the length of each of those intervals as you progress.

2. **Keep your monitor at eye level**  
Your screen is at about eye level, which will reduce stress on your neck and help you maintain a better posture.

3. **Adjust your keyboard and mouse**  
The position of your elbow will be slightly below the level of your shoulders, with a slight angle (around 90 degrees) of bending. While typing, try to keep your wrist relatively straight.

4. **Wear supportive shoes**  
Bare feet or poorly fitting slippers can cause discomfort when you are standing. It is best to select a pair of shoes that provides adequate support for your feet, or use an anti-fatigue mat.

5. **Use an anti-fatigue mat**  
Cushioned mats are effective at reducing the strain placed upon your feet, knees, and lower back — particularly when you're standing on hard surfaces.

6. **Move instead of simply standing**  
While on phone calls, you may choose to change positions by shifting your weight, stretching, walking around, or doing some calf raises. It's almost as bad to stand in one spot for hours as it is to sit in one spot for hours.

7. **Alternate positions regularly**  
A good aim is to transition from sitting to standing each half-hour to hour. It would be better for you to listen to what your body needs, as opposed to adhering strictly to a routine.

8. **Keep essentials within reach**  
Arrange your desk so that you can easily reach your keyboard, mouse, phone, and other commonly-used items. Having to continually stretch to obtain these items may result in additional physical discomfort.

9. **Mind your posture**  
Keep your shoulders down, keep your head directly above your spine and equally distribute your body weight among each foot. Do not lean on the desk.

10. **Make movement convenient**  
Keep a bottle of water close by, use walking meetings if you can, and try using a small foot rest or balance board to change up your routine.

A great standing desk setup will offer you a wider variety of options during your work hours and allow you to make changes to your position before physical discomfort occurs.

Mentorship is the cornerstone of remote apprentice programs because it fills the void left by the physical separation of mentor and student which would otherwise undermine the quality of the learning process. In a conventional setting, students gain knowledge from their mentors simply by being near them – watching how they use their tools, listening to them talk about solving problems, and being corrected when they make errors. However, since there are no unplanned opportunities for remote students to observe and learn from their mentors, intentional mentorship becomes even more important than it would be in an on-site program.

In an online setting, a good mentor will establish the structure that would normally occur naturally. For example, they will schedule regular meetings with the student, explain how they think about problems while sharing their screen, and provide an avenue for students to ask questions that could easily be asked as people pass each other. Rather than being just someone who the student can watch, the mentor is now intentionally creating the learning environment.

Building trust has a large role to play in building relationships. Because of the lack of opportunities for informal conversation (i.e. hallways, lunch), mentors will need to spend more time establishing a safe environment for apprentices to share their thoughts and feelings about their work. Mentors can do this by modeling transparency and check-ins regarding both professional and personal well-being.

In addition to connecting mentees with other professionals within the company (which would normally be done in person), remote mentors may also help introduce mentees to broader professional networks. Since remote apprentices cannot physically participate in company events or meetings, mentors will need to find creative ways to provide those opportunities. Some examples of how remote mentors can facilitate connections to larger professional networks include: introducing mentees to colleagues, inviting mentees to participate in virtual meetings outside of their assigned responsibilities, and advocating on behalf of mentees for increased visibility throughout the organization.

In the end, mentoring in remote apprenticeships evolves from being a natural result of working in close proximity to becoming a more purposeful and organized system of practices. Although this requires more thought and planning on the part of the mentor, if it is executed properly, it can provide for more significant, thoughtful learning connections between the mentor and mentee.

Experts say that while governments around the world are rushing to create new laws regulating facial recognition technology, both current and proposed regulations have fallen behind the fast-paced development of the technology itself. 

From the European Union's pioneering Artificial Intelligence Act, to local government prohibitions on the use of real-time biometric surveillance by police departments throughout the U.S., there has been a significant focus by governments on regulating public-sector deployment of AI technology. Specifically, governments are restricting the ability of law enforcement agencies to use real-time biometric surveillance. On the other hand, many legal scholars and technology experts contend that these restrictions create a false sense of security while leaving large gaps in the regulation of AI technologies.

One major barrier is that the technology has become so common. Facial recognition is now used in more places than just high resolution cameras on street lights. Private security systems, retail analysis, smart phone apps, and social media sites use facial recognition as well. Current laws have difficulty dealing with the spread of the technology into the private sector. Consumers are frequently asked to give their consent through long terms-of-service agreements which most consumers sign off on without ever reading.

In addition, the ability for companies to develop and deploy biometric software products on a global scale is hindered by the jurisdictional limitations that exist regarding the enforcement of privacy laws. Because biometric data can easily cross national boundaries, it is possible for developers of biometric software products to use training data from countries where there are fewer restrictions on how companies collect, store, and process personal information. Once the developer trains the algorithm using this training data, they may then deploy the product in other countries where there are stricter rules regarding the collection, storage, and processing of personal information. Mandating that companies provide transparency regarding what types of training data they collect and use (e.g., disclosing the source of the training data) are often met with resistance due to company trade secrets.

The advent of new technology presents a larger problem than ever before. Generative AI and synthetic biometrics have made it difficult to tell what is real from what is fake when viewing pictures. Therefore, what was previously defined as a "biometric identifier" in most laws is now obsolete. Due to the speed at which technology advances, by the time a law is proposed, created, and implemented, the technology that was used as the basis for the law has likely changed, making the law useless.

While some cities have banned the use of facial recognition by their local police departments, experts say these types of bans are only a temporary solution to the larger problem. Piece-meal regulation of this type of technology cannot prevent a globally commercialized technology from being used. Therefore, without a global standard for how to regulate private commercial use of this technology, as well as the underlying algorithms that make it work, the technology will grow at a much faster rate than the regulations intended to control it.

Community Supported Fisheries (CSFs) are an innovative way of supplying seafood to consumers. CSFs work by connecting consumers directly with local fishers, eliminating traditional long supply chains. They are based on Community Supported Agriculture (CSA). CSFs typically involve consumers investing in advance by buying shares of the catch of a fishing enterprise. This helps provide fishers with capital, stable prices and a guaranteed market. Consumers benefit by receiving fresh seafood, with traceability, and often sustainably sourced. The idea of CSFs has been around since the early 2000s in the US. More recently they have been popularised throughout North American coastal regions, and to a lesser extent, Europe and the rest of the world. This follows increased consumer demand for knowing where their food comes from, environmentally sustainable options and supporting local businesses.

The topic of CSFs has become increasingly popular among researchers across different disciplines. Many researchers have looked into CSFs for many reasons. For example looking at how they help small scale fishing communities become economically viable. They also look at how they encourage sustainable management of fisheries. Finally they look at how they represent alternative food networks. Despite the increase in literature surrounding CSFs there are still many issues which need to be addressed. These include understanding the long term viability of CSFs, environmental impact and conservation benefits.

This review has brought together research surrounding community supported fisheries to understand what we currently know about its origin, structure and effect on fishers, consumers and the marine environment. It will evaluate previous research to understand its strengths and weaknesses. This will show key themes within research, the methods used and any areas to be addressed within future research.

# Paint your kitchen in a day!

## Friday Evening

Empty everything out of your kitchen. Take all hardware off of your cabinets, lights and appliances. Cover your countertops, floors and any leftover fixtures with drop cloths and plastic to protect them.

## Saturday Morning

Clean your surfaces well with trisodium phosphate (TSP). Once everything is clean leave to dry. Any stained areas or dark walls should be primed. You will also want to sand any glossy areas so that paint can stick. This will create a good base to paint.

## Saturday Afternoon

Start painting! Begin by painting the ceiling and top of the walls. Use a roller for these areas to make it easier. Then paint around the trim and detailed areas with a brush. Buy good quality paint as this will give you better coverage and last longer. Leave the paint to dry properly between coats. It will usually take around 4-6 hours to dry depending on humidity.

## Sunday

Paint your second coat. You may wish to paint your doors and trim. Use painters tape to get nice clean lines around your windows and skirtings. When removing the tape leave it while the paint is still slightly sticky.

## Sunday Evening/Monday

Once everything is fully dry place your lights and cabinet hardware back in. Put your appliances back. Be careful when removing any protection.

## Top Tips

Buy everything you need on Thursday to save you time.

Use good quality low VOC paints.

Invest in good quality brushes and rollers. They really make a difference.

Have a damp cloth to hand to wipe up any mess.

Make sure there is plenty of ventilation.

By having a good plan and working efficiently you will have a brand new painted kitchen by Monday morning!

10 Tips for creating an effective evening routine.

You aren’t the only person who may feel like they can’t switch off at 10pm. We often become very busy during the day and struggle to fully unwind during the evening. Getting a good nights sleep is key and having a wind down routine will really help.

Here are 10 tips for creating an effective wind down routine.

Set a digital curfew. Decide on a time where you will turn off any screens. This should be at least an hour before bedtime. Blue light can affect melatonin.

Turn your lights down. As it gets dark outside turn your lights down to signal to your brain that you need to wind down.

Have a warm bath/shower. This will help to relax your muscles and your body temperature will drop slightly after.

Read a physical book. A physical book will help you to relax and won’t distract you.

Get ready for the next day. Lay out your clothes and pack your bag. This will help to reduce any decisions you have to make in the morning.

Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time. Our bodies love consistency.

It should be prioritised to provide more cycle lanes, than parking across cities. Whilst parking does provide a convenient service for drivers, public roads should be focused on providing a service to a wider range of people.

Cycle lanes can help reduce accidents within traffic, promote exercise and make cycling accessible to children, elderly and those who do not have a car. Cycle lanes can also help cities improve air pollution and reduce green house gas emissions. On busy areas, providing cycle lanes can allow more people to travel without contributing to congestion. Providing cycle lanes can also benefit local businesses as cyclists are often high frequent visitors that help local shops. Eye-catching roads can also boost business.

However it is important to consider those with disabilities, delivery workers, tradesmen and those who really do require their cars. With an intelligent policy in place, there can still be spaces for disabled access, loading bays and a small amount of short term parking. Improving public transport and implementing a permit or payment system can help ensure there isn’t too much free parking along the roads which is taking up precious public land.

Ultimately it depends on the area. If the cycle lane would not be useful due to being isolated, dangerous at junctions or there would not be much need for cycling there then it would be better to not provide one. Officials should research traffic flow, consult the relevant communities and monitor how effective it is. However, in busy urban areas the long term benefits to the public from having safe cycling usually outweigh having lots of convenient parking. Cycle lanes should be prioritised within a wider transport strategy however reasonable options should be provided for those who require their cars.

How Community Libraries Have Adapted to Become Digital Hubs

Community libraries are adapting to become a crucial source of digital access.

With more people working remote, studying online and accessing digital services, community libraries have evolved into providing a range of services such as free super-fast internet, computers and digital skills to those in hardship.

"Libraries are providing access to technology to everyone. For many people they are the only place they can access reliable internet and computers." said Maria Chen, director of digital initiatives at the American Library Association.

This has been especially beneficial during the pandemic with many students using the libraries for online classes and those looking for jobs using them to apply for roles remotely. Many libraries have now specific services such as coding classes, digital skills and help with government sites and telehealth.

Librarians have adapted to also provide digital coaching. They help people with learning how to use emails to understanding cyber security.

However, libraries are struggling to keep up with their limited budgets. They find it difficult to keep up with the latest technology, employ specialised staff and keep up with how quickly technology is advancing.

Despite this, community libraries are still extremely valuable. They are an affordable alternative to paying for internet and computer labs, provide a judgement free environment and are still a hub within the community.

Going forward they need to adapt. By partnering with technology companies, increasing government funding and incorporating new technologies such as virtual reality and artificial intelligence they can provide better services.

Community libraries are on the front line to ensure that everyone can access the tools they need to thrive in today’s world, regardless of their income.

The future is definitely hybrid. Whilst there are definitely purists who will be saddened by losing the traditional lecture, this is an unrealistic way of looking at things. Traditional lectures lack flexibility meaning they do not fit with the varied lifestyles of modern students. Many students have other commitments whilst studying so cannot attend a lecture at a specific time and place.

Hybrid learning can help solve this problem. Lectures can become a mixture of live online sessions, self-paced learning, and focussed face-to-face sessions. Self-paced learning means students can take their time to understand tricky concepts. They can revisit the material and learn at their own pace. This means they can make the most out of their face-to-face sessions where they can participate in more interactive tasks, such as in depth discussions, problem solving, and feedback sessions.

Having the technology available to offer hybrid learning develops students’ digital skills. It is our responsibility to teach students how to work in a digital world. Using a variety of online tools helps us achieve this. A well planned hybrid learning approach can lead to more independent students, increase accessibility and can create a more engaging learning environment. The future of Higher Education is definitely going to thrive with the use of technology.

Employee retention is an important issue for organisations due to increasing competition within the labour market. To help retain employees, many have introduced policies such as unlimited holiday. This allows employees to take the amount of paid holidays they want. Compared to standard policies, which provide employees with set amounts of holiday per year, unlimited holiday can allow employees to feel trusted, empowered and encourages them to be performance orientated.

Unlimited holiday can help retain employees due to various theories. The social exchange theory suggests that if employees feel valued and given flexibility they will be more loyal to the organisation. The self determination theory suggests that people are motivated by feeling empowered. Giving employees more flexible holiday may make them feel more in control, increasing satisfaction and psychological wellbeing. It may also serve as a token benefit to help attract new employees. This is often used in knowledge based industries where flexibility is important to employees.

However, there can be issues around unlimited holiday. Removing holiday entitlement can cause confusion around how much holiday should be taken. If employees do not know how much they should be taking they may not take as much. In a high performing culture, employees may feel they will look less committed to the organisation compared to their colleagues. In some cases unlimited PTO can cause the responsibility of taking breaks to fall on the employee. This will negate any benefits it could have had on wellbeing. How managers act, workload, team norms and fairness will most likely affect whether employees see unlimited holiday as a real benefit.

This literature review looks at unlimited holiday policies and how they can help retain employees. It looks at how giving employees flexibility can help create a supportive environment, whilst also looking at the benefits and limitations of using this method. It will look at how unlimited holiday can help create long term commitment from employees.

Start a book club in your neighbourhood to make new friends, try new authors and have a regular get together.

Start by contacting a few people to begin with. Using your neighbourhood email lists, social media, posters or just word of mouth. Six to twelve people is ideal to make sure you have enough people to keep conversations going but not too many to cause issues. At your first meet up set some ground rules about when you are going to meet, where you will meet, how you are going to choose your books and if everyone is expected to read the whole book.

Set a regular time, maybe the first Thursday of every month. Take it in turns to host or meet at a neutral place like a library, coffee shop, community centre or in a park. You could also do an online version occasionally.

Take it in turns to pick the books or have a vote. If needed set a page limit. Try to mix it up between different genres, authors and viewpoints. Read some popular fiction, non-fiction, memoirs, mysteries, local authors and shorter books. Tell everyone when you will be reading your next book and when your next meet up will be.

Set a few discussion questions to get them thinking. Ask them what they liked/disliked, were they surprised by anything? Which characters or ideas did they believe the most? How does this relate to their lives now? Having someone to lead the discussion each time can help.

Be friendly and flexible. Let people have their own opinions and don’t let one person take over. People may not always be able to make it or read the whole book. Have some snacks and drinks to make it feel more friendly but keep it simple to host.

Keep them motivated by reminding them, celebrating any achievements and mixing things up occasionally. Maybe do a theme night, author chat, visit a book store or do a swap. Your book club doesn’t need to be perfect, you just need to be consistent, friendly and have books to keep people coming back.

# The Limitation of Choices With Recommendation Algorithms

Despite recommendation algorithms changing how consumers find products, they are limiting their choices. These algorithms can make your choices more specific but ultimately limit the variety.

Recommendation algorithms work by learning about your behaviour, creating an echo chamber. Netflix suggesting similar movies to what you watched or Amazon suggesting products you might like based off what you bought will always suggest what you will be happiest with. This means consumers won’t be presented with any new choices. To have true choice you need to have a variety of options and recommendation algorithms do the opposite.

These algorithms also mean that there is less variety in the market. Recommendation algorithms tend to only recommend popular products and sellers. This means new or less popular products won’t be recommended. A small book shop won’t have any chance of having their first novel recommended whereas a well-known publisher would have a best-selling novel. This creates a monopoly effect meaning there isn’t much variety in consumer choices.

The lack of transparency makes it harder for consumers to know why certain products aren’t being shown. To make an informed choice you need to know what options you have.

Recommendation algorithms take advantage of peoples weaknesses. They will show you options that will keep you engaged. This means they aren’t trying to make you happy with your choices but instead trying to make money.

Whilst recommendation algorithms can be convenient they do have a cost. They do limit your choices as they are making your choices based off corporate wants. To truly empower consumers there needs to be less algorithms, more transparency and areas where people can be presented with unexpected choices.

To train for a century/100mile cycle you need to be consistent and gradually build up. Assuming you can easily cycle 20-25 miles.

Phase 1 – Base Weeks (Weeks 1-4)

Try to get into a habit of cycling 3-4 times per week. Two shorter sessions during the week (10-15 miles), one easy ride or other training session. One longer ride on the weekend. During week 1 you will begin your longer ride at 25 miles, building up by 5 miles each week until week 4 when you will hit 40 miles.

Phase 2 – Build Up Weeks (Weeks 5-8)

Keep doing your shorter sessions as mentioned. However you can begin to build up your mid-week rides by doing some hill work or intervals. On your longer rides at the weekend you will begin to push further. Starting at 45 miles in week 5, building up to 60 miles in week 8. These longer rides are also good to practice your riding nutrition. Try to consume 30-60g of carbs and a bottle of water/electrolytes every hour.

Phase 3 – High Volume Weeks (Weeks 9-12)

These will be your highest mileage weeks. Mid-week rides should be between 15-25 miles. Longer rides on the weekend will start from 65 miles, building up to a high of 75-80 miles in week 12. You do not need to do 100 miles before the event. As you have hit 80 miles you know you have the stamina to complete the distance.

Phase 4 – Taper and Event (Weeks 13-16)

Reduce your mileage so that your muscles can recover.

Week 13 – Long Ride 60 miles

Week 14 – Long Ride 45 miles

Week 15 – Long Ride 30 miles

Week 16 (Event Week) – Early in the week take a rest and do a gentle 10 mile spin 2 days before. Take a rest the day before.

Tips – Get your bike fitted by a professional to avoid injury from overuse. Make sure you get enough sleep. Do not try new food or equipment on the day of the event.

10 Tips for using a Standing Desk at Home

Standing desks can make your home workspace more versatile, comfortable and invigorating. Here are some top tips to make the most out of your standing desk:

Start with short periods of time

Avoid standing too long for your first go. Try short 15-30 minute sessions and build up over time.

Monitor height

Ensure that your screen is at eye level to avoid any strain on your neck.

Keyboard & Mouse

Ensure that your elbows are tucked in and at approximately 90 degrees. Ensure your wrists are straight.

Shoes

Standing with bare feet or no support can cause discomfort. Ensure you have some comfortable shoes. Alternatively use an anti-fatigue mat.

Anti-fatigue Mat

Using a cushioned mat will reduce pressure on your feet, knees and lower back. This is particularly useful if you have hard flooring.

Move!

Try shifting your weight, stretching, walking around whilst on a call or doing a few calf raises. If you are standing still for long periods of time it won’t really be much better than sitting.

Change positions

Try to alternate between seated and standing every 30-60 minutes. Listen to your body.

Organise your desk

Ensure that everything you need is easily reachable (keyboard, mouse, phone etc). Constant reaching can cause new aches.

Posture

Ensure your shoulders are relaxed, your head is balanced above your spine, and your weight is evenly distributed across both feet. Don’t lean on your desk.

Easy to move

Ensure you have a water bottle to hand, try to have walking meetings and consider using a small footrest or balancing board.

The best way to set up your standing desk is to give yourself more choice throughout the day and to change positions before you get any discomfort.

Governments around the globe are scrambling to introduce legislation around facial recognition. But experts say current and planned laws simply aren’t keeping up.

Across the world, from the EU’s groundbreaking Artificial Intelligence Act to local bans in the U.S., the focus has been on banning or limiting the use of real time biometric facial recognition by law enforcement in the public sector. However, experts in law and tech say this is creating a ‘false sense of security’.

The main issue is how widespread this technology is. Facial recognition is now being used everywhere from high definition police cameras on street lights to private security, in shops, on apps and social media. Current laws are struggling to address its expansion in the private sector, many times there are no clear consent forms that are readable by consumers.

There can also be issues with enforcement due to the nature of the technology. Biometric data is easy to transfer across borders. Developers can train their AI in areas with low privacy regulations but then apply it to their product worldwide. Many attempts to enforce more transparency such as forcing companies to tell consumers what they have trained their AI on often fail due to companies wanting to protect their trade secrets.

With the rise in generative AI and fake biometrics, it has become increasingly difficult to tell what is a genuine image and what isn’t. This means traditional laws often fail to define what biometric identifiers are. By the time a law is debated, written and put into place, the technology will have changed.

Whilst banning certain uses could help reduce over use by police in certain cities, experts say this won’t stop the global, commercialised technology. Without global, comprehensive laws around the use of this technology in the private sector along with the algorithm itself, facial recognition will grow at a much faster rate then the laws trying to stop it.
