# Repaint Your Kitchen in a Weekend

## Preparation (Friday Evening)

Get your kitchen ready for a makeover. Start by emptying it out - take down any hardware from the cabinets, and remove light fixtures and appliances if you can. Cover up your countertops, floors, and any fixtures that are staying with drop cloths and plastic sheets. This will save you a lot of hassle when it comes to cleaning up, and protect your space from any damage.

## Priming and Cleaning (Saturday Morning)

To get a smooth finish, start by giving all surfaces a good clean with TSP - that's trisodium phosphate - to get rid of any grease or grime that might be lurking. Let it dry completely, don't rush it. If you've got any stained areas or walls that were previously dark, now's the time to apply some primer. And if you're dealing with glossy surfaces, just lightly sand them to help the paint stick. Doing this groundwork will make all the difference and give you professional-looking results.

## First Paint Coat (Saturday Afternoon)

When you're painting, start with the ceiling and the upper parts of the walls - a roller is the best tool for this, it gets the job done quickly. For the trim and any areas that need a bit more detail, switch to a brush. Don't skimp on the paint, either - good quality paint might cost a bit more, but it covers better and lasts a lot longer. And be patient, make sure you leave enough time for each coat to dry properly, usually around 4-6 hours, depending on how humid it is.

## Second Coat and Details (Sunday)

Now it's time to add a second coat of paint to your walls and ceiling. If you want, you can also paint the doors and trim - it's up to you. To get nice, sharp lines around your windows and baseboards, use some painter's tape. And here's a tip: take the tape off while the paint is still a bit sticky, and you'll get really crisp edges.

## Final Touches (Sunday Evening to Monday)

Reinstall light fixtures and cabinet hardware once paint is completely dry. Return appliances to their locations. Remove protective coverings carefully to avoid dragging dust onto fresh paint.

## Pro Tips

- Purchase supplies Thursday to avoid weekend shopping delays
- Use low-VOC paint for better air quality
- Invest in quality brushes and rollers—they make a visible difference
- Keep a damp cloth handy for quick cleanup
- Ensure proper ventilation throughout the process

By the time Monday morning rolls around, your kitchen can be totally transformed - all it takes is a bit of planning and some hard work to get the job done. With a fresh coat of paint, your kitchen will be looking brand new and ready to go for the week ahead.

## 10 Tips for Building a Focused Evening Wind-Down Routine

Do you often lie awake at night, feeling wide awake and struggling to calm down? You're definitely not the only one. With our packed schedules, it's easy for the stress of the day to carry over into the evening, making it hard to unwind before bed. But getting a good night's sleep is really crucial for our well-being, and having a relaxing bedtime routine can make all the difference - it's like a secret ingredient that helps you switch off and prepare your body for a restful night's sleep.

Here are 10 tips to help you build a focused evening routine and drift off more easily:

1. **Switch off your screens on time**: Try to put away your phones, tablets, and laptops at least an hour before bedtime. You see, the blue light from these devices can really interfere with your body's production of melatonin, the hormone that helps you sleep.
2. **Dim the Lights:** When night starts to fall, turn down the lights inside. This helps your brain know it's time to unwind and relax. It's like a signal that says, "okay, it's time to slow down now."
3. **Warm Bath or Shower:** Taking a warm bath or shower can really help you unwind and relax your muscles. It's also a great way to lower your body temperature a bit, which is perfect for getting a good night's sleep.
4. **Read a Physical Book:** Ditch the e-reader and pick up a good old-fashioned paper book. It's calming and distraction-free.
5. **Gentle Stretching or Yoga:** Doing some simple stretches can really help you relax and feel better. It's a great way to release tension without getting you all pumped up. Just a few slow moves can make a big difference.
6. **Herbal Tea Time:** If you're feeling stressed, try a calming cup of chamomile or lavender tea - it can be really soothing. Just remember to steer clear of anything with caffeine in it.
7. **Journal Your Thoughts:** If your mind races, jot down your worries or to-dos. Get them out of your head and onto paper.
8. **Try Relaxing with Some Music or a Podcast**: You can listen to instrumental music, sounds from nature, or a podcast with a soft, storytelling style - these can be really great for unwinding.
9. **Get Ready for Tomorrow:** Take a few minutes to pick out your outfit and pack your bag tonight. This simple trick can make a big difference in the morning - fewer things to worry about and less stress to start your day.
10. ** Consistent Bedtime:** Our bodies love routine. Try to go to bed and wake up around the same time every day, even on weekends.

Making new habits stick can be tough, so don't get discouraged if it takes a while. Start by adding one or two small changes to your daily routine each week and see what works for you. Before you know it, you'll be sleeping better and feeling more confident - and that's the key to making lasting changes, so get ready to catch some sweet dreams!

For example, kids, older people, and those who don't have cars can all use these lanes to get around. Plus, they can help reduce pollution and make the air cleaner. # Community Libraries Evolve as Digital Hubs in the Modern Age

Community libraries are reinventing themselves as essential digital access points, bridging the technology gap for millions of underserved residents.

As remote work, online education, and digital services become increasingly prevalent, public libraries have expanded far beyond their traditional roles. Today, these institutions offer free high-speed internet, computer access, and digital literacy programs that prove vital for economically disadvantaged populations.

"Libraries are democratizing access to technology," says Maria Chen, director of the American Library Association's digital initiatives. " For many people, the library is their only gateway to reliable internet and computers."

Libraries have become really important, especially during the pandemic. They helped students with online classes and people looking for jobs with remote applications. Now, many libraries offer special programs like teaching people how to code, how to use the internet safely, and how to access government websites and online health services. This change has made libraries a vital part of the community, providing essential support to those in need. By offering these programs, libraries are not only helping people access information but also bridging the gap in digital literacy. As a result, libraries are no longer just places to borrow books, but hubs for learning and connection.

Beyond hardware and internet access, librarians have become digital coaches. Staff members help patrons navigate everything from email basics to cybersecurity awareness, recognizing that technological access alone doesn't guarantee digital competence.

However, this expanded mission strains already-limited budgets. Libraries struggle to maintain cutting-edge equipment, hire specialized staff, and keep pace with rapidly evolving technology—all while facing potential funding cuts.

Community libraries are still really important, even with all the challenges they face. They give people a cheaper way to get online and use computers, and they're a safe space where anyone can learn without feeling judged. Plus, they're still the heart of the community, bringing people together and providing a sense of belonging.

As we move ahead, it's clear that libraries need to keep changing with the times. By teaming up with tech companies, getting more funding from the government, and using new technologies like virtual reality and artificial intelligence, they can offer even more to their communities. This can help libraries stay relevant and provide better services to people.

As the digital divide persists, community libraries stand at the frontline, ensuring that everyone—regardless of income or background—has equitable access to the tools and knowledge necessary to thrive in an increasingly digital world.

This can lead to employees taking less vacation time, especially in workplaces where everyone is really driven and people don't want to seem like they're not trying as hard as their coworkers. In some cases, having unlimited vacation time can actually put the responsibility on the employee to make sure they're taking time off to rest and recover, rather than the company making sure they have a good work-life balance. So, things like how managers behave, how much work everyone has to do, what's considered normal in the team, and whether everyone feels like they're being treated fairly can all affect whether unlimited vacation time is seen as a real benefit or just something that sounds good but doesn't really mean anything.

This study looks at how offering unlimited vacation time can help keep employees from leaving their jobs. It brings together research on how much control employees have over their work, how much support they get from their organization, how well they balance work and life, and whether they plan to quit. The goal is to figure out if unlimited vacation time really helps employees feel committed to their company for the long haul, or if it's just a nice-sounding benefit that doesn't actually make a difference. The study also considers the good and not-so-good things about these policies, and tries to pinpoint the conditions under which they can really work to keep employees engaged.

Starting a neighborhood book club is a simple way to meet people, discover new authors, and create a regular gathering that neighbors look forward to.

To get started, reach out to a few people in your neighborhood through email, social media, or by putting up flyers. You can also just tell your friends and family about it. Try to get a small group together, around 6-12 people, so you can have some great conversations without it getting too crazy. At your first meeting, figure out the basics: how often you'll meet, where you'll hang out, how you'll pick books, and if everyone needs to finish the book before you discuss it.

To make your book club work, pick a regular meeting time, like the first Thursday of each month. You can take turns hosting at each other's homes, or meet at a library, café, or community center - even a park is a great spot. And don't forget about members who can't make it in person - having a virtual option every now and then is a good idea.

For book selection, take turns choosing titles or let members nominate books and vote. Set a page limit when necessary, and vary the genres, authors, and perspectives. Include popular fiction, nonfiction, memoirs, mysteries, local authors, and shorter works. Announce the next title and meeting date before everyone leaves.

To get a good conversation going, think about some questions that will make people think. You could ask what people liked or didn't like about the book, what surprised them, or which characters seemed the most real. It's also a good idea to talk about how the book relates to what's happening in the world right now or in your own community. Having someone different lead the discussion each time can help spread the work around and keep things interesting.

To make your club a comfortable space for everyone, be open to different views and try to avoid letting one person take over the conversations. It's also important to be understanding when members can't make it to a meeting or haven't finished the book. Adding some snacks and drinks can make things more welcoming, but don't feel like you need to go overboard with hosting duties. Keep things simple and relaxed, so everyone feels at ease. This way, your club can be a place where people feel free to share their thoughts and enjoy each other's company.

To keep your club going strong, make sure to remind everyone what's happening and celebrate the good times. It's also a great idea to mix things up a bit - like having a potluck with a fun theme, listening to an author talk, visiting a bookstore, or swapping books with each other. The key to a successful club isn't that everyone shows up every time or that you have super deep discussions - it's just about being consistent, being friendly, and picking books that people actually want to read and talk about.

# 10 Tips for Weekend Batch-Cooking Strategies

Let's be real—weeknight dinners are chaos. But you know what isn't? A fridge stocked with pre-made meals. Here's how to nail weekend batch cooking without losing your mind.

**1. Choose Simple, Freezer-Friendly Recipes**
Skip anything that gets soggy or weird after freezing. Curries, chili, soups, and roasted proteins? Gold.

**2. Plan Your Menu First**
Before you head out to buy ingredients, take a minute to write down exactly what you're planning to make. This simple step can save you money and prevent those frustrating moments when you're halfway through cooking and wonder what you were thinking.

**3. Prep Everything on Friday Night**
Get your ingredients ready, chop up those veggies, and measure out your spices. It's a good idea to do this ahead of time, so when Saturday morning rolls around, you won't be overwhelmed with a mess of onion peels and other clutter.

**4. Use Your Whole Kitchen**
Oven, stovetop, slow cooker, and rice cooker working simultaneously? Chef's kiss. This is how you maximize your time.

**5. Double (or Triple) Recipes**
You're already heating the oven anyway. Make enough to freeze portions for later.

**6. Invest in Quality Containers**
Glass or quality plastic containers are your MVPs. Label everything with dates so you're not playing freezer roulette in three weeks.

**7. Cook Proteins First**
Get your chicken, ground beef, or beans done early. Once those are cooling, you've basically won.

**8. Don't Forget About Breakfast**
Batch-cook egg muffins, oatmeal, or breakfast burritos too. Future you will be so grateful Monday morning.

**9. Clean as You Go**
Yeah, it's tempting to ignore the sink, but finishing with a clean kitchen beats facing Mount Dishmore on Sunday night.

**10. Give Yourself Grace**
Some days you'll get everything just right, while other days you'll be lucky to whip up a single decent meal - and that's okay, because let's be honest, it's still a lot better than relying on takeout for every dinner.

Your future self during week nights will be absolutely thriving.

As electric vehicle ownership rises, residents in older neighborhoods are confronting a challenge that newer developments were often designed to avoid: where to charge.

In the past, many neighborhoods were built without considering the need for garages, driveways, or off-street parking. As a result, the streets are often narrow, the electrical systems are outdated, and the homes are closely packed together, making it a challenge to charge electric vehicles at home. For people who have to park their cars on the street, they usually have to use public charging stations. On the other hand, those who have garages may still face problems, like having to pay for expensive electrical upgrades to make their homes charging-friendly. This can be a big issue for people who want to own electric vehicles but live in older communities.

Cities are coming up with different ways to deal with this issue. For example, some are putting charging stations right on the curb in areas where people don't have a lot of space to park off the street. Others are trying out chargers that are built into streetlights or parking meters, which means they don't need to put up new poles or do a lot of construction. In some communities, officials are also looking at the rules that let people run charging cables across the sidewalk, but they're still worried about safety and making sure everyone can get around easily.

The shift to electric vehicles has raised concerns about fairness. People with more money can easily install their own chargers at home, but those who rent or live in apartments often don't have that option. Supporters argue that the government should focus on putting chargers in neighborhoods where people don't have driveways or garages, rather than putting them in newer or richer areas. This way, everyone has a chance to use electric vehicles, not just the wealthy. It's not fair that some people have more access to chargers just because of where they live. The goal should be to make electric vehicles available to everyone, regardless of their income or where they live.

Preserving old buildings and areas can make things more complicated. When you want to put in new equipment, like charging stations, in older buildings or neighborhoods that are protected, you often need to get extra approvals. Also, the companies that provide electricity have to figure out if the existing transformers and power lines can handle the extra energy needed, especially since a lot of people tend to charge their cars at night.

Despite the obstacles, transportation planners say older neighborhoods can adapt with careful planning. They recommend combining curbside stations, workplace and public charging, and incentives for apartment owners to add shared equipment.

As people start using more electric vehicles, neighborhoods will have to update their systems to keep up. But they also need to make sure they don't lose what makes them special. The speed of this change will depend on how much money is available locally and what kind of infrastructure is already in place. This is a big challenge for communities that were built a long time ago, before anyone thought about charging cars. They need to find a way to modernize without changing the things that make them unique and interesting.

# The Constraining Effect of Recommendation Algorithms on Consumer Choice

Recommendation algorithms have fundamentally altered how consumers discover products, yet their pervasive influence actually narrows rather than expands genuine choice. While these systems promise personalized convenience, they ultimately limit the diversity of options consumers encounter and reinforce existing preferences in problematic ways.

Algorithms work in a way that seems a bit strange: they learn what you like and then only show you things that are similar. For example, when you're browsing Netflix, it recommends movies that are like the ones you've already watched. Or, when you're shopping on Amazon, it suggests products that are similar to the ones you've bought before. The problem with this is that it doesn't give you a chance to discover new things that you might like, but that aren't like what you've chosen before. This means you're not really getting to choose from all the options that are out there - the algorithm is limiting what you see. To really have a choice, you need to be able to see all the possibilities, not just the ones that the algorithm thinks you'll like.

These systems actually make it harder for new products to get noticed. They favor things that are already popular, so small businesses or unique items have a tough time getting seen. Imagine a small bookstore trying to promote a new novel - it's unlikely to show up in recommendations when compared to a bestselling book from a big publisher. This creates a situation where everyone ends up choosing the same things, and individual choices become less diverse. As a result, the market becomes dominated by a few big players, making it even harder for new entrants to break in. This can lead to a lack of variety and innovation, which isn't good for consumers in the long run.

The opacity of algorithmic decision-making compounds this problem. Consumers cannot easily understand why certain options are hidden from view or how rankings were determined. This absence of transparency undermines informed choice, which requires understanding the available alternatives and the reasoning behind their presentation.

Algorithms can take advantage of people's weaknesses by manipulating them. They do this by showing users options that are meant to keep them engaged, like sensational or addictive content, rather than giving them what they really want. This is because algorithms are designed to make money, not to truly satisfy consumers. They prioritize profit over people's actual preferences, which can be a problem.

When we use recommendation systems, they might make things easier for us, but they also take away some of our freedom to choose. Instead of giving us real options, they guide us towards what companies want us to pick. To really have control over our choices, we need to reduce the influence of algorithms and be more open about how they work. We also need to keep some spaces where we can discover new things by chance. Only then can we say we're really free to choose what we want.

To get ready for a big 100-mile bike ride in just 16 weeks, you need to be consistent and keep pushing yourself. This training plan is for people who can already ride 20-25 miles without too much trouble.

**Phase 1: Foundation (Weeks 1–4)**
To get started, aim to ride your bike three or four times a week. Try to do two shorter rides during the week, like 10 to 15 miles, and keep a moderate pace. You should also have one day for a recovery ride or try something different like cross-training. Then, on the weekends, plan a longer ride. Start with 25 miles on your first weekend and add 5 miles each week. By the time you get to week 4, you should be up to 40 miles. This will help you build up your endurance and make progress with your riding routine.

**Phase 2: Endurance Building (Weeks 5–8)**
To boost your cardiovascular power, try to stick to your usual weekday routine, but add a bit more challenge around the middle of the week. You can do this by incorporating hill climbs or interval training into your rides. As for your weekend rides, aim to increase the distance gradually - so if you're doing 45 miles in Week 5, try to get up to 60 miles by Week 8. These longer rides are a great opportunity to practice your nutrition while you're on the bike. A good rule of thumb is to consume between 30 and 60 grams of carbohydrates per hour, along with at least one bottle of water or electrolytes.

**Phase 3: Peak Volume (Weeks 9–12)**
This is the toughest part of your training, with the most miles to cover. During the week, you'll be riding around 15-25 miles. Then, on the weekends, you'll be doing longer rides, starting at 65 miles and working up to 75-80 miles by Week 12. The good news is, you don't need to ride 100 miles before the big day - if you can hit 80 miles, you'll know you've got what it takes to finish the whole distance.

**Phase 4: Taper and Event (Weeks 13–16)**
Take it easy and give your muscles a break, but still keep your legs loose and ready to go.
*   **Week 13:** 60-mile long ride.
*   **Week 14:** 45-mile long ride.
*   **Week 15:** 30-mile long ride.
*   **Week 16 (Event Week):** Try to get plenty of rest at the start of the week. A couple of days before the event, take it easy with a short 10-mile bike ride. Then, take the day before the event off to make sure you're feeling fresh.

**Key Tips:** Get a professional bike fit to prevent overuse injuries, prioritize sleep, and never try new foods or gear on event day.

Standing desks can make your home office feel more flexible, comfortable, and energizing—but only if you use one thoughtfully. Here are 10 practical tips to help you get the most from yours.

1. ** Start slowly**
Don’t stand all day on your first attempt. Begin with 15–30 minutes at a time, then gradually increase your standing periods.

2. ** Keep your monitor at eye level**
To sit comfortably, your computer screen should be at a height where the top of it is about level with your eyes. This way, you won't strain your neck and your posture will be more natural. It's all about finding a position that feels relaxed and comfortable for you.

3. ** Adjust your keyboard and mouse**
Your elbows should stay close to your sides and bend at about 90 degrees. Your wrists should remain fairly straight while typing.

4. ** Wear supportive shoes**
Bare feet or unsupportive slippers can make standing uncomfortable. Choose comfortable shoes, or use an anti-fatigue mat.

5. ** Use an anti-fatigue mat**
A cushioned mat can reduce pressure on your feet, knees, and lower back—especially on hard flooring.

6. ** Move instead of simply standing**
Shift your weight, stretch, walk around during calls, or do a few calf raises. Standing still for hours isn’t much better than sitting still.

7. ** Alternate positions regularly**
A good goal is to switch between sitting and standing every 30–60 minutes. Listen to your body rather than following a rigid schedule.

8. ** Keep essentials within reach**
Arrange your desk so your keyboard, mouse, phone, and frequently used items are easy to access. Reaching constantly can create new aches.

9. ** Mind your posture**
To stand comfortably, keep your shoulders relaxed and your head straight over your spine. Your weight should be evenly spread across both feet. Try not to lean forward onto the desk, it's better to stand up straight. This way, you can avoid straining your back and neck.

10. ** Make movement convenient**
Keep a water bottle nearby, use walking meetings when possible, and consider a small footrest or balance board for variety.

The best standing desk setup isn’t about standing nonstop. It’s about having more options throughout the day and changing positions before discomfort sets in.

Mentorship is really important for remote apprenticeships. It helps make up for the fact that the apprentice and mentor are not in the same place. Normally, when they're in the same room, the apprentice can learn a lot just by being around their mentor. They can watch what they're doing, listen in on conversations, and get feedback right away. But when they're not in the same place, they miss out on these casual learning moments. That's why it's even more important for the mentor to be intentional about teaching and guiding the apprentice.

A good mentor working with someone remotely needs to make an effort to create a structured approach. This involves planning regular meetings, clearly explaining their thought process when sharing screens, and setting up a system for asking questions that would normally come up in conversation. By doing this, the mentor takes on a more active role in shaping the learning environment, rather than just being someone the apprentice can watch and learn from. They need to be intentional about how they teach and communicate, since they can't rely on the apprentice picking things up naturally in a shared physical space. This way, the mentor can ensure the apprentice has the support and guidance they need to learn and grow, even from a distance.

Building trust is crucial in this setting. Since mentors and apprentices don't have the chance to chat in the hallway or grab lunch together, mentors need to make an extra effort to create a safe and supportive environment. This means making sure apprentices feel okay about asking questions or admitting when they're confused or made a mistake - even if it's just over text or video. To do this, mentors have to be willing to be vulnerable themselves and show their apprentices that it's okay to not have all the answers. They also need to check in regularly to see how their apprentices are doing, not just with their work, but with their overall wellbeing.

Mentors in remote apprenticeships play a key role in linking their mentees to a wider network of professionals. This can be really helpful for apprentices who aren't physically present in an office. Mentors can introduce their mentees to other colleagues, invite them to virtual meetings that go beyond their usual tasks, and speak up for them within the organization. By doing so, mentors can help their mentees become more visible and connected, which is crucial for their growth and success. This is especially important in a remote setup, where it's easy to feel isolated or left out. By taking on this connector role, mentors can help bridge the gap and provide their mentees with valuable opportunities to learn and network.

Ultimately, mentorship in remote apprenticeships shifts from an organic byproduct of shared space to a deliberate, structured practice—demanding more intentionality but often yielding deeper, more reflective learning relationships when done well.

Governments around the world are quickly creating laws to control the use of facial recognition technology, but experts are concerned that these laws are not being updated fast enough to keep up with the technology's rapid growth. This means that the rules in place may not be effective in addressing the issues that come with this technology.

Policymakers have been paying a lot of attention to how artificial intelligence is used in the public sector, especially when it comes to law enforcement using real-time biometric surveillance. For example, the European Union has passed a big law about artificial intelligence, and some cities in the United States have banned certain uses of it. But some experts think these rules are not enough and might even make people feel safer than they really are. They say there are still big gaps in the rules that need to be fixed. These experts, who are lawyers and technologists, believe that the current measures do not go far enough to address the issues with biometric surveillance.

The big problem is that facial recognition technology is everywhere. It's not just used in high-quality cameras on the streets, but also in security systems for private companies, stores that want to know more about their customers, apps on our phones, and social media sites. The laws we have now are having a hard time dealing with how common this technology is in the private sector. A lot of times, when we sign up for something online, we just click "agree" without reading the long terms of service, which can include consent for facial recognition. This makes it tough to know what's happening with our personal info.

The rules that govern how personal information is used are often not strong enough. This is a problem because biometric data, like facial recognition, can be shared easily across the world. As a result, companies can develop their technology in places with weak privacy laws and then use it everywhere. When governments try to make companies be more open about how they use this data, they often hit a roadblock. Companies don't want to share their secrets, so they use trade-secret laws to avoid being transparent about what they're doing.

Technological shifts present an even greater challenge. The rise of generative AI and synthetic biometrics has blurred the line between authentic and artificial images, rendering traditional definitions of "biometric identifiers" obsolete in many legal frameworks. By the time a law is debated, drafted, and enacted, the underlying technology has often shifted, rendering the legislation ineffective.

Experts say that banning facial recognition in a few cities might help stop police from misusing it, but this won't solve the bigger problem. Since facial recognition is a global technology that's being used more and more for business, we need international rules that cover everything, including how companies use it and the technology behind it. Without these rules, facial recognition will keep spreading faster than the laws that try to control it. This is because the technology is not just limited to one place, it's being used all over the world, and companies are making a lot of money from it. So, we need to have a comprehensive approach to regulate it, otherwise, it will be hard to keep up with its rapid growth.

People should back the repair-and-refurbish electronics industry because it cuts down on waste, helps save consumers money, and is the antidote to a culture of planned obsolescence. If we rely on our phones, laptops, tablets, and other electronic appliances every day, it shouldn't mean that we have to buy new ones just because our batteries are dying, our screens have cracked, or one small part has given out. 

Electronic waste is one of the fastest growing types of waste in the world. When old electronics are thrown away, they often contain lead, mercury, and other toxic chemicals that can end up polluting the environment if they're not properly managed. Meanwhile, all those valuable metals and parts inside our electronics have to be mined or manufactured. Repairing a phone or laptop for another few years means we don't have to make a new one, saving the resources and pollution involved in making it, shipping it, and disposing of the old one.

Repair also makes technology more accessible. The cost of buying a new laptop or smartphone can be in the hundreds or even thousands of dollars, while replacing a battery or a broken charging port or screen may cost only a fraction of the original price. Refurbished electronics give a good alternative to students, families, and small businesses looking to upgrade their technology without paying full price for a new product. Greater availability of refurbished electronics could also help close the digital divide by giving more people access to essential electronic tools.

Some people might say that new devices will work better or be more secure, and there might be cases where replacing is the best option. But that's no excuse for companies to design devices that are hard to fix or cannot be fixed at all. They should make parts, repair guides, diagnostics, and software updates available for those who want to fix things themselves. We need right-to-repair legislation to make sure independent repair shops and individual owners have the ability to fix the products they've bought.

In short, the repair-and-refurbish movement is a movement toward responsibility. Instead of treating electronics as throw-away accessories, it encourages us to see them as valuable tools that deserve to last longer. Supporting repair helps protect the environment, supports consumer choice, and makes for a more sustainable future with technology.

The term community-supported fishery (CSF) describes an approach to seafood distribution in which consumers purchase products directly from local fishers without the need to go through the traditional supply chain, which is long and frequently non-transparent. Conceptually based on community-supported agriculture (CSA), these programs operate by having consumers buy in advance a share of a fishery’s yield, giving fishers working capital, fixed prices, and guaranteed sales. In return, consumers are able to receive locally-sourced, fresh, traceable seafood, which is often produced in an environmentally sound manner. The first CSFs were established in the U.S. in the mid-2000s, and since then similar initiatives have spread throughout the coastal areas of North America, as well as to Europe and other regions in the world, spurred by a growing consumer demand for knowing the provenance and production methods of the foods they eat and supporting local economies. As CSFs have become increasingly popular, they have also drawn attention from scholars in several disciplines, ranging from economics to sociology and marine policy to food systems studies. Much of this research is dedicated to exploring whether CSFs provide an opportunity to improve the livelihoods of small-scale fishers competing in the global economy and facing ever-decreasing resources, promote sustainability through greater accountability between producers and consumers, and represent another iteration of the alternative food movement seeking to counter the negative effects of industrial food production. Despite the increasing volume of published work on CSFs, much remains unknown about how these enterprises are faring economically, what impact they are having on conservation efforts, and why certain CSFs succeed while others do not. This review summarizes what we know about CSFs and identifies ways in which the current literature can be improved upon through further study of the social, economic, and ecological aspects of these fisheries.

# Kitchen Makeover in 48 Hours

### Friday: Prep

Clear your kitchen completely and remove cabinet hardware. Take down any hanging lights, ceiling fans, blinds, and appliances if they’re lightweight enough. Lay down drop cloths and plastic sheeting on floors and any surfaces you’ll be working near. This will save you time when you’re done painting.

### Saturday: Priming and Cleaning

Wash walls, ceilings, and cabinets with trisodium phosphate (TSP). Rinse off the cleaner and allow everything to dry. Prime stained or previously dark walls. Sand down any glossy surfaces before painting. 

### Saturday Afternoon: First Coat

Paint your ceiling and walls first using a roller. Next, tackle trim and other detailed areas using a paintbrush. Invest in high-quality paint; it’ll save you a lot of time and effort in the long run. Allow proper drying time between coats (about 4-6 hours).

### Sunday: Second Coat and Details

Paint another coat on your walls and ceiling. If you want to repaint your doors and trim, now’s the time to do so. Use painter’s tape around windows and baseboards to create clean lines. Pull off tape while the paint is still a bit tacky.

### Sunday Night to Monday: Finishing Touches

Put up lights and cabinet knobs/handles after the paint has dried. Put your appliances back in place. Remove drop cloths and plastic sheeting. 

### Extra Tips

Buy your painting supplies on Thursday so you don’t have to go shopping on the weekend. Use low-VOC paint to keep your house smelling fresh. Buy good quality brushes and rollers; the finish will look better. Keep a wet rag nearby for easy cleanup. Make sure your house is properly ventilated during the entire process.

Follow these steps, and you’ll have a sparkling clean kitchen painted on Monday morning!

In general, I believe cities should install bike lanes instead of parking spaces when this will result in safer, more effective, and more sustainable transit. Street parking has its advantages; it’s easy for drivers to park, and it might benefit businesses. However, public streets can be used by more people when they’re utilized for transit as opposed to storing cars. Bike lanes are safer for the rider, which reduces the number of traffic-related injuries. They can promote exercise and provide mobility for children, senior citizens, and those who don’t own a car. They can also reduce air pollution and carbon dioxide emissions. In densely populated areas, streets that include bike lanes could enable more people to get around without making the traffic worse. And they might even help the local economy, since cyclists and pedestrians have been shown to frequent local businesses more often and spend more money there, and bike lanes might attract more visitors to commercial areas.

But cities shouldn’t eliminate parking spaces without considering the needs of disabled people, deliveries, contractors, and others who need cars. The city could keep some spaces for accessible parking, loading, and limited, short-term parking while turning other spaces into bike lanes. They should also invest in public transit and implement paid parking or parking permits to manage the remaining spaces. Street parking, especially free curbside parking, should not be prioritized over other forms of transit. It’s hard to say whether one solution is always better than another because each situation is different. A bike lane isn’t very helpful if it doesn’t connect to anything, if it’s dangerous at intersections, or if it’s built in a location where few people would want to ride. Cities should investigate traffic patterns, consult the residents who will be affected, and evaluate the results before deciding what to do. However, in congested urban areas, the potential benefits of creating safe cycling routes usually outweigh the benefits of creating more parking spaces. Cities should make installing bike lanes their first choice and offer reasonable parking options for people who need them.

How Libraries Are Adapting to Meet the Digital Needs of Underserved Communities

Public libraries are becoming increasingly important as digital hubs and essential resources for low-income populations. With the rise of remote work, online learning, and digital government services, libraries are playing a crucial role in providing free internet access and technology to those who might otherwise lack it.

"In many cases, libraries are the only place where people can access reliable internet and computers," says Maria Chen, director of the American Library Association's digital initiatives.

During the pandemic, libraries were instrumental in supporting students and families navigating distance learning. Many branches now offer digital skills training, computer workshops, and access to government resources. Librarians are also playing a more active role in teaching digital literacy, helping patrons learn everything from basic computer skills to online safety.

But as the demand for technology continues to grow, libraries face the challenge of maintaining their services and equipment while operating under tight budgets. Despite this, community libraries continue to provide an important service by offering affordable access to technology, computer labs, and digital training programs.

As the digital divide widens, the role of community libraries in providing access to technology will only continue to grow. Experts suggest that libraries should consider increasing their partnerships with private technology companies and pursuing additional funding from local and state governments to meet the needs of their communities.

As the world becomes more digital, community libraries will play a critical role in ensuring that all people have access to the information and technology they need to succeed.

So what will the university lecture look like in the future? There will be no doubt that it will take on a hybrid form, and that will not necessarily be a bad thing. It is all too easy to pine for the days of the old-fashioned lecture, but that is just the sort of backward-looking attitude that will prevent us from seeing how much better hybrid learning could be. In reality, the traditional format has been inflexible, requiring students to go to a specific place at a specific time. Not everyone can afford to do that.

A hybrid lecture would consist of online learning, face-to-face teaching and some combination of the two. It could use asynchronous methods such as online videos or quizzes so students could complete them at a time that suits them, and then spend class time doing things they couldn’t do online, like group discussion or working through exercises. The use of technology also helps prepare students for the modern world in which most jobs require them to know how to use computer systems. Instead of trying to cling to the traditional university lecture as though it was the best way of educating students, we should embrace the opportunities offered by digital technologies to give them a richer experience.

Retaining skilled employees is a persistent challenge for businesses in today’s competitive labor market, driven by increasing turnover costs, shifting employee preferences for flexibility and well-being, and evolving workplace expectations. One policy that has emerged to address these challenges is unlimited vacation, sometimes referred to as discretionary paid time off or unlimited paid time off (PTO). This type of policy allows employees to take as much time off as they want while maintaining their pay, in contrast to traditional vacation policies that provide a set number of days per year. While there is limited empirical evidence regarding the impact of unlimited vacation on employee retention, some researchers suggest that these policies may increase organizational commitment by signaling organizational trust and autonomy. The social exchange perspective holds that employees may reciprocate organizational support with increased loyalty and lower turnover intentions. Meanwhile, the self-determination perspective argues that granting employees more control over their time away from work can enhance motivation and satisfaction. By offering employees greater flexibility to schedule time away from work as needed, unlimited vacation may foster higher job satisfaction and stronger employee commitment. Furthermore, the symbolic value of unlimited vacation may strengthen organizational differentiation and attract candidates who value flexible work arrangements. Despite the potential benefits, unlimited vacation may also have unintended consequences for employee retention. Without a set limit on days off, employees may be less likely to take advantage of their vacation benefits, fearing negative repercussions from managers if they do. Alternatively, the absence of formal vacation entitlements may shift the burden of taking time off from employers to employees, leading to decreased work-life balance and increased stress. Managers’ practices, workloads, and team norms, as well as employees’ perceptions of fairness, may influence how effectively unlimited vacation serves as a retention tool. To gain a clearer understanding of the effectiveness of unlimited vacation as a retention strategy, this literature review will explore relevant studies on employee autonomy, organizational support, work-life balance, and turnover intentions. The review will also consider the potential benefits and drawbacks of these policies, as well as the conditions under which they may contribute to increased employee retention.

One of the easiest ways to build a sense of community and meet your neighbors is with a book club. You’ll have a new reading list, get to know some new authors, and establish a recurring event that will be a great talking point among neighbors. To get started, invite a handful of people via email list, social media, flyers, or word-of-mouth. Six to 12 members is usually a good size, large enough to provide a robust conversation, but small enough to stay organized. At the first meeting, decide the frequency and location of meetings, the method of selecting books, and whether people are expected to read all of the books. Decide on a meeting schedule, like the first Thursday of every month. The hosts can rotate from house to house, or you could gather at a library, coffee shop, community center, or local park. Consider occasionally offering a virtual option for those who can’t attend in person. Take turns selecting books, or ask members to nominate them and vote on the choices. Set a page limit if necessary. Vary the genres, authors, and points of view. Mix in popular fiction, nonfiction, memoirs, mysteries, local authors, and smaller volumes. Let everyone know the next title and meeting time before you disperse. Come up with a few open-ended questions that will prompt discussion. Ask what they liked or didn’t like about the book, or what surprised them. Ask which characters or ideas were the most believable. Discuss how the book relates to their life or your community. Rotate the role of discussion leader among members to share the responsibility. Keep the group inclusive and open-minded. Allow space for diverse opinions. Don’t let one person hog the floor. Remember that members may skip a meeting or not finish every book. It’s nice to offer snacks and drinks, but don’t make it a big deal if no one brings anything. Send out regular reminders and celebrate milestones. Occasionally do something different: a themed potluck, an author talk, a bookstore trip, or a book exchange. You don’t need 100% attendance or intellectual rigor to be successful. You just need consistency, hospitality, and enough interesting books to keep people coming back.

# 10 Weeknight Batch-Cooking Hacks

Look, we all hate weeknight cooking. We don’t love it either. But there is one thing we do love: having leftovers in the fridge. These tips will help you make meal prep easier, faster, and more enjoyable.

**1. Pick recipes that freeze well.**
Some foods, like pasta and potatoes, just aren’t the best for freezing. So stick to things like chili, curries, soup, or even roast chicken that will freeze perfectly.

**2. Make a list of what you’re going to cook.**
This will save you money and help you stay organized. Plus, no one wants to go to the grocery store to buy one ingredient at a time.

**3. Do most of your prep on Friday night.**
Prepping the night before is the best way to make cooking on the weekend much easier. Take the time to chop your veggies and measure out your spices.

**4. Use the entire kitchen.**
If you have the space, use the oven, stovetop, slow cooker, and rice cooker at the same time. It’s the best way to get everything ready quickly.

**5. Make extra.**
Since you’re cooking anyway, why not make more? You can always freeze it for another day.

**6. Get good containers.**
Glass and quality plastic containers are the best way to keep your food fresh. Label them with the date so you know what you’re looking at when you open your freezer.

**7. Start by cooking proteins.**
Whether you’re using ground beef, chicken, or beans, start with that. Once it’s done, you’re pretty much set.

**8. Don’t forget about breakfast!**
Make some egg muffins or oatmeal to go with it. You’ll thank me in the morning.

**9. Clean up as you go.**
It’s so tempting to leave everything for last, but I promise you’ll be happier if you clean up as you cook. There’s nothing worse than coming home from work and finding a dirty kitchen.

**10. Be flexible.**
Some weeks you'll nail it; some weeks you'll manage one meal. And that’s okay! That’s still better than ordering out four times a week.

Making financial literacy a requirement for high school graduation is important because students need to be prepared for the real world. In the real world, young people need to make tough financial decisions, such as taking out student loans, getting a credit card, and budgeting. Most young people do not receive any financial education in school and therefore struggle financially throughout their lives, accumulating high-interest debt and bad credit. By making financial literacy a requirement, every student will have access to the tools necessary to make sound financial decisions. Requiring financial literacy in high school is important because it creates equality between students. Students from wealthier families have parents to teach them about personal finance, while students from lower income families often do not have that advantage. By making financial literacy a requirement, all students will have the opportunity to learn how to manage their money. This can be a key step toward financial independence and a strong foundation for building a financial future. Some might argue that adding more requirements to high school graduation is a burden on schools and students. However, financial literacy can be added as a semester-long class for seniors or integrated into existing classes such as math or social studies. The cost to schools and students is minimal and the benefit to students is great. Ultimately, the goal of education is to prepare students for life after school. If students are not taught about finance, they will not know how to make smart financial decisions in the future, which can lead to financial ruin. Making financial literacy a requirement is an important step to ensure that students are prepared for life after school.

With more people driving electric cars, homeowners in established neighborhoods are grappling with an issue that builders of newer subdivisions usually have plans for: Where do they plug their cars in?

Lots of old neighborhoods weren't built with garages, driveways or off-street parking. And even if residents have garages, narrow streets and cramped lots and outdated electrical systems can make charging at home difficult. People whose cars park on the street often will need to use public chargers; residents with garages sometimes will have to upgrade their wiring.

Local governments are tackling the problem by deploying a range of solutions. In some places, officials are putting charging stations along the curb in areas where few residents have off-street parking. Other cities are experimenting with installing chargers on streetlights or parking meters. That requires less construction and no need to dig up sidewalks and lay conduit for more utility poles, like what's needed for a charging station. And in some towns, regulators are considering allowing residents to run cords from their houses to parked cars on the sidewalk, although there are still issues around safety and pedestrians' right of way.

There's also the issue of equity. Wealthier residents are likely to be more able to install charging stations at home than low- and middle-income residents who rent or live in multifamily housing. Some advocates have suggested that cities should prioritize investing in chargers in places where residents don't have garages or driveways, rather than building them in newly developed areas where they're easier to deploy.

Preserving historic architecture also could create complications, since installing chargers in a historic building or district may require special approvals. Utility companies, too, will need to figure out whether local power grids and transformers can support additional demand when tens of thousands of drivers start charging at night.

Transportation experts say old neighborhoods can work with a combination of charging on the curb, workplace and public charging, and encouraging landlords to invest in chargers at apartment complexes. It will be up to individual municipalities to decide how quickly to make upgrades as electric vehicles become more common.

But do algorithms enhance choice? In fact, recommendation algorithms significantly limit consumer choice. Algorithms predict what consumers will like based on their previous behavior, effectively restricting them to only those choices the algorithm predicts they will like. By definition, they will never find things that surprise them. Consumers will never see any choices beyond those predicted. Algorithm recommendations also tend to reward those products and providers that are already popular, limiting consumer choice further by only offering the same products and services from the same sources. Consumers cannot be offered the full range of available options if a small bookshop’s newest book can never compete with the latest novel from a bestselling author on an algorithmic recommendation list. Finally, algorithms make consumers' choice more difficult as consumers don’t know what other options are available to them. They can’t even know that other options exist. And worse, these algorithms manipulate consumer behavior by showing them things they want to see to keep them engaged for longer periods, rather than things they want to see because they like them. Sure, there may be some benefits to using these algorithms, but it doesn’t mean that consumers are truly making the choices they want to. To improve consumer choice, we need to reduce our dependence on algorithms.

To train for a 100-mile bike ride in 16 weeks you must be consistent, progressively overload your body, and fuel properly. Assuming that you can comfortably ride 20-25 miles right now, here’s what you should do.

**Phase 1: Foundation (Weeks 1-4)**
Your goal this phase is to build a routine of three to four rides per week: two short weekday rides (10-15 miles) at a moderate pace, one recovery ride or cross-training session, and one weekend long ride. Start off riding 25 miles on your first weekend and increase your weekend ride by five miles each week. The final weekend in phase 1 should be 40 miles.

**Phase 2: Endurance Building (Weeks 5-8)**
This phase has the same schedule as Phase 1 but you’ll want to make your mid-week rides more intense by adding in some hill climbs or interval training to increase your cardiovascular power. Continue your long weekend rides from 45 miles in week 5 up to 60 miles in week 8. Use these rides to practice your on-bike nutrition. You’ll need 30-60 grams of carbs and one bottle of water or electrolyte drinks per hour when riding 100 miles.

**Phase 3: Peak Volume (Weeks 9-12)**
Phase 3 consists of the most riding of the plan. The mid-week rides should be 15-25 miles and the long weekend rides should range from 65 miles up to a maximum of 75-80 miles in week 12. You don’t have to ride 100 miles leading up to event day so don’t worry about riding 100 miles in this phase, the 80 mile rides will prove you have enough endurance to complete 100 miles.

**Phase 4: Taper and Event (Weeks 13-16)**
The last phase should consist of lighter riding so that your muscles can recover but your legs still feel fresh. Week 13 should have 60 miles, week 14 should be 45 miles, week 15 should be 30 miles, and week 16 should be a light 10 mile spin two days before the event and no riding the day before. 

Also make sure you get a professional bike fit to avoid overuse injuries, get plenty of sleep, and NEVER try anything new on event day!

10 ways to make the most of your standing desk

A standing desk can bring more flexibility, comfort and vitality to your home workspace, but only if you use it correctly. Here are 10 ways to get the most out of yours.

1. Start slowly. Don’t stand all day on your first try. Instead, start by standing for 15 to 30 minutes at a time. Then, work up to longer periods of standing. 2. Position your monitor at eye level. The top of your computer screen should be about at eye level. This reduces strain on your neck and can improve your posture. 3. Position your keyboard and mouse. Your elbows should be close to your sides and bent at about a 90-degree angle. Your wrists should be straight as you type. 4. Wear comfortable shoes. Standing barefoot or in flimsy slippers can be uncomfortable. Opt for comfortable shoes or use an anti-fatigue mat. 5. Use an anti-fatigue mat. A thick, soft mat can reduce pressure on your feet, knees and lower back, especially if you’re working on hard floors. 6. Move while standing. Shift your weight, stretch, pace during phone calls or do calf raises. Standing still for several hours isn’t much better than sitting still. 7. Change positions often. You should aim to alternate between sitting and standing every 30 minutes to an hour. But don’t feel like you have to stick to a strict schedule. Pay attention to what your body needs. 8. Keep things within arm’s reach. Make sure you can easily access your keyboard, mouse, phone and other things you need without stretching or bending. Reaching can cause its own aches. 9. Watch your posture. Keep your shoulders relaxed, your head aligned with your spine and your weight evenly distributed on both feet. Avoid leaning on your desk. 10. Make it easy to move. Keep a water bottle nearby, take walking meetings and keep a footstool or balance board handy for additional options. A great standing desk setup is not about standing the entire time. It’s about giving yourself more options during the day and changing positions before you feel pain.

Mentorship is crucial to a remote apprenticeship. In a remote setting, the apprenticeship lacks the benefit of being in the same location with someone who has a lot of experience, which is important because the learning aspect of an apprenticeship can be diminished if the parties are not in close proximity. 

In an in-person setting, the apprentice can learn from the mentor's actions, observations, and conversations. However, in a remote setting, there are fewer opportunities for an apprentice to learn from a mentor's day-to-day activities. Thus, a good mentor should take the initiative in providing learning opportunities to the apprentice. They should schedule regular check-ins and ask about any challenges the apprentice may be facing, share their own experiences, provide feedback and guidance, explain their thought process, and encourage questions and curiosity.

The relationship between a mentor and an apprentice is a trust-based relationship. Since remote interactions lack face-to-face interaction, the mentor should be mindful of the apprentice's well-being. Remote mentors can still maintain trust and rapport with apprentices by scheduling regular check-ins and providing feedback, guidance, and support. They can also build trust by showing interest in the apprentice's personal life and asking about their well-being, encouraging open communication, and being available to answer questions and provide support.

A mentor can help an apprentice develop a professional network by introducing them to others in the field, including professionals they may not have had access to. Remote mentors can introduce apprentices to their network via social media platforms, online forums, and email lists. A remote mentor can also invite the apprentice to events or meetings where they can meet others in the industry. Overall, mentorship is a key component of remote apprenticeships and should be taken seriously.

With countries rushing to create laws about facial recognition technology, the prevailing consensus among experts is that current and pending laws simply cannot keep up with the technology.

The EU’s recently passed Artificial Intelligence Act, for example, along with bans passed in several American cities, focus on the government’s use of facial recognition. Laws around the world tend to be focused on restricting law enforcement’s access to the technology.

Yet facial recognition is not only used by law enforcement; there are plenty of applications that exist outside the realm of policing. Facial recognition software isn’t just used to scan police bodycam footage for suspects anymore, it’s being deployed in video surveillance systems that don’t require law enforcement involvement. Laws have difficulty addressing this problem because people sign away their rights to consent in agreements they don’t read when signing up for a new phone app or software service.

Moreover, most laws only work within a country’s own borders, and biometric data can easily cross borders. This means that the software used to train facial recognition models can operate from countries that have less strict data protection laws, or even no laws at all. Some laws attempt to address these issues by forcing companies to disclose how their models were trained, but this often conflicts with intellectual property laws, making it difficult to enforce.

Even if laws are able to successfully regulate facial recognition’s current applications, the technology is still growing and changing. Some laws struggle to define what facial recognition actually is. For instance, some laws define biometric data as data based on physical characteristics, which does not account for the ability to generate images using artificial intelligence. Laws might also become outdated quickly, since they need to go through the legislative process before becoming law. By the time they are passed, they might not apply to the technology they were supposed to be regulating.

Although many laws might temporarily prevent law enforcement from using facial recognition technology, this is not enough to regulate the technology fully. Facial recognition technology will continue to outpace laws unless governments and organizations around the world work together to establish broad regulations.

People should support the repair-and-refurbish electronics movement because it helps to reduce waste and save consumers money, and challenges a wasteful culture of planned obsolescence.

Phones, laptops, tablets and other devices are becoming increasingly essential to our daily lives. There's no reason for any of the devices to be forced into an early retirement, whether because a battery weakens or because a screen cracks.

Electronic waste is one of the fastest-growing waste streams in the world. Discarded devices, if not handled properly, can contaminate soil and water with lead, mercury and other hazardous chemicals. And the products we once were forced to discard contained valuable metals that also required a significant amount of energy to extract through mining.

Repairing a device and keeping it for several more years helps to minimize all of those impacts.

Repair also makes technology more affordable, giving people options. A new smartphone or laptop can cost hundreds or thousands of dollars; maybe you just need to replace a battery, charging port, or display instead. Or maybe you can get a refurbished device for your student or small business. The more of the old devices we fix, the more we can stop the toxic waste boom.

We’re the first to admit that some newer devices might be more efficient or secure, and we get that in some cases you might need to replace something. But that doesn’t relieve manufacturers of their duty to make devices that are easy, or even possible, to fix. They can’t just stop selling replacement parts, or deny access to repair manuals, or put the billion-dollar price tag on their awesome new diagnostic tool, or totally restrict that new software update to themselves. If they do, and if right-to-repair laws don’t stop them, these companies could soon make maintaining and refurbishing their products all but impossible—and get you every time with their needlessly frequent new device replacements.

The repair-and-refurbish movement is an important response to manufacturers’ shameful and wasteful tendency to replace responsibility with convenience, as if electronics were fashion items. Community-supported fisheries (CSFs) have gained attention as an alternative seafood distribution model, similar to the community-supported agriculture (CSA) model for vegetables. In CSFs, consumers buy a share of a fishing operation’s anticipated catch, assuring fishers of some upfront capital, price stability, and a guaranteed market, as well as providing consumers with greater access to fresh seafood. A handful of CSFs appeared in the mid-2000s in the United States, and interest in CSFs as a model for effectively and efficiently distributing seafood continues to grow in coastal regions of North America, Europe, and elsewhere around the world.

Although community-supported fisheries (CSFs) are a burgeoning phenomenon, they exist in an ocean of ink. Disparate scholarly disciplines including economics, sociology, and marine policy study CSFs through various lenses—from examining the economic viability of small-scale fisheries competing with globalization and overexploitation to investigating their role in promoting alternative food systems. An array of peer-reviewed articles have reported both successful and purported outcomes of CSFs, resulting in knowledge gaps about their long-term economic viability, their real conservation outcomes, and more speculative results that require further exploration. The objectives of this review are twofold: to synthesize the existing research on CSFs, and to identify what is and is not known about them. In dissecting their origins and operational models, this review addresses their impacts on constraints faced by fishers and seafood consumers, and marine ecosystems. Given the proliferation of CSFs currently taking root, synthesis of the existing body of work is a critical first step from which to determine what prior studies have revealed, and to pose future inquiries where knowledge is lacking.

Repaint Your Kitchen in a Weekend

Preparation (Friday Evening)

You'll have an easier time painting if you have an uncluttered work area. So, when you start your project on Friday evening, clear your kitchen completely. Remove hardware from the cabinets, light fixtures, and, if possible, appliances. Then, cover the countertops, floors, and any fixtures you couldn't remove with drop cloths and plastic sheeting to avoid any delay when it comes time to clean up.

Priming and Cleaning (Saturday Morning)

Clean, clean, clean! If you want to get professional results, you need to get old grease and grime off the surfaces to be painted. Use trisodium phosphate (sold as TSP) to clean everything, and be sure to let the surfaces dry completely. If there are stained areas, apply primer before you start painting. If the walls were previously dark, you'll need to apply primer to the whole surface, but that's not usually necessary. If the surfces are old and glossy, give them a light sanding before you start painting.

First Paint Coat (Saturday Afternoon)

The ceiling and upper parts of the walls can be painted with a roller; do trim work with a brush. Make sure to use good-quality paint; it will cover much better than cheap stuff, and it will end up saving you time and money. Make sure to allow the paint to completely dry (4 to 6 hours, depending on temperature and humidity) before applying a second coat.

Second Coat and Details (Sunday)

If you're going to apply a second coat to the door or trim, that's the next step. If you want to paint the doors, now's a good time to get those out of the way, too. When the walls have completely dried, tape around windows and baseboards, then apply a coat of paint to these areas. Remove the tape when the paint feels slightly tacky.

Final Touches (Sunday Evening to Monday)

Once you have a 2nd coat and it’s all completely dry, reinstall the light fixtures and cabinet hardware and return the appliances to their locations. Remove all the protective coverings, taking care not to drag any dust with you.

Pro Tips

Buy your supplies on Thursday to avoid weekend shopping delays.

Use low-VOC paint for better air quality.

Invest in good brushes and rollers, it makes a visible difference.

Have a damp cloth handy, it helps with quick clean-ups.

Keep the area well-ventilated.

By Monday morning, your kitchen will be ready for the week ahead.

Taking time to create a soothing and noise-free break before bed allows your brain to start winding down for sleep. Making time for a “digital sunset,” while also creating an atmosphere of calm with dim lights and warm water, prepares you to welcome sleep. Here are more things you can do to wind down before bed:

Set a "Digital Sunset" Time

This goes hand-in-hand with turning down the lights. The blue light emitted from our phones, TVs and computers tricks the brain into thinking it’s still daylight and doesn’t help with our melatonin production.

Dim the Lights

Mimicking the sunset and allowing your indoor lights to dim as it gets dark outside signals to your brain that it’s time to start winding down.

Giving your body the gift of a warm soak can relieve tension, while lowering your body’s temperature shortly afterwards signals that it’s time to sleep.

Read a Physical Book

Of course you can read, but ditch the e-reader. Reading a paper book can be calming and free of distractions.

Doing a few simple stretches can ease any tension, while allowing your mind to focus without getting too energized.

Cities may occasionally remove street parking to add protected bike lanes. In such cases, cities should prioritize bike lanes. More people will be able to get where they’re going more safely, while cities reduce air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions. Denser neighborhoods will also accommodate more residents without additional congestion. And studies show that businesses tend to thrive in areas with more cyclists and pedestrians.

It’s important for cities to consider residents with disabilities and people who rely on cars such as delivery workers and tradespeople. Cities can create more accessible parking, loading zones and short-term parking as they remove other parking spots to create new protected lanes.

Cities should also expand public transportation before they remove street parking. But in addition to supporting protected bike lanes, cities should manage the remaining street parking more effectively, using a permit system, meter pricing and other means to reduce the amount of free curb-storage. It should be beyond dispute that much of the city is too valuable to be devoted primarily to the storage of private vehicles at no cost.

The best decision depends on local conditions. A bike lane is less useful if it is disconnected, unsafe at intersections, or built where cycling demand is minimal. Before reallocating space, officials should study traffic patterns, consult affected communities, and measure results. Nevertheless, in crowded urban areas, the long-term public benefits of safe cycling usually outweigh the convenience of abundant street parking. Cities should prioritize bike lanes as part of a broader transportation strategy, while providing reasonable alternatives for essential car access.

Stateline, by Michael Macagnone :   After years of communities across the country debating whether to close local libraries or reduce their staff and budgets, a larger conversation is starting to bubble up: how municipalities will support their libraries in a digital age.

In response to massive shifts in how information is consumed, many libraries are striving to develop new material, programs and technology dedicated specifically to online access. This includes digitizing old collection material to make it available to patrons thousands of miles away to building computer labs to provide public access for those in need. Some libraries, like those in Chicago and New York City, even allow patrons to take classes in virtual reality.

"At its core, that's what libraries are for: providing equal access to information and technology available to everyone, regardless of who they are or where they come from," said Maria Chen with the American Library Association's digital initiatives. "The internet has become so fundamental to so many services today, but not everyone has access at home. That's something libraries are still trying to solve."

Affordability, particularly for economically disadvantaged populations, as well as the ability to make using technology comfortable, are two areas where libraries can continue to play a large role, Chen said.

The expanded mission has added further strain to already-limited budgets.

Many libraries are cutting back on programs in order to maintain the latest equipment or hire specialized staff. Even less are able to find ways to fund pay-walls and subscriptions to specialized services, especially as their funding is often targeted for potential cuts.

Still, it’s hard to argue against the case that community libraries are more indispensable than ever: Often serving as the last affordable alternative for many communities as major corporations eliminate commercial internet providers, serve as community computer labs or act as a judgment-free zone for learning. Libraries are also vital community anchors.

Some experts recommend libraries forge strategic partnerships with tech companies or actively seek increased government funding.

Some endorse the incorporation of new technologies.

The future of university lectures is hybrid — and that’s a good thing.

Anyone who thinks otherwise is romanticizing a model of education that is rigid, inflexible and antiquated.

While there is much to be said for the value of sitting in a room, focusing your attention on a professor during set times and locations, that model simply doesn’t work for everyone.

It also doesn’t make the best use of students’ time. When lectures are available in an asynchronous format — such as pre-recorded or interactive modules — students can learn at their own pace. It also gives them an opportunity to re-visit material when their receptiveness is highest.

In turn, students and educators can use that precious time together in person on more dynamic, interactive materials. Imagine deep dive discussions, problem solving workshops or personalized feedback sessions — interactions that encourage real academic engagement and discourage the passive learning style of being lectured to.

Furthermore, the technological infrastructure supporting hybrid models fosters digital literacy, a crucial skill for today’s graduates. Universities are obligated to prepare students for a digitally integrated world. Through the incorporation of diverse online tools into the learning process, hybrid education can cultivate greater student agency and accessibility. Rather than diluting the quality of education, a thoughtfully designed hybrid approach may create a more engaging and effective learning environment than the singular, often unidirectional, university lecture of the past. The future of higher education lies not in merely surviving with technology but thriving because of it.

Employee retention is a key issue for many organizations battling competitive labor markets, rising turnover costs, and employee expectations for more flexibility and well-being. Organizations have introduced a variety of policies, such as unlimited vacation (also called discretionary paid time off or unlimited paid time off [PTO]), that may set them apart. Typically, rather than allotting employees a fixed number of vacation days each year to take as needed (subject to managerial approval), organizational members are free to take as much paid leave as they want and need, as long as their workloads and organizational expectations permit.

Although there is little academic scholarship on the effects of unlimited vacation, on a retention rational alone, such policies might be beneficial. Social exchange theory might predict that supplemental organizational policies that provide such supportive behaviors by employers would increase employee reciprocation in the form of reduced intentions to quit. From a self-determination theory perspective, unlimited vacation allows employees choice in the timing of time off and can help meet employee needs and enhance employee motivation and performance.

Unlimited vacation also provides a symbolic benefit that employers can use to attract and retain employees, especially if organizations are competing in knowledge-intensive domains.

Critics of unlimited time off point to a lack of data about the real impact on time off. For unlimited vacation to work in an organization, people must truly take vacation days.

When there aren’t parameters around vacation in terms of how long is the maximum allowed, it’s not uncommon for culture to dictate people taking less time off since it’s not clear what is acceptable. In high-performance cultures, there can be a perception that taking fewer vacation days puts you on par, with your other team members who are possibly logging in and taking on other assignments while they’re on vacation.

There’s also the question of whether our working environments truly support the rest and recovery that unlimited time off is intended to address. If managers don’t pull back on workload, if team norms dictate friction or displeasure with coworkers who take time off, or if it creates an inequity, then unlimited time off is more a promise than anything else.
