Starting a neighborhood book club is an easy way to meet people, discover new authors, and get together regularly with neighbors. Begin by sending a few email invitations on your neighborhood email list, posting to social media, putting up flyers or just spreading the word. Ideally, you want a group of about six to twelve members that can discuss a book and keep to a manageable size. At the first meeting, agree on how often to meet, where to meet, how the group will choose books and whether everyone is expected to finish the book each time. You might decide to meet the first Thursday of every month, for example, and rotate hosting at members’ homes or meet at the library or a local cafe. If you have members who can't attend in person, you might offer a virtual option. Decide how the group will select a book. You could all take turns, or have people nominate books and then vote. If your group is ambitious, set a page limit; mix up the genres, authors and perspectives you’re reading. You might throw a popular fiction in with some nonfiction or a memoir or mystery, read a few works by local authors or select shorter works. Announce the next book and when you’ll get together before everyone goes home.

Set the stage for meaningful conversation by preparing some open-ended questions to start with and encouraging members to share their own questions. You may want to ask members what they enjoyed or disliked about the book, or what was surprising. You may want to ask which character or idea they found most convincing, or how they related to some aspect of the book in their current life or local area. If you'd like to share the responsibility, you can also rotate the discussion leader from meeting to meeting. To keep the discussion interesting and welcoming, keep in mind that: Everyone is entitled to their opinion and all opinions are valid. If someone else disagrees with an opinion, it's acceptable to discuss it, but don't let it take over the meeting! It is also important to remember that it is acceptable to miss a meeting or not finish the book! Lastly you'll want to provide snacks and drinks if you can, and letting club members know who is hosting each meeting is a good idea! If you aren't going to be there, it's best to let someone else know it is their turn! You might also want to keep things going with reminders and make a special occasion of milestones -- check in on meeting yourself, or start a new year with a themed potluck, or decrease attendance by bringing to members who only attend occasionally what they can do to keep their club going -- answers may include rights, conveniencing, hosting, etc. Entrance could be a reminder to read, decorate their space, or get members more involved in the process by hosting meetings themselves or providing good snacks.

As we prepare students for whatever their future holds, making financial literacy one of the required classes for graduation has never been more important. Young people are entering adulthood with an overwhelming amount of financial decisions to make, such as how to manage student loans and credit cards. There are also many decisions to make when it comes to budgeting and investing now that most have entered the workforce. Without an understanding of how to do these things, students will not be preparing themselves for their careers as well as their long term financial stability. Furthermore, so many students come from different backgrounds and may never have learned the basics of financial literacy. Adding this requirement would help level the playing field for the future generations and put each and every one of them on the same path to success.

Some opponents of a financial literacy requirement argue that teaching it would add another thing to an already packed list of graduation requirements. But financial literacy could be combined with existing math or social studies courses, or offered as a one-semester class during senior year. Besides, the values to be gained would be high-yield for students, as learning to be financially savvy now would improve practically every facet of their lives.

Ultimately, the purpose of public education is to prepare students for the independent, successful lives we as a nation want for them. Teaching financial literacy could ensure a reduced ignorance of basic financial principles, with all its personal and societal costs, thus adding a great deal of value to the high school diploma.

As electric vehicle ownership continues to rise, residents of some older neighborhoods could have some challenges because those communities were built before the advent of garages and driveways for off-street parking. Those narrow streets and aging electrical systems with closely spaced homes can make charging your car an issue.

Many drivers in areas with street parking will need to rely on public chargers. For some residents with garages their situation may require costly electrical upgrades.

Cities are trying to come to grips with the situation from a couple of angles. In some communities charging stations are being installed at the curb to help areas with limited off-street options. Others are trying chargers attached to streetlights and parking meters reducing the need for new utility poles and construction.

And in some places rules are being considered to allow a resident to run a charging cable across a sidewalk as chargers in the present configuration would make that difficult.

There are questions of fairness as well because higher-income homeowners will be in a better position to install private chargers while renters and those in multifamily buildings may have limited options. Advocates call for public investment first in areas where residents don’t have driveways and garages.

Historic preservation and older buildings may present challenges to planning electric vehicle infrastructure, especially in historic districts. In addition to additional reviews for historic preservation, utility companies will also need to assess whether local transformers and power lines will be able to handle the demand of many vehicles charging overnight.

“People in the older neighborhoods, the communities, need to realize that it’s not going to happen overnight,” says David Kaczor of Boyle Engineering, in reference to the funding and infrastructure required for vehicle-charging stations. He recommends a combination of curbside stations, workplace and public charging, and incentives for apartment owners to provide shared equipment.

Recommendation algorithms lack true understanding, with net consequences most damaging.

The debate about recommendation algorithms has raged for years, with some experts warning that their under-the-hood workings can affect even how highly educated and critical users access new information as well as products in ways they do not expect or may not even want. Fortunately, intrepid software developers are likely to come up with new and creative ways to lessen any adverse effect on consumer choice.

However, the myriad studies pointing to the constraining effect of search engines on research and algorithms on recommendation lists have led us to appreciate this paradox: that these systems designed to benefit us do not always have our best interests at heart. Algorithms are trained to pre-match consumer preferences as closely as possible.

This concentrates the market on a smaller number of shops that can afford to run the algorithms while they learn what enough users want. While it is true that consumer choice is not good for sellers in the long run.., the fun part will be to watch actors in a winner-take-all market with so much concentration of real patterns, how our consumer choices evolve over time.

Not only can algorithmic decision-making adapt to, and exploit, consumers’ psychological vulnerabilities but it can also conceal how options are ranked and hidden from consumers view, cutting down on the likelihood consumers will make informed choices. Because recommendation systems are all about maximizing engagement or profit —looking at the most sensational or addictive content rather than serving consumers’ authentic preferences—they have all the power to manipulate, and everything to gain by doing so. We advocate reducing —empowering consumers to lessen their algorithmic mediation experience and add back in the ‘moments of serendipity’ where consumers encounter goods not suggestively catered to them, in order to balance the genuine cost to consumers’ autonomy that recommendation systems require to offer their convenience.

What makes the newsletter writer so unique and so versatile?

Introduction

For decades the role of trusted commentator has historically belonged to the familiar ranks of newspaper columnists, television pundits or academic voices. The democratic potential of the internet and growing public skepticism towards mainstream media has challenged this model, creating a desire for alternative voices and viewpoints.

In this paper, we will explore the unique affordances of newsletters, how these affordances are harnessed by newsletter writers, and ultimately, what these voices might mean for society at large. We will touch on the growing economic viability and social platform made available to newsletter writers and how their ability to cultivate niche audiences using their own assessment of what’s needed in the marketplace of ideas provides the potential for novel perspectives and previously unaddressed issues.

Training for a 100-Mile Bike Ride: 16-Week Plan

Are you ready to tackle that 100-mile (century) bike ride? With 16 weeks to go, your focus needs to be on training consistently. Gradually adding distance and duration is critical to success. Progressive overload, good nutrition, and rest are equally important. If you can currently ride 20–25 miles comfortably, you’re ready to start the plan.

Follow This 16-Week Program to Prepare for a 100-Mile Ride

Phase 1: Foundation (Weeks 1–4)

The most important part of training for any big ride, race, or event is to get into a routine. Aim for three to four rides weekly. Plan for two short weekday rides (10–15 miles) at a moderate pace. Add a recovery ride or cross-training workout. Spend your time on the weekend with a long ride. Start with 25 miles and add 5 miles each week until you reach 40 miles.

Phase 3: Now is the Time to Put in the Heaviest Mileage (Weeks 9–12) This is where the magic happens! Your mid-week rides should be between 15 and 25 miles and your weekend rides should be 65 miles for Weeks 9 through 11 and 75–80 for Week 12. In the past, people have said that you have to ride 100 miles before the event to be able to complete the ride. Not true. Train up to 80 miles to be prepared for the event. Phase 4: Tapering to the Event (Weeks 13–16) During this phase, you will be tapering (i.e., reducing volume) so that your muscles have a chance to repair while keeping your legs fresh. Week 13: Long ride: 60 miles Week 14: Long ride: 45 miles Week 15: Long ride: 30 miles Week 16 (event week): Rest early in the week, light 10 mile spin two days before, rest day before Key tips: Get a professional bike fit to help avoid overuse injuries. Prioritize sleep; the body's best recovery tool. Don't forget event day. You will want to test other things during training too, like food and gear.

10 Tips for standing desks for home offices

Standing desks can help your home office feel more balanced and energetic, but only if used correctly and thoughtfully. Here are 10 tips for maximizing your standing desk setup:

Start slowly  
Only you know how tolerant your body is of new activities, so give your body time to adapt to your new standing desk. Start with 15–30 minutes of standing, then slowly increase your standing periods from there.

Monitor position  
Keep your monitor at eye level, with the top of the screen roughly even with your eyes. This helps reduce neck strain and will allow you to keep a more natural posture.

Arm/hand position  
Elbows bent at 90 degrees and close to your sides while typing will help keep your wrists fairly straight while using the keyboard and mouse.

Shoes  
Standing desks support your bare feet or illfitting slippers poorly. Wear comfortable shoes or, better yet, standing desk anti-fatigue mat.

Anti-fatigue mat  
Speaking of which, anti-fatigue mats add cush to your feet, knees and lower back, and are essential if you’re using a standing desk on hard flooring.

Move!  
Standing still is not the only alternative to sitting still. Experiment with shifting your weight, stretching, taking walks during calls, and doing occasional calf raises.

Rotate positions regularly  
Changing from sitting to standing every 30–60 minutes is a good goal. But listen to your body rather than stick to a rigid schedule.

Keep everything within reach  
If you have to reach too far to grab your keyboard, mouse, phone, or frequently used items, you can create new aches and pains.

Keep your posture in check  
Your shoulders should be relaxed; head stacked directly over your spine; weight evenly distributed between your feet. You shouldn’t be leaning into your desk.

Make moving more convenient  
Keep a water bottle close by, schedule walking meetings, and use a small footrest or balance board to encourage movement.

Remember, the best standing desk setup isn’t one where you stand non-stop; it’s one that offers more options throughout your day and encourages you to change positions before you get uncomfortable.

Mentorship is the bedrock of remote apprenticeships and fills the gaps left by not being able to learn by proximity. In a co-located environment, apprentices absorb a great deal through incidental moments — watching their mentor work hands-on, overhearing problem-solving conversations, and receiving spontaneous correction. Without these moments, remote apprentices depend on their mentors for intentional and deliberate guidance.

First, a strong remote mentor will proactively create structure. There are things you can do easily in person that are much harder to replicate in a remote setup — moments of spontaneous learning or connection, for example. The burden of providing structure, in terms of time and space, weighs more heavily on a remote mentor. Second, a remote apprenticeship significantly ramps up the need for building trust. Without in-person interactions, you need to work harder to create a level of psychological safety which allows an apprentice to feel comfortable admitting things like confusion or mistakes. That comes with being vulnerable yourself, but it also means caring enough to check in with an apprentice’s wellbeing as well as their technicalwork.

The importance of mentorship in apprenticeships has long been recognized in-person. The same can be said for remote apprenticeships as well. When it comes to remote apprenticeships, mentors help connect their mentees with the employer’s professional network, which helps them gain a network of their own, something they might not have been able to grow in an office setting. Mentors are also expected to introduce their mentees to colleagues, invite them to virtual meetings, and ensure apprentices are visible to the organization. Ultimately, the difference relates to the fact that you have to be more deliberate about the mentorship aspect of a remote apprenticeship.

The lag between laws and the technology often outpaces them has led to cries for reform. Lawmakers have poured over facial recognition laws, with some countries - like the European Union - introducing proposed laws covering artificial intelligence. Others have focused on how facial recognition can be used by public services, with FMJ and other outlets covering various municipal bans on how law enforcement deploys the technology.

But jurists and technologists claim that these measures have given the public a false sense of security over the technology, and that instead, these pieces of legislation have created massive blind spots. The chief issue, they say, is that the legislation right now focuses almost exclusively on public sector deployment - as opposed to the private sector proliferation that these jurists warn is much closer to most people’s day to day lives.

These laws, far more extensive than most proposed federal facial recognition or biometric laws in the United States, also are not able to handle the proliferation in private use.

Outside of consent forms buried in terms-of-service documents, the majority of these laws avoid any conversation about how private companies like security firms or retailers are allowed to use facial recognition. This is largely because of the difficulty in policing where this data is collected and how it is used, judged or sold.

Technological shifts further confuse the landscape. Generative AI and synthetic biometrics make it difficult to tell what’s authentic versus what’s artificial. We already see systems demonstrating this effect, and “biometric identifiers” will be incompletely and inappropriately defined in these legal frameworks. Also, by the time a law is debated, drafted, and enacted, the technology has shifted, making the legislation ineffective.

Targeted bans may give specific cities a respite from police overreach, but experts agree that piece-meal regulation cannot corral this global, commercialized technology. Faced with the technological impossibility to contain or limit the underlying algorithmic architectures, only comprehensive international standards addressing both private commercial use and underlying algorithmic architectures have hope of slowing the expansion of facial recognition.

The electronics repair/refurbish movement deserves broad public support. It cuts down on waste, saves consumers money and calls into question a culture of planned obsolescence. More and more, phones, laptops, tablets and appliances support everyday lives. And yet, too often, people are encouraged to buy a new one if their screen cracks, their battery dies or some other part breaks.

Every year, the world sees electronic waste grow faster than almost any other stream. Often, in devices, toxic substances (e.g. lead, mercury and chemicals) are found that could leak into water and soil if they aren't disposed of properly. And electronics themselves contain valuable components and metals. They take energy and mining to produce. By repairing a device and using it for a few more years, people avoid unnecessary production of a new one. And society avoids the environmental cost of mining materials, making a product and getting rid of the old one.

In many cases, repair costs much less than buying a new phone, laptop or tablet. And refurbished electronics could well meet the needs of small businesses, families and students who want reliable technology but can't afford a new device. Through refurbished devices, more people could access the technology they need. That could help close the so-called digital divide.

Some might say a new device is more secure, more efficient or simply better than an old one. That doesn't mean manufacturers shouldn't build products that can be repaired. In particular, they could sell replacement parts for their products, include repair instructions, diagnostic tools and reasonable access to software updates. With the right laws, repair shops and individual consumers could keep their purchased products working.

In this way, the repair/refurbish movement favors responsibility over convenience. It sees electronics more as useful tools than as disposable fashion accessories. Through repair, people save the environment, have more choice as consumers and build a more sustainable relationship with technology.

Community-supported fisheries (CSFs) are an alternative way of delivering seafood from local fishers to consumers, cutting out much of the long, hidden supply chain. In some ways, they are an extension of community-supported agriculture (CSA). In a CSF, consumers would, for example, pre-purchase a share of the catch from a fishing operation. In return, the fisher would have a market, price certainty and capital. And the consumer would get seafood that is often sustainably harvested, traceable and fresh. Since the mid-2000s, CSFs have spread in coastal areas of North America and, to a lesser extent, in Europe and elsewhere. They reflect increasing consumer concern about the provenance of their food, its environmental impact and the health of local economies.

Increasingly, academics from a range of disciplines (e.g. economics, sociology, food systems and marine policy) have explored CSFs. They have looked at CSFs, for example, as a way of improving the livelihoods of small-scale fishing communities in the face of declining fish stocks and increasing competition; as a way of encouraging sustainable management of fisheries through a closer relationship between fisher and consumer; and as part of broader movements toward alternative food networks which question our existing food system.

Taken together, these studies have thrown up much evidence of the appeal of CSFs. But little is known about their longer-term economic sustainability, their environmental and conservation impact and the social and cultural factors supporting their success or otherwise in different settings.

In this paper the existing literature on CSFs is brought together. The aim is to consider what is known of their roots, their model and their impact for fishers, consumers and the marine environment. Drawing on strengths and weaknesses of previous work, the review identifies themes, methods and questions for future policy and research on this increasingly important model of sustainable seafood provision.

Repainting a Kitchen in a Weekend

Preparation (Friday Evening)

First, empty the kitchen. Take down cabinet hardware, light fixtures and appliances. Then, using drop cloths and plastic, cover the floor, countertops and any remaining fixtures. This will help keep the space protected and make cleanup easier. Wipe down all surfaces with TSP to cut through grime and grease. Let them dry.

Priming and Cleaning (Saturday Morning)

If there are dark walls or stained surfaces, paint a primer over them. If there are glossy surfaces, lightly sand them to help the paint stick. With this groundwork, there is a good chance of excellent results.

First Paint Coat (Saturday Afternoon)

Start on the walls and ceiling. A roller will make quick work of these. Brush on the trim and other detailed areas. Use good quality paint. It will last longer and cover better.

Second Coat and Details (Sunday)

Between coats, let the paint dry. Depending on humidity, that will take 4-6 hours. Second coat on the walls and ceiling. If desired, paint the trim and doors.

Final Touches (Sunday Evening to Monday)

To get clean lines at the baseboards and around windows, use painter's tape. Take it off when the paint is still slightly tacky for sharp lines. When the paint is dry, put back cabinet hardware, light fixtures and appliances. Put the appliances back in place.

Pro Tips

Take off the plastic and drop cloths carefully, so dust is not smeared onto the new paint. Buy supplies on Thursday. Otherwise, there might be trouble finding them over the weekend.

Consider using low-VOC paint for better air quality.

Good brushes and rollers make a real difference.

Have a damp cloth handy to wipe up any paint splatters.

Make sure the space is kept well ventilated.

With good planning and good execution, by Monday morning the kitchen could be freshly painted for the week ahead.

10 Tips for Building a Focused Evening Wind-Down Routine

Many of us lie awake at 10 pm, wanting to tune out but unable to. This is a common experience. Often our days are long by then and we haven't had a chance to unwind before bed. The following 10 tips can help you build a focused evening routine and fall asleep more easily: Good sleep is essential. And with a good wind-down routine, we could improve our sleep.

Here are some ideas:

1. Pick a "digital sunset" time. That's when you'll turn off your screen, at least an hour before bed. Blue light from screens suppresses melatonin.
2. Turn down the lights as it gets dark outside. That's a cue in our brain that it's time to wind down.
3. Take a warm bath or shower. This can ease muscle tension and drop your body temperature. And that's good for sleep.
4. Read a paper book. Put away the e-reader and pick up a physical book. Reading a paper book is distraction-free and soothing.
5. Do some gentle stretching or yoga. Slow, simple stretches can ease tension but won't rev up energy.
6. Have a cup of herbal tea. Chamomile or lavender tea can be very relaxing. Stay away from anything with caffeine.
7. Write down your thoughts. If your mind won't settle, try writing down to-do lists or worries. That way they're out of your head and on paper.
8. Put on some quiet music or a podcast. A storytelling podcast, nature sounds, or instrumental music could work well.
9. Get ready for the next day. Pack your bag and pick out what you'll wear. If you do this the night before, you'll have fewer decisions to make in the morning and less stress.
10. Try to go to bed and wake up at roughly the same time every day (even on weekends). Our bodies like routine.

It may take some time to develop a routine. Don't get discouraged. Try one or two of these ideas each week and see which ones work best for you.

Sweet dreams.

Cities would be better off with bike lanes than with street parking in most cases. Often, street parking is convenient for drivers and helpful for local businesses. But more people can use a street for movement than for storing their car.

Protected bike lanes can cut traffic injuries, promote physical activity and open up cycling for older people, children and people without cars. They can help cut greenhouse gas and air pollution in cities. In a dense neighborhood, a street with fewer parking spaces and more bike infrastructure might well let more people move around without increasing congestion. And local businesses could benefit. Cyclists and pedestrians tend to pass by local shops regularly. And good streets can spur more activity in the area.

But in reallocating space, there is a need to think about people with disabilities, tradespeople, delivery workers and people who need cars. A good policy could keep limited short-term parking, loading spaces and parking for disabled people, but turn other spaces into protected bike lanes. And cities could improve their bus network and use pricing or permits on any remaining parking. Too often valuable public land is used for free curb parking.

Whether a bike lane would work depends on each local situation. A bike lane won't add much value if it's unsafe at intersections, isn't well connected, or is built in an area with little demand for cycling. Before cutting back on parking, local authorities should look at traffic flows, talk to local people and assess the impact. But in many urban neighborhoods, over time the public value of safer cycling would outweigh the value of plentiful parking on the street. Bike lanes should form part of a city's transportation strategy. And where necessary, they should be accompanied by reasonable provision of car access.

Community Libraries Evolve as Digital Hubs in the Modern Age

Community libraries are increasingly stepping up to be key points of digital access for millions of residents from underrepresented communities.

More and more, people are using online education, digital services and remote work. And in response, public libraries have moved well beyond their original role. Today, through free access to high-speed internet, computers and digital literacy programs, they serve many of the economically disadvantaged in their communities.

"Libraries are opening up technology to everyone," says Maria Chen, director of digital initiatives at the American Library Association. "Often for people, the library is their only access to a computer and the internet."

In particular, during the pandemic, as more students moved to online learning and more people applied for jobs remotely, libraries proved invaluable. Many now run programs such as coding, digital citizenship, using government websites and using telehealth.

But beyond computers and internet access, librarians have increasingly taken on the role of digital coach. They help people, for example, with email, cybersecurity and more. They recognize that simply having access to technology doesn't necessarily mean someone will know how to use it.

Yet in many cases, libraries' budgets simply don't stretch to keep up with fast-changing technology, to employ staff with specialist skills or to replace outdated equipment. And they risk losing funding.

Nevertheless, libraries remain a valuable resource. They offer a more affordable option to computer labs and internet providers. They offer a judgment-free space to learn. And they remain an anchor in their communities.

Going forward, many believe libraries need to keep evolving. With support from technology companies, more government funding and use of emerging technologies (e.g. artificial intelligence, virtual reality) they could build on what they already do.

In an increasingly digital world, community libraries are at the front line in helping everyone, whatever their background or income, access the tools and knowledge they need to succeed.

The university lecture of the future will be hybrid. In this form, it can only deepen, not reduce, the academic experience. Many traditionalists lament the passing of the traditional, face-to-face lecture. But this is an obstacle to progress. In its fixed time and place, the traditional lecture fails to meet the needs of many of today's students, who may have family, work, or geographical constraints.

Through the use of in-person interaction, asynchronous content and synchronous online sessions, hybrid learning can meet these needs. And in doing so, it adds value to the lecture. For example, in a hybrid model, students could watch a lecture at a time and place of their choosing, go back to difficult parts of it, and engage with it when they feel most able to do so. In-person time could then be used for more engaging, collaborative work (e.g., problem-solving workshops, discussions of the lecture, and feedback on students' work). Too often in large lecture halls these are the elements missing.

In addition, through its use of technology, a hybrid model would build up students' digital literacy. In an increasingly digital world, universities need to equip their students with digital skills. And part of doing that is bringing a range of online tools into their learning. A well-designed hybrid approach could well produce a more engaging, effective learning experience for students than the often one-way, fixed-time, fixed-place university lecture. And it could bring greater accessibility, agency and depth to their learning. More than simply surviving technology, the future of higher education lies in its use.

Employee retention is a concern for many organizations in an increasingly competitive labor market, in the face of increasing turnover costs and evolving expectations of flexibility and well-being among employees. In response to these concerns, increasing attention has been given to policies such as unlimited vacation (sometimes called discretionary paid time off or unlimited paid time off). Under such policies, rather than having a set number of vacation days each year, employees could take paid time off at the discretion of their manager, depending on workload, organizational expectations and their own needs. Proponents of such policies see in them values of autonomy, trust and results. They believe this could in turn increase employees' commitment to their organization.

Underlying much of the case for using unlimited vacation as a retention tool are well-known themes in the organizational literature. Social exchange theory suggests, for example, that employees could reward perceived flexibility and support from their organization with less desire to leave and greater loyalty. Equally, self-determination theory highlights the value of autonomy for employees. In theory, by giving employees more discretion over their time off work, they could feel more in control of their lives, more satisfied at work and more psychologically well. Unlimited vacation could also act as a benefit of working at an organization, distinguishing it from others in retention and recruitment, particularly in knowledge-intensive sectors where employees value flexibility and integration of work and life.

But there is not necessarily a clear link between unlimited vacation and retention. Some argue that, in effect, by moving away from fixed entitlements, the appropriate use of time off becomes unclear. And in a high-performance culture, employees may well worry they would seem less committed than their colleagues if they took time off. In other circumstances, under an unlimited PTO policy, responsibility for rest and recovery could fall on the employee, rather than the employer. That might well reduce its value to their well-being. Whether this policy is seen as a benefit or as a non-starter would depend on workload, norms in the team, equity across the workforce and the approach of the manager.

In this review, the author considers the use of unlimited vacation as a tool for retention. The review draws on research on work-life balance, employee autonomy, organizational support and turnover intentions. In this note, the study explores possible advantages and drawbacks of unlimited vacation policies. In particular, the study considers under what circumstances unlimited vacation could support long-term commitment in employees, as opposed to simply becoming another perk of working in a particular company.

In my home, a coastal city, I saw at first hand the conflict between ecological conservation and economic development. Local industrial centers brought more jobs, but at the expense of air quality and marine ecosystems. And in that conflict lay an important question supporting my own academic path: How might we structure our economic system so that our own prosperity doesn't come at the expense of the environment?

In my undergraduate economics program, I developed skills in policy analysis, quantitative methods and market mechanisms. But too often, in that program, environmental degradation would be treated as an "externality" of economic activity. That changed for me when I undertook a project looking at resource allocation. In it, I explored the impact of different mechanisms for pricing carbon on corporate decision-making. In that project, I realized that in many cases it isn't economics that conflicts with sustainability. Rather, it's that we have tended to undervalue our natural capital.

I'd like to study environmental economics. Through it, I want to develop more sophisticated valuation tools and econometric techniques to provide a basis for market-based responses to climate change. In particular, I'd like to explore how, in developing countries, private incentives could be brought into line with public interest in conservation, through, for example, biodiversity credits and local incentive schemes.

What I value about your program is its focus on policy-relevant, analytical economics and its access to outstanding faculty and cutting-edge research centers. Through them, I could build market-based, scalable solutions. And in the end, I'd like to go on to advise an international development agency on economic policies informed by evidence. Policies that would help drive sustainable growth. Only through a grounding in environmental economics could I see market mechanisms as our best tool for restoring the environment.

A neighborhood book club is a good way to meet neighbors, try out new authors and build up a regular, anticipated event in your neighborhood.

Start by letting a small group of neighbors know about your idea via social media, email, flyers or word of mouth. You'll want between six and twelve members, so you'll have enough to discuss a book, but not too many to manage it. At your first meeting, work out where and how often to meet, how to pick books and whether you want everyone to read the book.

Try meeting on the first Thursday of each month. You could rotate hosting, or meet at a park, community center, library or café. And every so often, you could consider a virtual meeting for members who aren't able to join in person.

Members could each pick a book for the group, or they could put books forward for discussion and vote on them. Mix up the authors, genres and perspectives. Maybe include nonfiction, fiction, memoirs, mysteries, local authors and shorter books. Let people know when and where the next book will be discussed.

To help discussion at each meeting, you could ask members to consider: what they liked or didn't like about the book, what they found most believable about the characters or ideas, and in what way it might relate to their own lives or experience in the neighborhood. At each meeting, you could have a different person lead the discussion.

Keep your club friendly and open. Let people express different views. Don't let one person dominate. And keep in mind that not everyone will read the book, or will read all of it. Drinks and snacks could add to a meeting, but don't overburden the host.

And to keep things moving, you could send out reminders of each meeting, mark milestones (e.g. the 10th book) and every now and then try a different kind of meeting (e.g. an author talk, trip to the bookstore, book swap, potluck with a theme tied to the book). A good book club doesn't need perfect attendance or deep discussion. What it does need is regularity, friendliness and books that draw people back to each meeting.

Ten Strategies for Weekend Batch Cooking

Weeknight dinners tend to be a mess. But with a refrigerator full of meals you can take out and heat up, much of that mess disappears. Here are a few tips for more successful batch cooking on the weekend.

1. Choose Simple, Freezer-Friendly Recipes
Don't use anything that will get soggy or take on an unappealing texture in the freezer. Good options include roasted proteins, chili, curries and soup.

2. Plan Your Menu First
Before you go shopping, decide what you'll be making. Otherwise you'll end up spending money on ingredients you won't use and realizing halfway through that your meal wasn't well planned.

3. Prep Everything on Friday Night
Chop your veggies, measure your spices and lay out your ingredients. On Saturday morning, when you open the fridge, you'll be glad you did. Otherwise you might end up wrestling with onion skins.

4. Use Your Whole Kitchen
Run the oven, stovetop, rice cooker and slow cooker all at once. That's the best way to make use of your time.

5. Double (or Triple) Recipes
In the process of warming up the oven, prepare more of whatever you're making so you could freeze some for another day.

6. Invest in Quality Containers
Best equipment for this kind of cooking is a good-quality plastic or glass container. Date each meal as you put it in the freezer. Otherwise in three weeks you'll be playing freezer roulette.

7. Cook Proteins First
Try to finish up your ground beef, chicken or beans early in the day. By the time they're cooling down, you'll be well on your way to having a meal.

8. Do Not Forget About Breakfast
And in the same batch, make breakfast burritos, oatmeal or egg muffins. On Monday morning, your future self will thank you.

9. Clean as You Go
It's easy to put off cleaning up, but it's better to have a clean kitchen at the end of the week than to be staring at a pile of dishes on Sunday night.

10. Give Yourself Grace
Some weekends you'll pull off a great batch of meals. Other weekends you might only make one meal and count that a success. But better than four takeout meals.

Your future self will appreciate your weeknight meals.

To succeed in today's world, students need financial literacy as part of graduation requirements. Too often, young people step into adulthood with important financial decisions to make (about credit cards, student loans, investing, budgeting, etc.) but little or no education on these issues. As a result, they often accumulate high-interest debt, develop poor credit and struggle financially over the long term. Through financial education in high school, every student could gain key tools for economic well-being throughout his or her life.

In addition, a graduation requirement in financial literacy would advance social and economic fairness. Often, young people from wealthy families pick up money management skills at home. But those from less well-off families may not. A curriculum in financial literacy would ensure that all students, regardless of background, had access to important life skills. With that foundation, young people could more easily escape cycles of poverty in their families and build up their own wealth.

Some might argue that another graduation requirement would stretch an already full high school curriculum and stretch limited educational resources. But financial literacy needn't take the form of a multi-year course. It could easily be woven into a social studies or math class. Or, for greater value, a one-semester course in the senior year could add real value to students' academic paths.

At its core, the purpose of public education is to enable students to lead successful lives on their own. In personal and societal terms, it's costly when young people lack even basic financial knowledge. With a graduation requirement in financial literacy, a high school diploma would signal both academic success and readiness for life beyond high school.

As more people drive electric vehicles, residents of older neighborhoods are facing a problem newer neighborhoods were designed to avoid: charging.

Historic neighborhoods were often built before driveways, off-street parking and garages. Their often narrow streets, old electrical systems and close-set homes can make it difficult for residents to charge at home. And those who park on the street may be forced to use public chargers. Others with garages may need expensive upgrades to their electrical system.

In response, cities are trying a range of approaches. Some are adding charging stations on the street for people without driveways or garages. Others are experimenting with parking meters and streetlights that include a charger. And in some communities, officials are looking at whether residents could string up a charging cable from their garage across the sidewalk. There's concern this could pose safety risks and may not be accessible to everyone.

In some ways, the shift to electric vehicles raises an equity question. Typically, it's easier for higher-income homeowners to add a charger at their home. Renters and residents of multifamily buildings may not have that option. Some advocates think public investment should be directed to neighborhoods where people don't have garages or driveways. Too often, they argue, chargers end up going in wealthier and newer neighborhoods.

Another consideration in historic neighborhoods is the need to consider adding equipment to older buildings or in historic districts. And utility companies would need to ask whether their power lines and transformers could handle more demand, especially from drivers charging at night.

Transportation planners believe, with thoughtful planning, even older neighborhoods could add charging. They point to curbside charging, public and workplace charging and incentives for owners of apartment buildings to install equipment.

Depending on their local infrastructure and funding, residents of older neighborhoods may see more or less change over time. More people are moving to electric vehicles. And in neighborhoods built well before charging was common, they'll need to change without sacrificing what makes them special.

The Constraining Effect of Recommendation Algorithms on Consumer Choice

Recommendation algorithms have transformed product discovery for consumers. But in doing so they tend to narrow, rather than widen, choice. In theory, such systems would bring convenience for consumers. In reality, they limit the range of options available to them and entrench existing preferences in damaging ways.

At their core, algorithms work on a contradiction. They learn from consumers, but in doing so tend to confine them to a small range of options. Take, for example, Netflix's movie recommendations or Amazon's product suggestions. They draw on what a user has already watched or bought, and aim to maximize likely satisfaction. In practice, this means consumers rarely see alternatives beyond what the algorithm predicts. And choice depends on exposure to a range of options. In fact, algorithms actively narrow that range.

Equally importantly, such systems tend to favor well-known products and vendors. A niche book from a small publisher, for example, is unlikely to be picked up by an algorithm as it would, say, a bestseller from a major publisher. In this way, over time there is increasing sameness in what consumers choose across the population.

But consumers have little sense of why some options might not appear in recommendations, or of how options are ranked. And without that sense, they can't make informed choice between alternatives. Informed choice requires awareness of the range of options available, and of why they are presented in one form rather than another.

Equally, algorithms exploit psychological weaknesses in consumers. In picking content likely to engage users, they tend to promote the most sensational, addictive content. They seek to drive profit, not satisfaction of consumers' preferences.

In short, through recommendations, such systems may well make consumers' lives easier, but at considerable cost to autonomy. Rather than supporting choice, they drive it in ways that serve corporate interests.

To empower consumers, there is a need for less algorithmic influence, more transparency and more opportunities for individuals to encounter options they would otherwise miss. Only in this way could choice become free.

Over the past 20 years, the world of digital media has changed radically. More platforms have emerged and the production and consumption of information has shifted. In an era of increasingly polarized public debate, declining trust in news media and the noise of social media, we have seen the emergence of trusted commentators in the form of newsletter writers. In this literature review, I consider what supports this development. In particular, I look at how platforms such as Substack, Ghost and Patreon have allowed academics, experts and journalists to engage directly with their audience, without going through traditional media gatekeepers.

In the past, trusted commentator tended to be newspaper columnists, TV pundits and prominent academics. Their credibility often rested on editorial input and their links to institutions. But increasing skepticism of narratives in mainstream media, the affordances of the internet and, importantly, the emergence of the newsletter, have opened up space for other voices. Here I consider aspects of the newsletter format (intimacy with the reader, personalized delivery and often a funding model based on subscriptions) which many readers find reinforces the independence and authenticity of newsletter writers. I also consider how, using their specialist knowledge and often distinctive perspectives, they can add original reporting and analysis to the often superficial or sensationalist content elsewhere online. Drawing on work on audience engagement, media trust and platform economics, this sets the stage for a consideration of the newsletter writer as an increasingly important figure in public debate.

To prepare for a 100-mile (century) bike ride in 16 weeks, you need progressive overload, consistency and nutrition. Let's assume you could do a 20-25 mile ride comfortably right now.

Phase 1: Foundation (Weeks 1–4)
Over the next 16 weeks, the aim of this phase would be to build into your routine three or four rides a week. Two shorter, moderate-paced rides on weekdays (10-15 miles), one recovery ride or cross-training, and a longer ride on the weekend. Start your weekend long ride at 25 miles in Week 1. Each week add 5 miles until by Week 4 it's 40 miles.

Phase 2: Endurance Building (Weeks 5–8)
Keep up your weekday rides, but add a bit more intensity to them (for example, intervals or hill climbs) to develop cardiovascular power. In Week 5, up your weekend long ride to 45 miles. In Week 8, up to 60 miles. On these rides, start thinking about nutrition on the bike. Try to take 30-60g of carbs each hour, plus a bottle of water or electrolytes.

Phase 3: Peak Volume (Weeks 9–12)
This is the longest mileage phase. Over the week, try to do 15-25 miles on the weekday rides. Each weekend, build up your long ride from 65 miles to 75-80 miles in Week 12. You don't need to do a 100-mile ride before event day. If you could do 80 miles, you could make it all the way.

Phase 4: Taper and Event (Weeks 13–16)
Cut back on mileage in this phase so your muscles can recover, but so your legs stay fresh.
Week 13: Weekend long ride: 60 miles
Week 14: Weekend long ride: 45 miles
Week 15: Weekend long ride: 30 miles
Week 16 (Event Week): Rest early in the week. Two days before the event, do a 10-mile easy ride. Rest the day before.

Key Tips:
Consider getting a professional bike fit to avoid overuse injuries. Get plenty of sleep and don't introduce new gear or food on the day of the event.

10 Tips for Standing Desks for Home Offices

A standing desk can make your home office more comfortable, more energizing and more flexible. But to get the most from it, you need to use your desk well.

Here are 10 tips to help you make the most of yours.

1. Start slowly
Don't try to stand all day at first. Try 15-30 minutes at a time and gradually work up to longer stretches of standing.

2. Keep your monitor at eye level
Your screen should be about eye level. That will avoid strain on your neck and will more naturally position your body.

3. Adjust your keyboard and mouse
Keep your elbows close to your body, at about 90 degrees. While typing, keep your wrists straight.

4. Wear supportive shoes
Standing is uncomfortable in bare feet or with slippers. Use a good pair of shoes, or an anti-fatigue mat.

5. Use an anti-fatigue mat
If you stand on hard floor, try a cushioned mat under your feet. It could help take pressure off your feet, knees and lower back.

6. Move instead of simply standing
Stretch, walk during phone calls, or try a few calf raises. Standing for hours is no better than sitting for hours.

7. Alternate positions regularly
Try to spend 30-60 minutes in the chair and then 30-60 minutes standing. But follow your body, not a clock.

8. Keep essentials within reach
Set up your desk so your phone, keyboard, mouse and other items you use often are within easy reach. Constant reaching can lead to aches.

9. Mind your posture
Keep your shoulders loose, your head over your spine and your weight evenly on both feet. Don't lean on the desk.

10. Make movement convenient
Keep a water bottle at your desk, try walking meetings and maybe try a balance board or small footrest.

A good setup for your standing desk isn't necessarily standing all day. But it could mean more choice in your day, and a move from standing to sitting before you start to feel uncomfortable.

Mentorship forms the foundation of remote apprenticeships, helping offset the loss of learning that might result from physical distance. In traditional apprenticeships, knowledge is picked up by proximity to the mentor. The apprentice sees the mentor's hands at work, hears conversations between the mentor and others, and is corrected on the fly. In a remote setup, these kinds of learning opportunities are lost. And so mentorship becomes more important than it would be in a co-located situation.

A good remote mentor will consciously build in much of what would naturally happen in a co-located situation. He or she might, for example, set up regular check-ins, explain their own thinking in a screen-share, and set up avenues for the apprentice to ask questions that might otherwise arise in conversation with the mentor. In other words, the mentor would be more of a builder of the learning environment than someone the apprentice could simply watch.

More importantly, trust becomes more important. In a co-located apprenticeship, the apprentice might pick up a question in the hallway or at lunch. In a remote setting, that's more difficult. The mentor therefore needs to do more to ensure the apprentice feels safe in raising a question or acknowledging a mistake in a video or text message, rather than face-to-face. Often this means the mentor needs to be more open about his or her own limitations, and check in on the apprentice's wellbeing as well as his or her learning.

Often in a remote apprenticeship, the mentor would also be drawing on wider professional networks of the employer that the apprentice wouldn't otherwise encounter in an office. It would be up to the mentor, for example, to bring the apprentice to meetings outside his or her own role, to invite them along on virtual meetings, and to push for their inclusion in other parts of the business.

In a remote apprenticeship, therefore, mentorship becomes more deliberate and structured than in a co-located one. It requires more intention on the part of the mentor, but can well result in more reflective learning between mentor and apprentice.

As governments around the world rush to put in place legislation on facial recognition technology, many experts argue that proposed and existing laws are lagging behind the fast-moving technology.

In the United States, there have been local bans of facial recognition. In the EU, a sweeping new Artificial Intelligence Act would in effect prohibit real-time use of facial recognition by police. But legal scholars and technologists argue such laws give a false sense of control, and leave big gaps in regulation.

A key problem is that facial recognition technology is now found in private security systems, social media, smartphone apps and in retail analytics. Existing laws struggle to pick up this use in the private sector. Often embedded in long, unread terms of service, consent to its use is taken for granted.

Biometric data easily crosses borders, allowing developers to train algorithms in regions with lax standards before deploying them globally. And frequently, when laws seek to require transparency of a company's use of facial recognition, they clash with the company's right to protect trade secrets.

Even more challenging is fast-moving technology. Increasingly, using generative AI and synthetic biometrics, it has become hard to tell the difference between a real image and one produced by an algorithm. In many legal frameworks, this undercuts the concept of biometric identifiers. And by the time a law is written, debated and passed, the technology underlying it may well have moved on.

In some cities, targeted bans of facial recognition in the public sector could well restrain overreach by police. But, say experts, piecemeal regulation of a global, commercial technology will not work. Without international rules covering use of facial recognition in the private sector and its underlying algorithms, the technology will develop much more quickly than the laws seeking to limit it.

The repair-and-refurbish movement deserves strong public support because it reduces waste, saves consumers money and challenges a culture of planned obsolescence. With increasing reliance on phones, computers, tablets and appliances, people should not be required to replace equipment solely because a battery fails, a screen breaks or a minor component malfunctions.

Electronic waste is one of the world's fastest growing waste streams. Disposed equipment contains toxic materials and hazardous substances that can contaminate soil and water if not properly managed. Plus, equipment contains valuable metals and components that require substantial amounts of energy and mining. Extending equipment life through repair avoids unnecessary manufacturing and reduces costs associated with extraction of raw materials, transportation of equipment and disposal of old equipment.

Using repaired equipment also provides greater access to technology at reduced costs. The price of a new cellular phone or computer is often hundreds or thousands of dollars, whereas replacement of a battery, power supply or display is substantially less costly. Availability of refurbished equipment offers an additional means of providing affordable technology to students, families and small businesses. Increased availability of repaired equipment will contribute to reduction of the digital divide and provide greater availability of essential equipment for more people.

Critics may contend that newer equipment is more efficient or safer and, in some instances, replacement is appropriate. However, this does not relieve manufacturers of the obligation to design equipment that is difficult or impossible to repair. Manufacturers should provide access to replacement parts, repair instructions, diagnostic equipment and appropriate availability of software updates. Implementing laws to promote right-to-repair will facilitate access of independent repair shops and individual consumers to equipment they have purchased.

Finally, the movement toward repair and refurbishment reflects a commitment to responsibility rather than convenience. It provides an alternative to disposal of equipment as a form of disposable consumer fashion, and instead emphasizes the value of equipment that should be maintained. Protection of the environment, enhancement of consumer options and development of a more sustainable relationship with technology will result from support for repair.

Community-supported fisheries represent an alternative model of seafood distribution that directly links consumers to local fishers and therefore eliminates conventional long and largely opaque supply chains. Based conceptually on models of community-supported agriculture, consumers purchase shares of a fishery's anticipated harvest in advance, providing fishers with immediate access to capital, price stability and a guaranteed market and consumers with opportunities to obtain fresh, traceable and often sustainably harvested seafood. Since establishment of the first documented programs in the mid-1990s in the United States, this model has rapidly expanded throughout coastal regions of North America and to a lesser extent in Europe and elsewhere, reflecting increasing consumer interest in food origins, environmental sustainability and support for local economies.

Concurrent increases in the volume of scientific information on community-supported fisheries reflect diverse disciplinary perspectives including economics, sociology, marine policy and studies of food systems. Research has focused on several aspects of this alternative fisheries model, including its potential to improve economic viability for small-scale fishing communities in a globalized environment of declining fish stocks; to promote sustainable management of fisheries by strengthening relations between producers and consumers; and to represent components of broader movements toward alternative food systems. However, major gaps remain concerning long-term economic viability of community-supported fisheries, actual levels of environmental sustainability and details of the social and institutional conditions that contribute to success or failure of this alternative fisheries model in different geographic and institutional settings.

This review integrates and evaluates existing information on the origins, operational characteristics and effects of community-supported fisheries on fishers, consumers and marine ecosystems. This critical evaluation of strengths and limitations of previous studies identifies major themes, methods of investigation and unresolved issues that should guide future research and development of policies for this emerging system of sustainable seafood production.

Repaint Your Kitchen in a Weekend

Preparation (Friday Evening)

Remove all cabinet hardware, light fixtures and appliances. Cover counters, floors and remaining fixtures with drop cloths and plastic sheeting to protect your space and prevent delays in cleanup.

Priming and Cleaning (Saturday Morning)

Thoroughly clean all surfaces with TSP to remove grease and dirt, and allow complete drying. Apply primer to all stained areas and to previously dark walls. Lightly sand glossy surfaces to improve adhesion of paint. This preparation will provide a basis for excellent results.

First Paint Coat (Saturday Afternoon)

Begin with ceiling and upper walls using a roller for maximum efficiency. Paint trim and other detailed areas with a brush. Use high quality paint for better coverage and longer durability. Allow adequate time for drying between coats (generally 4 to 6 hours depending on humidity).

Second Coat and Details (Sunday)

Apply a second coat of paint to walls and ceiling. Paint doors and trim at your discretion, and use painter's tape to produce sharp results at window and baseboard locations. Remove tape while paint is slightly tacky to obtain excellent edge definition.

Final Touches (Sunday Evening to Monday)

Reinstall hardware for light fixtures and cabinets after complete drying of paint. Return appliances to their original locations. Carefully remove all protective coverings to avoid deposition of dust on fresh paint.

Pro Tips

Obtain all supplies on Thursday to avoid delays associated with shopping on weekends. Use low-VOC paint to achieve better quality of indoor air. Invest in high quality brushes and rollers that will provide excellent results. Maintain a damp cloth for rapid cleaning. Provide excellent conditions for ventilation throughout the entire procedure.

As a result of careful planning and efficient implementation, your kitchen will be completely transformed into a freshly painted environment by Monday morning and will be ready for use throughout the remainder of the week.

10 Tips for Building a Focused Evening Wind-Down Routine

Hey everyone!
Have you ever still felt wired at 10 p.m., staring at the ceiling and wishing you could just shut down? You're not alone. Our hectic days often spill over into our evenings and make it difficult to achieve true relaxation before bedtime. However, good quality sleep is essential, and a well-developed wind-down routine can make all the difference.

Here are 10 tips to help you build a focused evening routine and drift off more easily:

1. Establish a "digital sunset" time. Turn off all screen time at least 1 hour before bedtime. Exposure to blue light disrupts melatonin production.

2. Dim lighting. Reduce indoor light levels to match the decreasing amount of daylight outside. This will signal to your brain that it is time to slow down.

3. Take a warm bath or shower. This will relax your muscles and slightly lower your body temperature, both of which are ideal for the attainment of good quality sleep.

4. Read a physical book. Avoid electronic reading devices and instead use a traditional paper book. This is a calming and non-distracting activity.

5. Perform slow, gentle stretching exercises or practice yoga. This will relieve tension without increasing alertness.

6. Enjoy a session of calming herbal tea. Avoid all caffeinated beverages.

7. Record your thoughts in a journal. If your mind is racing, write down your concerns or to-do items. This will remove them from your mind and transfer them to paper.

8. Listen to soothing music or to a quiet storytelling podcast.

9. Prepare for the next day. Lay out your clothing and pack your bag the night before. This will minimize the number of decisions you must make in the morning and reduce your level of stress.

10. Maintain a regular bedtime. Our bodies function optimally with routine. Try to sleep and awaken at approximately the same times every day, including on weekends.

Developing a new habit requires time, so be patient with yourself. Incorporate one or two of these suggestions each week and determine which procedures work best for you. Sweet dreams!

Cities generally should give priority to bicycle lanes over street parking whenever this provides a safer, more efficient and more sustainable transportation system. Although parking is convenient for drivers and supports adjacent businesses, public streets serve more people when they accommodate movement rather than storage of private vehicles.

Protected bicycle lanes reduce traffic injuries, promote physical activity and provide access to bicycling for children, older adults and persons without private vehicles. They also contribute to reductions in air pollution and emissions of greenhouse gases. Replacing parking spaces with bicycle infrastructure subsequently provides access to transportation for more residents without contributing to traffic congestion. On top of that, businesses benefit because frequent visits by cyclists and pedestrians enhance sales of local goods, and attractive streets stimulate commercial activity.

However, parking should not be eliminated without consideration of needs of persons with disabilities, delivery workers, tradespersons and individuals who truly require motor vehicles. Implementing an appropriate policy will maintain areas of accessible parking, loading zones and limited short-term parking, and convert other areas to protected bicycle lanes. Improvements in public transportation and management of remaining parking by means of permits or pricing will also reduce the dominance of free curb storage on valuable public space.

The optimal course of action depends on local conditions. A bicycle lane is of little value when it is disconnected, unsafe at intersections or applied to locations with minimal demand for bicycle travel. Officials should evaluate traffic conditions, consult with affected residents and quantify results prior to reallocation of space. However, in densely developed urban areas, long-term benefits of safe bicycle travel generally are greater than the convenience of extensive street parking. Because of that, priority should be given to bicycle lanes as a component of an overall strategy for transportation, with adequate alternatives for essential needs for motor vehicle access.

Community Libraries Evolve as Digital Hubs in the Modern Age

Community libraries are transforming themselves into essential gateways to digital access, and reducing the technology gap for millions of underserved residents.

With increasing reliance on remote work, online education and digital health care, public libraries have expanded well beyond their traditional functions. Today they provide free high-speed internet, computer access and training in digital literacy that are critical for populations with limited economic resources.

"Libraries are providing universal access to technology," said Maria Chen, director of the digital initiatives of the American Library Association. "For many people, the library is their only source of reliable internet and computer access."

The result has been especially important during the pandemic, when libraries provided critical support for students enrolled in online courses and for job seekers applying for remote positions. Many branches now offer specialized programs in computer programming, digital citizenship and access to government and health care Web sites.

In addition to providing equipment and access to the Internet, librarians serve as digital instructors. Staff teach such skills as basic operation of e-mail and awareness of security threats, and recognize that access to technology does not necessarily produce competence with it.

But implementation of this expanded mission is limited by already inadequate financial resources. Libraries are unable to maintain state-of-the-art equipment, to employ specialists or to keep pace with rapidly developing technologies in the face of potential reductions in funding.

Still, community libraries remain essential. They provide an economical alternative to commercial providers of Internet access and computer laboratory services, offer a setting of non-judgmental learning and continue to function as a focus for community life.

Future efforts will require continued adaptation of library services. Collaboration with technology companies, increased support from government and incorporation of emerging technologies such as virtual reality and artificial intelligence should further improve service capabilities.

Finally, as the digital divide persists, community libraries are at the forefront of efforts to provide equal access to the tools and knowledge needed for successful participation in an increasingly technological world.

The future of the university lecture is certainly hybrid, a necessary adaptation that should enhance rather than diminish the experience of learning. Although traditionalists lament the loss of the conventional, face-to-face lecture, this represents an impediment to progress based on unrealistic expectations. The inflexibility of the conventional system with fixed times and locations is inadequate to meet the diverse needs of contemporary students who often combine academic work with family obligations or geographic limitations.

Hybrid methods provide an effective solution with components of synchronous online instruction, asynchronous materials and individualized face-to-face interactions. This results in no loss of quality, but rather in an increased capacity for learning. Students are able to review difficult concepts and interact with material at times of optimal cognitive readiness. On top of that, valuable face-to-face time is available for more interactive and collaborative experiences such as intensive discussions, problem-solving workshops and individualized sessions of feedback. This restores to the system of large, passive lecture halls those very components of active, interactive instruction that were previously lost.

Finally, the use of technology to support hybrid methods develops the information skills essential for graduates to function effectively in a technologically integrated world. The responsibility to prepare students for such a future is fulfilled most completely through use of a wide variety of online instructional tools. Rather than reducing the quality of education, an appropriately designed system of hybrid instruction provides greater opportunities for student autonomy, increases accessibility and ultimately produces a more stimulating and effective experience of learning than does the largely one-directional experience of the conventional university lecture. The result is a future of higher education in which survival with technology is replaced by success achieved through technology.

Employee retention remains a major challenge for organizations competing for scarce labor resources, experiencing increasing costs of turnover and changing expectations regarding flexibility and well-being. Of the policies adopted to address these concerns, unlimited vacation (i.e., discretionary or unlimited paid time off) has received increasing attention. Compared with traditional systems of fixed annual allocations of vacation days, policies of unlimited vacation allow employees to receive paid time off as needed with approval of managers, based on demands for work and expectations of organizational performance. These policies are intended to convey perceptions of trust, autonomy and a results-oriented work environment that should increase employee commitment to the organization.

The rationale for implementing policies of unlimited vacation is based on several well-established approaches to organizational research. According to social exchange theory, perceived organizational support for and flexibility of work schedules should elicit greater employee loyalty and less intent to leave. Also, provision of greater freedom to control the amount of time away from work should increase perceptions of control, satisfaction and well-being. Finally, unlimited vacation should serve as a symbol of competitive advantage in efforts to attract and retain employees, especially in high-tech industries where employees place high value on flexibility and integration of work and family roles.

However, the relationship between unlimited vacation and retention is not necessarily simple. Elimination of formal limits on entitlement to vacation may result in ambiguity concerning acceptable patterns of use of time off. Therefore, employees should receive less vacation when expectations regarding acceptable patterns of behavior are not well developed, particularly in high-performance settings in which concern about apparent differences in commitment relative to coworkers is intense. In some instances, unlimited provision of time off may shift responsibility for management of periods of rest and recovery from the employer to the employee, and therefore eliminate potential benefits for employee well-being. Finally, behaviors of managers, levels of workload, norms of team performance and perceptions of equity ultimately will determine whether the policy is experienced as a meaningful opportunity for retention or merely as a symbol of managerial generosity. 

This review of the literature supports the use of unlimited vacation as a strategy for increasing employee retention, and highlights conditions under which this strategy should be especially effective.

Starting a neighborhood book club is a simple way to meet people, discover new authors and develop a regular opportunity for which neighbors will look forward.

Begin with a small group recruited by neighborhood e-mail lists, social media, flyers or word of mouth. Aim for 6 to 12 members to achieve an atmosphere of lively discussion that is still easy to manage. At the first meeting, agree on basic details of frequency, location, methods of book selection and expectations for completion of the book.

Select a consistent schedule, such as the first Thursday of each month. Rotation of homes will facilitate management of the meeting, or alternatively, meetings may be held at a library, café, community center or park. Provide an occasional opportunity for virtual participation for members unable to attend in person.

For selection of books, alternate among titles chosen by members or selected by member vote. Limit the number of pages required when appropriate, and vary the types of authors, genres and perspectives. Include popular fiction, nonfiction, memoirs, mysteries, works by local authors and short books. Announce the title of the next book and the date of the meeting before members depart.

To stimulate discussion, prepare a few open-ended questions. Obtain reactions to aspects of the book that were enjoyable, displeasing or unexpected; to the degree of believability attributed to characters or concepts; and to the extent that the experience of reading relates to aspects of current life or to experiences within the neighborhood. Use a rotating moderator to distribute responsibility for the meeting.

Maintain an atmosphere of warmth and flexibility. Encourage expression of different views, avoid domination by any one member and recognize that occasional absence from meetings or incomplete reading of the book are inevitable. Add further comfort with refreshments, but maintain a minimum of expectations for the experience of hosting.

Finally, sustain interest by providing reminders of meeting dates, celebrating achievements and occasionally introducing new features of meeting such as a theme-based potluck, discussion with an author, visit to a bookstore or exchange of books. The success of the club requires neither perfect attendance nor profound interpretation of books, but only consistency of operation, a friendly atmosphere and books that provide good reasons for continued participation.

I am pleased to announce a new initiative designed to promote a healthier work-life balance and protect personal time: Effective immediately, we will implement a "no internal e-mail after 6 p.m." policy.

For that reason, we will avoid sending internal e-mail to colleagues, direct reports or supervisors between 6:00 and 8:00 a.m., and at all times on weekends. This will help establish a clearer distinction between work and personal time, and enable all employees to achieve true separation from work and time to restore energy.

We recognize that there are occasionally urgent situations requiring immediate attention. However, consideration should be given to whether such situations represent true emergencies. Otherwise, e-mail messages should be prepared and scheduled for transmission during hours of regular business operations.

This action reflects our commitment to the health and productivity of our employees. With mutual respect for hours away from work, we will all return to work with renewed energy and greater capacity for concentration.

Thank you for your support and assistance in achieving a successful implementation of this policy.

Best,
