Making financial literacy a required component of graduation is essential for preparing students to participate in the modern world. Today, young adults enter adulthood with complex financial responsibilities that include management of student loans and credit cards, budgeting and investment, and generally receive no formal instruction in these areas. Therefore, they experience high rates of interest-related debt, poor credit ratings and long-term financial instability. Implementing financial education within the high school curriculum will provide all students with the fundamental tools necessary for lifelong economic well-being.

Plus, requirements for financial literacy increase social and economic equity. Wealthy students generally receive instruction in money management from their families, whereas students of low socioeconomic status often lack access to this informal education. Standardized instruction eliminates these inequities and provides all students with equal opportunity to develop important skills for life. Finally, this experience enables young people to escape cycles of intergenerational poverty and to achieve financial security.

Critics will argue that addition of another requirement for graduation is excessive and further strains already overburdened educational resources. However, financial literacy need not be achieved with a separate, multi-year course. Instead, it may be readily incorporated into existing programs for mathematics or social studies. Alternatively, completion of a concentrated, one-semester course in the final year of high school provides substantial experience with practical financial skills without interference with academic training.

Ultimately, the purpose of public education is to prepare students for independent, successful lives. The lack of knowledge about fundamental principles of financial management results in high costs to individuals and to society. Requirement for financial literacy therefore ensures that high school diplomas reflect not only academic achievement, but also complete readiness for life in the real world.

With growing adoption of electric vehicles, residents of older neighborhoods are experiencing a challenge that developers of newer neighborhoods typically sought to avoid: where to charge.

Most historic communities predate widespread availability of garages, driveways and off-street parking. Narrow streets, aging electrical systems and close spacing of buildings make it difficult to provide home charging. Street-parked residents must rely primarily on public charging facilities, whereas those with garages generally require costly improvements in electrical capacity.

Cities are responding with a variety of strategies. Some are providing curbside charging stations for areas with little or no off-street parking. Others are testing integrated charging systems on streetlights or parking meters to eliminate the need for new utility poles and construction. Officials of several communities also are revising regulations to permit installation of charging cables across sidewalks, although concerns remain about safety and accessibility.

The resulting situation has raised questions about equity. Wealthier homeowners generally have greater capacity for installation of private charging facilities, whereas renters and residents of multi-family buildings have fewer options. Advocates emphasize that public investments in charging facilities should give priority to neighborhoods with no driveways or garages, rather than to newer or more affluent areas.

Historic preservation further complicates the situation. Installation of equipment on older buildings or within historic districts requires additional review. Plus, it will be necessary to determine whether existing capacity of local transformers and electric distribution lines is sufficient to accommodate increased demand, especially for large numbers of vehicles charging overnight.

Even so, transportation planners believe that older neighborhoods can achieve adaptation with careful planning. Integrating curbside charging, workplace and public electric vehicle charging, and incentives for owners of multi-family buildings to provide shared equipment should be especially effective.

The rate of future change will depend on availability of local financial resources and infrastructure. With increasing use of electric vehicles, older communities will need to be modernized without loss of those characteristics that provide the basis for their uniqueness.

The Constraining Effect of Recommendation Algorithms on Consumer Choice

Recommendation algorithms have revolutionized the ways consumers discover products, but ultimately reduce rather than expand true freedom of choice. Although these systems provide personalized convenience, they limit diversity of consumer experience and reinforce existing patterns of preference in a manner that is potentially harmful.

Algorithms reflect an inherent paradox in which learning about consumer behavior produces echo chambers that limit exposure to novel experience. When Netflix recommends movies similar to those previously viewed or Amazon suggests products based on past purchases, the system is optimized to predict satisfaction rather than to promote serendipity. Because of that, consumers rarely receive exposure to truly novel alternatives outside the bounds of algorithmic expectations. Complete freedom of choice requires exposure to a full array of alternatives, and algorithms achieve this by selectively limiting the range of available options.

Also, these systems enhance the degree of market concentration achieved for existing products and vendors. Products and services that are new or of limited commercial importance receive little opportunity for exposure because algorithms give priority to measures of consumer engagement and rates of conversion to sales. A novel book published by a small bookstore has virtually no chance of appearing in algorithmic recommendations of products compared with a best-selling book published by a major commercial publisher. This results in a highly competitive situation in which consumer freedom of choice becomes progressively more uniform for the entire population.

The lack of transparency associated with algorithmic methods of decision making exacerbates these problems. Consumers have difficulty understanding why certain alternatives are excluded from consideration or how treatment rankings are obtained. This lack of information impairs the ability to make informed choices based on complete knowledge of available alternatives and of the criteria used to present them.

Finally, algorithmic methods of recommendation exploit psychological weaknesses and manipulate consumer behavior. Presenting alternatives designed to maximize consumer engagement (particularly those involving highly stimulating or addictive modes of experience) results in greater emphasis on commercial profitability than on true satisfaction of consumer preferences.

In the end, although clearly of value, systems of recommendation represent a major cost to consumer autonomy. Rather than facilitate freedom of choice, they determine it in accordance with commercial objectives. Maximum achievement of consumer freedom of choice will require reduction of algorithmic control, enhancement of the degree of transparency and maintenance of conditions in which consumers experience unexpected alternatives. Only then will freedom of choice be completely and truly realized.

The digital media environment has experienced a dramatic transformation over the past 20 years, characterized by rapid proliferation of platforms and major changes in modes of information dissemination and consumption. In the cacophony of social media, declining public trust in traditional news media and increasing polarization of public debate, a new phenomenon has emerged: the emergence of independent newsletter writers as highly trusted commentators. Here we describe and discuss factors contributing to this development, and illustrate how individual journalists, academics and experts have been enabled to develop direct relationships with their audiences and bypass traditional mechanisms of media gatekeeping.

Previously, the role of trusted commentator had been largely restricted to established newspaper columnists, television commentators and prominent academic researchers who derived additional authority from institutional affiliations and editorial oversight. However, the capacity for democratization provided by the Internet and increasing public skepticism of conventional media representations have facilitated development of alternative modes of communication. We test the extent to which unique characteristics of the newsletter format (e.g., high degrees of personalization, perceived intimacy and reliance on subscription-based funding) contribute to perceptions of authenticity and independence that are highly attractive to readers. On top of that, we examine the ways in which specialized knowledge and subtleties of perspective enable newsletter writers to provide detailed analyses and original reporting that are markedly superior to much of the superficial or sensational content available elsewhere on the Internet.

Finally, our synthesis of existing research on media trust, platform economics and patterns of audience interaction provides a basis for a complete description of the newsletter writer as a major and increasingly influential component of contemporary public communication.

Training for a 100-mile bike ride in 16 weeks demands consistency, progressive overload and appropriate nutrition. This program is based on your ability to ride comfortably for 20 to 25 miles.

Phase 1: Foundation (Weeks 1–4)
Develop a training routine of three to four weekly rides consisting of two short weekday efforts at moderate intensity (10 to 15 miles), one session of cross-training or recovery riding and one long weekend ride. Begin with a distance of 25 miles in week 1 and increase weekly mileage by 5 miles to achieve a maximum distance of 40 miles by week 4.

Phase 2: Endurance Building (Weeks 5–8)
Increase the intensity of midweek training with hill climbs or intervals to develop capacity for cardiovascular power. Extend your long weekend rides to 45 miles in week 5 and to 60 miles by week 8.

Phase 3: Peak Volume (Weeks 9–12)
Use these opportunities to practice techniques for on-bike nutrition, with a goal of consuming 30 to 60 grams of carbohydrates and one bottle of fluid containing electrolytes per hour. This phase of training represents your maximum weekly mileage.

Phase 4: Taper and Event (Weeks 13–16)
Midweek sessions should provide distances of 15 to 25 miles, and long weekend rides should progress to 65 miles and ultimately to a maximum of 75 to 80 miles by week 12. You will not need to complete a distance of 100 miles before race day, since achievement of 80 miles is sufficient to confirm your capacity for completing the full race distance.
Week 13: 60-mile long ride.
Week 14: 45-mile long ride.
Week 15: 30-mile long ride.
Week 16 (Event Week): Rest early in the week, take a light 10-mile spin two days prior, and rest the day before.

Key Tips:
Reduce training volume to allow adequate recovery of muscle function and maintenance of leg freshness. Obtain a professional bike fit to prevent excessive risk of overuse injuries, optimize sleep and avoid use of new types of food or equipment on the day of competition.

10 Tips for standing desks for home offices

Standing desks can make your home office more adaptable, comfortable and energizing - but only if you use them with care. Here are 10 practical tips to help you get the most benefit.

1. Start slowly
Don't attempt to stand for the entire day. Start with periods of 15 to 30 minutes and gradually increase the length of your standing time.

2. Keep your monitor at eye level
Position your screen so its top is approximately at eye level to minimize neck strain and achieve a more natural posture.

3. Adjust your keyboard and mouse
Keep your elbows close to your body and flexed to about 90 degrees. Maintain a relatively straight wrist position during typing.

4. Wear supportive shoes
Using bare feet or poorly supportive slippers will be uncomfortable. Wear comfortable shoes or use an anti-fatigue mat.

5. Use an anti-fatigue mat
This will reduce pressure on your feet, knees and back, particularly on hard surfaces.

6. Move instead of simply standing
Change positions frequently, stretch, walk about during telephone calls and perform a few exercises to strengthen your calf muscles. Prolonged standing is no better than prolonged sitting.

7. Alternate positions regularly
Ideally, alternate sitting and standing every 30 to 60 minutes. Respond to the needs of your body rather than to a rigid schedule of activities.

8. Keep essentials within reach
Arrange your workstation so that your keyboard, mouse, telephone and other frequently used equipment are easily accessible. Constant reaching will produce new discomforts.

9. Mind your posture
Maintain relaxed shoulders, a posture of upright head position relative to the vertebral column and equal distribution of body weight between both feet. Avoid leaning on the desk.

10. Make movement convenient
Keep a container of water readily available, use opportunities for ambulatory meetings whenever possible and consider the use of a small footrest or a device to promote body balance for added variety.

The optimal configuration for your standing desk is not continuous standing, but rather greater flexibility throughout the day with frequent changes in position before development of discomfort.

Mentorship provides the critical structural foundation for remote apprenticeships, overcoming the limitations of physical distance on the learning experience. Apprentices in traditional settings learn primarily through proximity to mentors, with direct observation of hand movements, incidental participation in discussions of problem-solving and spontaneous correction of errors. Remote arrangements eliminate these opportunities for incidental learning, and require substantially greater efforts to achieve the goals of effective mentorship than are achieved with co-located apprentices.

Successful mentorship in a remote setting requires active creation of structures that otherwise develop spontaneously. This includes scheduling frequent contacts, explicitly describing the thought processes during computer-based or video conferences and providing well-defined channels for communication of questions that otherwise would be addressed informally. Because of that, the mentor becomes a deliberate designer of the learning experience, rather than a passive component of the apprentice's experience.

Developing trust is of exceptional importance. In the absence of casual interactions in the hallways or at meals, mentors must expend substantially greater efforts to achieve a sense of psychological safety that permits apprentices to readily express confusion or errors by electronic or video methods instead of in person. This necessitates active modeling of vulnerability and frequent attention to the well-being of apprentices, and not merely to their technical performance.

Also, mentors for remote apprenticeships function as conduits to large professional networks that otherwise would not be accessible to apprentices by virtue of their physical absence from an office. Exposure of apprentices to colleagues, participation in meetings that extend well beyond their immediate tasks and advocacy for increased visibility within the organization represent major responsibilities of the mentor.

Finally, mentorship for remote apprenticeships represents a fundamental shift from an organic consequence of shared physical space to a highly structured and deliberate process requiring substantially greater efforts of organization and control, but ultimately producing significantly more intensive and reflective experiences of learning when performed successfully.

As governments around the world scramble to enact laws regulating facial recognition technology, experts note that existing and proposed regulations fail to keep pace with rapid technological development.

From the landmark artificial intelligence legislation of the European Union to local prohibitions throughout the United States, policymakers have concentrated primarily on public sector applications and restrictions on real-time use of biometric surveillance by law enforcement. However, legal scholars and technologists argue that these measures provide a false sense of security and leave enormous gaps in regulatory coverage.

The major difficulty reflects the ubiquity of the technology. Facial recognition is no longer limited to high-resolution cameras on street lights, but is integrated into private security systems, commercial applications for retail analytics, smartphones and social media. Current laws are inadequate to regulate this expansion of private-sector applications in which consent is routinely obtained by signing lengthy terms-of-service agreements that are never read.

Plus, limitations on jurisdiction severely impair enforcement. Biometric data readily cross national borders to permit development of algorithms based on low standards of privacy protection, followed by global deployment of the finished products. Attempts to require disclosure of training data were frustrated by protection of commercial trade secrets.

Finally, rapid changes in technology represent an additional major challenge. Development of systems for generating and manipulating synthetic biometric images has eliminated distinctions between real and artificial images, and rendered most existing definitions of "biometric identifiers" obsolete for purposes of legal regulation. By the time legislation is discussed, drafted and enacted, the underlying technology has generally changed to a degree that renders the legislation ineffective.

Restrictions on police activities may temporarily limit abuses of facial recognition technology in certain cities, but overall, piecemeal regulation is incapable of containing a worldwide commercial technology. Absent complete international standards applicable to both commercial applications and underlying methods of algorithmic processing, development of facial recognition technology will continue to proceed at a rate far greater than that of associated legal controls.
